title: 2026 年 9-12 月雅思口语题库

questions.prompt: Do you prefer to sit by the window when travelling?

answers.basic: Yes, especially on a train. I like watching the view change outside, and it gives me a reason to put my phone away for a while. On the train back to Hunan, I especially like seeing the buildings give way to fields as we leave the city.

questions.prompt: Did you have a long journey with your family as a child?

answers.basic: Yes, I remember taking a long train journey from Hunan with my family. I spent most of it looking out of the window and asking how much longer we had. It felt like a big adventure because I'd never been on a train long enough to eat more than one meal there.

questions.prompt: Did you recycle when you were a kid?

answers.basic: A little. We used to keep cardboard boxes and empty bottles separate at home. I didn't think much about why we were doing it at the time. I mostly remember folding the boxes flat so we'd have enough room to stack them by the door.

questions.prompt: Is waste sorting common in your country?

answers.basic: It's quite common where I live in Shanghai. The bins near my building have different labels, and people are used to checking them before throwing things away. For example, when I finish unpacking a delivery, I know where to take the cardboard before it piles up at home.

questions.prompt: How do you recycle things like paper and plastic?

answers.basic: I flatten boxes so they take up less space, and I empty bottles before putting them with the recyclables. I usually take them downstairs together. I keep a bag near the door for the smaller things, so I can take it with me when I go out.

questions.prompt: What do you do when you see rubbish on the street?

answers.basic: If it's something clean and easy to pick up, like a bottle, I put it in a bin. If it looks sharp or dirty, I leave it alone. There's often a bin near a subway entrance, so I can usually get rid of a bottle without going out of my way.

questions.prompt: What do you do when you feel tired?

answers.basic: I step away from the computer and get some water. If I've been sitting for hours, a short walk usually helps more than another coffee. Even walking around the block gives my eyes a break and makes it easier to concentrate when I sit down again.

questions.prompt: When would you feel tired?

answers.basic: I get tired after a long day of debugging, especially if I have a badminton lesson to teach in the evening. By the time I get home, I'm ready to sleep. On those days, I can feel the difference when I'm packing up my racket bag and realise I've barely sat down all evening.

questions.prompt: Do you often feel tired?

answers.basic: Some days, yes. It mainly happens when work and coaching fall on the same day, so I try to leave one or two evenings free each week. A quiet evening at home usually gives me enough energy to enjoy the next lesson instead of rushing through it.

questions.prompt: Which do you prefer, fashionable shoes or comfortable shoes?

answers.basic: Comfortable shoes, definitely. When I play badminton, I care about how stable the shoes feel when I move sideways. The colour is a bonus. A pair that grips well gives me more confidence when I have to stop suddenly near the edge of the court.

questions.prompt: How much money do you usually spend on shoes?

answers.basic: For everyday shoes, I'd spend a few hundred yuan. I'm willing to pay a bit more for badminton shoes if they fit properly and feel stable on court. I usually try a few side steps in the shop because walking around in a straight line only tells me so much.

questions.prompt: Have you ever bought shoes online?

answers.basic: Yes, usually when I already know the brand and my size. For a new pair of badminton shoes, I'd rather try them on first. I've ordered a replacement pair online before because I'd worn the same model for months and knew it suited my feet.

questions.prompt: Do you like buying shoes? How often?

answers.basic: I buy shoes when a pair is worn out, so maybe once or twice a year. I quite enjoy trying on court shoes, though. It's satisfying to find a pair that feels right, especially when the old ones have started slipping on court.

questions.prompt: On what occasions should we be polite?

answers.basic: It matters when you're asking someone for help or sharing a space with strangers. For example, I'd keep my voice down when taking a call on the subway. Small things like that make it easier for everyone to share a crowded place without getting irritated with each other.

questions.prompt: What did you do to show your politeness as a child?

answers.basic: I used to greet relatives when they came over and thank them if they brought something. My family would remind me if I forgot. I wanted the adults to feel welcome, so I'd sometimes bring them a chair or get them some water as well.

questions.prompt: Do you think being polite is very important?

answers.basic: Yes. A polite request usually makes it easier for both people to deal with a problem. That matters when you're busy or when you disagree. Even at work, asking someone to check one specific thing politely can make a difficult conversation go much more smoothly.

questions.prompt: How did you learn to be polite as a child?

answers.basic: I mostly learned from watching my family. They would say thank you to the people who helped them, and I gradually started doing the same. I remember being reminded to wait until someone had finished speaking before I jumped in with my own story.

questions.prompt: Do people in your country like planting vegetables?

answers.basic: Some people do, even if they only have a balcony. Back in Hunan, growing a few spring onions or chillies at home felt quite normal. A relative of mine grows them in pots because she likes being able to cut a few fresh ones when she's cooking.

questions.prompt: Were there any kind of fruits and vegetables you disliked as a child?

answers.basic: I didn't like bitter melon when I was little. I remember taking one bite and then trying to eat the rest of my rice around it. The bitter taste was much stronger than I expected, and even mixing it with other food didn't help much.

questions.prompt: What kind of fruits and vegetables do you dislike?

answers.basic: Bitter melon still isn't my favourite because the taste stays in my mouth for a long time. I'm happy with most other vegetables. I quite like vegetables with a little heat, though, so I'd happily have something like peppers with my dinner.

questions.prompt: Where do you usually buy fruit and vegetables?

answers.basic: I usually pick them up at a supermarket near home. If I get back late from coaching, I sometimes order a few things to be delivered. I like being able to choose the fruit myself when I have time, especially if I'm buying enough for several days.

questions.prompt: How often do you eat fruit and vegetables?

answers.basic: I try to have vegetables with lunch or dinner every day. Fruit is usually a snack, especially if I'm hungry between work and badminton. A banana is easy to carry in my bag, so I sometimes eat one on the way to a lesson.

questions.prompt: Do you often see advertisements when you are on your phone or computer?

answers.basic: Yes, I notice them more on my phone, especially between short videos. On my computer I'm usually reading documentation, so I see fewer of them. A typical example is opening a video for one quick tip and having to wait through an ad before it starts.

questions.prompt: What kind of advertising do you like?

answers.basic: I like ads that show the product being used. If it's a badminton racket, for example, I'd rather see someone play with it and explain how it feels. Seeing how the racket moves gives me something concrete to think about, especially if the person explains what they noticed.

questions.prompt: Do you like advertisements?

answers.basic: I like a useful ad once in a while. I get annoyed when the same one interrupts three videos in a row. An ad for a new badminton shop nearby might actually help me, but a repeated video ad usually makes me close the app.

questions.prompt: Do you see a lot of advertising on trains or other transport?

answers.basic: Yes, there are ads in Shanghai subway stations and inside the trains. I notice the big posters more when I'm waiting for a train. If I'm standing on the platform for a few minutes, I'll sometimes read a whole poster without even meaning to.

questions.prompt: Is there an advertisement that made an impression on you when you were a child?

answers.basic: I remember a sports ad that showed a player practising the same movement over and over. I was more interested in the sound and the movement than in what it was selling. I think it stayed with me because I'd just started playing badminton and already knew how much practice one movement could take.

questions.prompt: Do you carry paper and pens with you when you go out?

answers.basic: Usually I just take my phone. I sometimes bring a small notebook to a badminton session if I want to write down a few things to cover. It's handy on court because I can glance at a short list between drills without getting distracted by a notification.

questions.prompt: Do people still keep handwritten letters today?

answers.basic: Yes, especially letters from relatives or people they don't see often. A handwritten note feels personal, so I can see why someone would keep it for years. A friend might keep a letter from home because even the handwriting can remind them of the person who sent it.

questions.prompt: Do you still write physical letters?

answers.basic: Hardly ever. I send messages for most things, but I'd still write a few lines by hand in a birthday card. A card gives me a good reason to slow down and write something specific about the person I'm giving it to.

questions.prompt: What did you like to do with paper as a child?

answers.basic: I used to fold paper planes and change the wings to see how far they'd go. Half the fun was seeing whose plane would land first. I liked that a small fold could make one plane turn sharply while another one flew almost straight across the room.

questions.prompt: Have you made any crafts with paper?

answers.basic: Yes, I made simple paper boats and planes as a child. I remember trying to make a boat strong enough to float in a bowl of water. I enjoyed seeing whether a different fold made it float longer, even when it sank almost as soon as I let go.

questions.prompt: Is there anything you miss about your secondary school?

answers.basic: I miss the time after class when it was easy to see my friends. Now that everyone is working, even finding one evening that suits us can take a while. Back then we could decide to play badminton after school without checking anyone's calendar, which made getting together feel easy.

questions.prompt: What was your favourite subject at secondary school?

answers.basic: I liked maths because I enjoyed working out how to get from the question to the answer. I still get a similar feeling when I solve a problem at work. I liked questions where the first step wasn't obvious and a small clue suddenly made the rest of the problem fit together.

questions.prompt: Were there any subjects that you found difficult at secondary school?

answers.basic: English speaking was hard for me. I could work through a written question at my own speed, but it took me much longer to put an answer together out loud. I especially remember knowing the words I wanted on paper and then forgetting half of them when someone asked me a question.

questions.prompt: Do you remember your first day at secondary school?

answers.basic: I remember being a little nervous because I knew very few people. Once I found my classroom and talked to the person next to me, I felt more at ease. I don't remember what the first lesson was about, but I remember how relieved I was to have someone to talk to.

questions.prompt: Do you often forget people's names?

answers.basic: Sometimes, especially when several people introduce themselves at once. I usually remember a face or a conversation before the name comes back to me. That happens most at a new badminton session, where I'm trying to learn names and work out who's playing on which court.

questions.prompt: How do you remember people's names?

answers.basic: I try to use the name once when I say goodbye. If we met at badminton, I also link it to the session or the court we played on. By the next session, thinking about a rally we played together usually helps me bring the name back.

questions.prompt: Is it easy for you to remember people's names?

answers.basic: It's easier if I have a proper conversation with someone. If I just hear their name in passing, I might need to ask again next time. A short chat gives me something to connect with the name, like the place they work or a sport they enjoy.

questions.prompt: How do you feel when people can't remember your name?

answers.basic: It doesn't really bother me. I just say my name again, because I know how easy it is to forget when you're meeting a lot of people. At a busy court I sometimes introduce myself again first, which takes the pressure off both of us.

questions.prompt: Do you prefer to sad or happy music?

answers.basic: I usually prefer cheerful music. I like having something upbeat on the way to a badminton session, especially after a long day. A lively song on the subway can wake me up enough to look forward to the game again.

questions.prompt: Does happy music make you feel more excited?

answers.basic: Yes, a fast song can put me in a better mood quite quickly. I notice it most when I'm walking somewhere and start matching my steps to the beat. If I've been sitting at my desk all day, that change of pace makes the walk feel much shorter.

questions.prompt: Have you taken any music classes?

answers.basic: I had music classes at school, but I haven't taken private lessons. Most of what I listen to now comes from playlists or recommendations from friends. At school we mostly learned songs as a group, and I enjoyed hearing everyone get the rhythm right together.

questions.prompt: Do you listen to music while doing other things?

answers.basic: Yes, I play music when I walk or do chores. I usually turn it off when I'm debugging because I want to hear myself think. I'll happily put a playlist on while I wash the dishes, when having something in the background makes the job feel quicker.

questions.prompt: Do you have a favorite teacher?

answers.basic: One of my favourite teachers was my secondary school maths teacher. They were good at showing how to get started when a problem looked too hard. I remember them starting with a smaller example, which often made it clear why the same idea worked in the bigger question.

questions.prompt: Do you want to be a teacher in the future?

answers.basic: I already teach badminton part-time, and I enjoy it. I'd like to keep coaching alongside my work as a software engineer. I get a lot out of seeing someone understand a movement, like when a student suddenly finds a more comfortable grip.

questions.prompt: Do you have a teacher from your past that you still remember?

answers.basic: Yes, I still remember my maths teacher. They used to ask how I got an answer, which made me pay more attention to the steps. One thing that stuck with me was having to explain a shortcut to the class, because it made me see what I'd missed.

questions.prompt: Are you still in touch with your primary school teachers?

answers.basic: No, I've lost touch with them over the years. I still remember a few things they used to say in class. We moved on to different schools, so there wasn't much chance to see them again except when I happened to pass the old building.

questions.prompt: In what way has your favourite teacher helped you?

answers.basic: My maths teacher showed me how to break a big question into smaller ones. I use that habit when I'm stuck on a problem at work now. If a service is slow, for instance, I'll check one request step by step instead of trying to fix everything at once.

questions.prompt: Do you like your primary school teachers more than your high school teachers?

answers.basic: I remember my high school teachers more clearly because I was old enough to ask them questions about what to do next. I have good memories of primary school too. A high school teacher might talk through a choice of subjects with me, which felt useful because it affected what I could study later.

questions.prompt: Have you ever posted anything on social media?

answers.basic: Yes, I've shared the odd update about what I'm learning or working on. My own blog gives me more room to write about a topic properly. A quick post might be a photo from a session, while a blog entry gives me space to explain a drill in more detail.

questions.prompt: When did you start using social media?

answers.basic: I started using it when I was at school, mainly to stay in touch with classmates. Now I use it to follow people with similar interests. I remember using it to make plans after school, whereas now I'm more likely to save a video that helps me with a skill.

questions.prompt: Do you think you spend too much time on social media?

answers.basic: Sometimes. I can open an app to answer one message and spend much longer scrolling through videos. It helps if I put my phone away when I have something else planned. If I open a clip during a break, for example, I try to stop when I've seen what I came for.

questions.prompt: Do your friends use social media?

answers.basic: Yes, most of my friends use it. We share clips, arrange badminton sessions and occasionally send each other something useful about work. Our group chat is especially useful because somebody can post a free court time and see who can make it within a few minutes.

questions.prompt: What do people often do on social media?

answers.basic: They chat, watch videos and keep up with friends. Some people also use it to show their work or build a name in their field. I often see people share a small thing they've made, which can start a conversation with someone who has the same interests.

questions.prompt: Do you like to keep things tidy?

answers.basic: Yes, I like knowing where everything is. At work that goes for files and notes as much as the things on my desk. If a teammate asks about a decision from last week, I like being able to find the note while we're still talking.

questions.prompt: Did you keep your room tidy as a child?

answers.basic: My room was fairly messy as a child. I'd leave books or sports gear out and put them away when I was asked. My badminton gear was usually the first thing I dropped by the door because I knew I'd want it again the next day.

questions.prompt: How do you keep your work or study space tidy?

answers.basic: I keep just the things I'm using on my desk. On my computer I try to give files clear names so I can find them again. For example, I keep notes for each project together, so I can pick up where I left off without searching through downloads.

questions.prompt: Do you think that it is necessary to be tidy?

answers.basic: Some tidiness is useful because it saves time. I care more about being able to find things than about getting every object to line up. A desk can look a bit lived-in, and I'm happy as long as I can put my hands on the right notebook.

questions.prompt: What kinds of websites do you often visit?

answers.basic: I often visit documentation sites for work and personal blogs when I'm learning a new skill. I also look at badminton sites for drills or match clips. I usually go in with a question, such as how to fix an error or show a beginner what their feet should do.

questions.prompt: What is your favourite website?

answers.basic: I use GitHub a lot. I like being able to see how other people built something and read the discussion when they run into a problem. A small example in a repository can tell me more about how something works than a long explanation with no code.

questions.prompt: Are there any changes to the websites you often visit?

answers.basic: Yes, I see more video and interactive examples than I used to. I still look for the plain written instructions when I want to check a detail quickly. When I'm learning a new tool, it's nice to run a small example in the browser and see the result immediately.

questions.prompt: What kinds of websites are popular in your country?

answers.basic: Video sites, shopping sites and social platforms are all popular. In my line of work, people also spend a lot of time on developer forums. It's useful when someone posts a problem I recognise and the replies show several ways to deal with it.

questions.prompt: Do you prefer getting information from websites or books?

answers.basic: For a quick question, I go to a website because I can search for the exact thing I need. For a subject I want to understand in depth, a book is nice. If I'm fixing a setting on my site I'll search online, but I'd sit down with a book to learn a subject from the beginning.

questions.prompt: Would you like to have your own website?

answers.basic: Yes, and I've already started one. I wanted a place to share what I'm learning and build a personal brand around my interests. I can use it for longer posts about backend work or badminton, then add to those posts as I learn more.

questions.prompt: What have you learned from websites that help with your life or studies?

answers.basic: I've learned how to fix coding problems and set up my own website. I can also find training drills and try them out in my badminton sessions. A clip of a coach slowing down a movement can give me a practical way to explain it in my next lesson.

questions.prompt: Do you wear a watch?

answers.basic: I don't wear one every day. My phone is usually close by, and on court I prefer to keep my wrists clear. I'll sometimes wear one for a longer walk so I can see the time without pulling my phone out of a bag.

questions.prompt: Have you ever got a watch as a gift?

answers.basic: Yes, I remember getting a simple watch as a gift when I was younger. I wore it to school for a while. I liked checking the time myself between classes, and I remember trying to see how quickly I could learn to read the face.

questions.prompt: Why do some people wear expensive watches?

answers.basic: Some people enjoy the design or the way it was made. A watch can also remind someone of an important event if they bought it to celebrate. Someone might buy one after their first promotion and wear it for years because it brings that moment back.

questions.prompt: Do you think it is important to wear a watch? Why?

answers.basic: I find it handy when I need to check the time without taking my phone out. For most days, though, my phone does the job. A watch makes more sense to me when I'm walking with a bag or trying to stay off my phone.

questions.prompt: Do you like shopping?

answers.basic: I enjoy shopping when I know what I'm looking for, especially if it's for badminton. I get tired of walking around shops without a clear idea. I can happily spend time comparing two rackets because the choice matters to me and I know what I want to feel in my hand.

questions.prompt: How often do you go shopping?

answers.basic: I buy groceries most weeks. For clothes or sports gear, I shop when I actually need to replace something. That usually means a quick supermarket trip for a few meals and a separate trip if my shoes start to wear out.

questions.prompt: Do you prefer online shopping or in-store shopping?

answers.basic: For things I already know, online shopping is easier. I prefer a physical shop when I want to try on shoes or feel the weight of a racket. I might reorder shuttlecocks online, but I'd want to feel how a new racket swings before I commit to it.

questions.prompt: Have you ever returned anything you bought online?

answers.basic: Yes, I sent back a piece of clothing once because the size was off. I usually check the measurements and reviews more carefully now. The sleeves were shorter than I'd expected, so I sent it back and compared the measurements with a shirt I already liked.

questions.prompt: Did you enjoy traveling by car when you were a kid?

answers.basic: Yes, especially if we were going somewhere new. I liked sitting by the window, though I used to get restless if the journey went on too long. I could look out at places I hadn't seen before, and I always looked forward to getting out for a snack halfway through.

questions.prompt: What types of cars do you like?

answers.basic: I like practical cars that are easy to park and have room for a sports bag. I don't need anything particularly large or flashy. I'd be happy with something compact that I could fit into a tight parking space after an evening at the sports hall.

questions.prompt: Do you prefer to be a driver or a passenger?

answers.basic: I'd rather be a passenger on a long trip because I can look around or listen to something. For a short trip on my own, driving is fine. As a passenger, I can check the route or talk to whoever's driving, which makes a long journey feel a bit more relaxed.

questions.prompt: What do you usually do when there is a traffic jam?

answers.basic: If I'm a passenger, I usually check the map or put some music on. If I'm driving, I just leave enough space and wait. I find it easier to stay patient when I allow extra time in the first place, especially if I'm heading to a lesson.

questions.prompt: Do you think car colours are important?

answers.basic: I'd choose a colour that's easy to keep looking clean. Beyond that, I care much more about how the car feels and what it costs to run. Grey would probably suit me because a bit of dust wouldn't stand out much between washes.

questions.prompt: Will you buy an expensive car in the future?

answers.basic: Probably not. The subway covers most of my journeys in Shanghai, so I'd only consider a car if I had a regular reason to use one. If I did need one to carry gear regularly, I'd look for something reliable and easy to park before thinking about a nicer model.

questions.prompt: Did you like going to parks as a child?

answers.basic: Yes. In Hunan I liked having space to run around with other children. I paid more attention to the games than to the plants. Sometimes we'd bring rackets and see how many times we could hit the shuttle back and forth before the wind took it.

questions.prompt: Do you still like going to parks now?

answers.basic: Yes, although I go for a walk now. After sitting in front of a screen for most of the day, I enjoy being somewhere green. A loop around a park gives me a chance to stretch my legs and notice something beyond what's on my screen.

questions.prompt: Would you like to see more parks in your city?

answers.basic: Yes, especially small parks near places where people live and work. Even a short walk at lunchtime can make the afternoon feel better. If there were a small green space near the office, I'd use it on days when I only have twenty minutes to spare.

questions.prompt: Are there any parks you want to go to in the future?

answers.basic: I'd like to spend more time in the bigger parks on the edge of Shanghai. It would be nice to have a whole afternoon to walk around without rushing. I'd pick one with a path around some water and bring something to eat so I could stay as long as I felt like.

questions.prompt: Would you prefer to play in a personal garden or public garden?

answers.basic: I'd choose a public park because there's more space, and I can meet a friend there. If I wanted to grow plants, a private garden would be nice. I like being able to walk in a different direction each time and find a bench when we want to stop.

questions.prompt: How are the parks today different from those you visited as a kid?

answers.basic: The parks I remember from childhood were fairly simple. A lot of the ones I see now have marked walking paths, exercise equipment and more places to sit. Even a small park near my apartment has a marked route, so I can fit in a short walk before dinner.

questions.prompt: What do you like to do when visiting a park?

answers.basic: I usually take a walk and look for a quiet spot to sit. If a friend comes along, we often talk until we've gone all the way around. When I go by myself, I usually leave my headphones in my pocket and see what I can hear around me.

questions.prompt: Do you like science?

answers.basic: Yes, especially when it explains something I can see. In badminton, for example, it's interesting to think about how the angle of the racket changes the shot. It's quite satisfying to change something small on the court and see straight away what it does to the flight of the shuttle.

questions.prompt: When did you start to learn about science?

answers.basic: I started at primary school, with simple things like plants, water and magnets. I remember liking the lessons where we got to try something. I remember using a magnet to see which things on my desk it would pick up, which made the lesson feel like a game.

questions.prompt: Which science subject is interesting to you?

answers.basic: I find physics interesting because it explains ordinary movements. Even a shuttlecock slowing down in the air can give me something to think about. When I'm coaching, I sometimes think about that because the same swing can produce different results depending on when you hit the shuttle.

questions.prompt: What kinds of interesting things have you done with science?

answers.basic: I've used slow-motion video to look at how a shuttle leaves the racket. Comparing two clips helped me see a difference I couldn't catch in real time. I could see where my racket was pointing when I made contact, which gave me a better idea of what to change.

questions.prompt: Do you like watching science TV programs?

answers.basic: I watch the occasional documentary or short science video. I like the ones that show a real experiment and explain what happened in simple terms. I remember watching someone show how a small change in shape affects the way an object moves through the air.

questions.prompt: Do Chinese people often visit science museums?

answers.basic: I think they're a popular choice for families on weekends or school holidays. An exhibition is more fun when children can touch things and try them. Something like a hands-on display about light can keep a child busy for longer than a row of objects behind glass.

questions.prompt: Have you ever bought mirrors?

answers.basic: Yes, I've bought a small mirror for checking how I look before I leave. I wanted something simple that would fit in the space. I put it near the door because that's where I usually notice that my collar is folded or my hair needs fixing.

questions.prompt: Do you usually take a mirror with you?

answers.basic: No, I don't usually carry one. If I'm out and need to check something, I'll find a mirror in a bathroom. I try to keep what I carry fairly light, especially if I already have a racket bag with me.

questions.prompt: Would you use mirrors to decorate your room?

answers.basic: I'd use one if it made a small room feel brighter or gave me somewhere to check my clothes. I'd probably stick with a simple frame. I'd hang it somewhere it catches daylight, because that would make more of a difference to me than a fancy design.

questions.prompt: Do you like looking at yourself in the mirror? How often?

answers.basic: I check the mirror when I get ready and again before I go out. Most days it's just a quick look at my hair or clothes. I wouldn't say I enjoy it much, but it saves me from getting to work and finding out I've missed a button.

questions.prompt: Have you ever learnt about outer space and stars?

answers.basic: Yes, I learned a little at school and picked up more from videos. I still find it surprising how far the light from a star has to travel. A video about the night sky made it click for me that looking at a distant star also means looking back in time.

questions.prompt: Do you like science fiction movies? Why?

answers.basic: Yes, when the story makes me think about what life would be like in a different place. I enjoy the quieter parts as much as the space battles. I like films that spend a bit of time showing how ordinary people get used to living somewhere completely unfamiliar.

questions.prompt: Do you want to know more about outer space?

answers.basic: Yes. I'd like to understand how people find planets around other stars. It's interesting that they can learn so much from a tiny change in light. I'd probably start with a short video showing what scientists see when a planet passes in front of its star.

questions.prompt: Do you want to go into outer space in the future?

answers.basic: I'd love to see the Earth from above, but I don't think I'd enjoy the launch or being far from home. Watching footage is enough for now. I can picture myself spending ages by the window, but the idea of being strapped into a rocket makes me nervous.

questions.prompt: Do you like singing? Why?

answers.basic: A little, mostly when I'm on my own. I enjoy singing along to a song I know well, even if I miss a few notes. If a song I know comes on while I'm making dinner, I'll sometimes join in without really thinking about it.

questions.prompt: Have you ever learnt how to sing?

answers.basic: I learned a few songs in school music lessons. I never trained seriously, so I mostly just follow the tune when I sing now. At school it was easier to keep going when the whole class sang, because nobody could hear every mistake I made.

questions.prompt: Who do you want to sing for?

answers.basic: I'd sing for a small group of friends if we were doing karaoke. It's easier to enjoy it when nobody is taking it too seriously. I'd pick a song we all know, so people could join in when I forget a line or go off key.

questions.prompt: Do you think singing can bring happiness to people?

answers.basic: Yes. Singing a familiar song together can get people laughing and make a room feel less awkward, especially at a party. At karaoke, someone will often start out shy and then smile once everybody else joins in on the chorus.

questions.prompt: Do you like listening to others singing?

answers.basic: Yes, particularly when someone sounds like they're enjoying themselves. Even a friend singing at karaoke can be fun to listen to. At a live show, I enjoy the little differences in how someone sings a song compared with the version I've heard before.

questions.prompt: Have you ever taken a singing class?

answers.basic: Only as part of school music lessons. I've never taken a separate singing class, although I'd be curious about how people learn to control their breath. It would be interesting to see if one lesson could make it easier for me to hold a note without running out of air.

questions.prompt: What kind of clothes do you like to wear?

answers.basic: I like simple, comfortable clothes, such as a T-shirt and trousers. On a day when I'm coaching, I usually have sports clothes in my bag. A plain shirt works for most things I do, and I can switch into a lighter top once I get to the hall.

questions.prompt: Do you prefer to wear comfortable and casual clothes or smart clothes?

answers.basic: I prefer casual clothes because I spend a lot of time at a desk or on court. I still dress a little smarter for a formal occasion. A neat T-shirt and comfortable trousers are enough for an ordinary day when I'm going straight from work to badminton.

questions.prompt: Do you like wearing T-shirts?

answers.basic: Yes, they're easy to move in and go with most things I own. I wear lighter ones when I'm playing badminton. On a warm day, I notice straight away if a shirt feels heavy or sticks to me after a few rallies.

questions.prompt: Do you spend a lot of time choosing clothes?

answers.basic: Usually I decide in a minute or two. I spend longer only when the weather is changing or I need to dress for an event. I often leave a clean top by my bag the night before if I'm going to a lesson straight after work.

questions.prompt: Do you wear different styles of clothes on weekdays and weekends?

answers.basic: A bit. On weekdays I wear simple clothes that are fine for work. At weekends I often end up in sports clothes because I'm heading to a court. If I'm meeting friends after a game, I'll usually take a spare shirt and change once we finish playing.

questions.prompt: What colour clothes do you like?

answers.basic: I like navy, grey and black because they're easy to put together. Sometimes I'll pick a brighter T-shirt to play badminton in. A navy top with grey trousers is the kind of thing I can put on without having to think about it.

questions.prompt: Are you good at telling jokes?

answers.basic: I'm better at making a quick comment in a conversation than telling a full joke. I sometimes forget the good part if I try to tell a long one. I can usually get a laugh if something funny has just happened and everyone already knows what I'm talking about.

questions.prompt: Do your friends like to tell jokes?

answers.basic: Yes, especially when we're relaxing after a game. We usually joke about a missed shot or something funny that happened that day. If someone completely misses an easy return, we might bring it up over noodles and end up laughing all over again.

questions.prompt: Do you like to watch comedies?

answers.basic: Yes, a good comedy is an easy way to relax. I like humour that comes from an ordinary situation going a little wrong. A scene where someone tries to get out of an awkward conversation can make me laugh because it feels so familiar.

questions.prompt: Have you ever watched a live show?

answers.basic: Yes, I've been to a small live comedy show. I liked hearing the audience react together because it made the performance feel different from a clip. When somebody at the front laughed early, it made everyone else laugh too, and I could see the performer adjusting to the room.

questions.prompt: Are comedy shows popular in your country?

answers.basic: Yes, comedy shows and short comedy clips get shared a lot. I usually hear about a good one because a friend has sent me a bit of it. Friends sometimes send a clip during lunch because they know I'll recognise the situation, even if I've never watched the full show.

questions.prompt: Do you use headphones?

answers.basic: Yes, I use them on the subway and when I want to listen to something without disturbing anyone. They're also handy for work calls. On a noisy train, I can follow an English recording much more easily once I've put my earbuds in.

questions.prompt: What type of headphones do you use?

answers.basic: I mostly use wireless earbuds because they're easy to carry. For a longer call at home, I sometimes use a headset with a microphone. The earbuds fit in a small pocket in my bag, so I usually have them even when I've left the bigger headset at home.

questions.prompt: When would you use headphones?

answers.basic: I use them to listen to music on my way to work or to take a call. Sometimes I put on an English recording during a walk. A walk is a good time to play the same short clip a couple of times and listen for phrases I've missed.

questions.prompt: In what conditions would you not use headphones?

answers.basic: I take them out when I'm cycling or crossing a busy road. I also leave them off when I'm coaching so I can hear the players. On court I often need to hear a question from the other side of the net, even while people are playing nearby.

questions.prompt: Is wearing headphones comfortable?

answers.basic: They're comfortable for a short trip. If I wear earbuds for too long, my ears start to feel tired, so I take them out for a while. I notice it most after a long call, when taking them out for five minutes feels like a proper break.

questions.prompt: What subjects are you studying?

answers.basic: I'm studying computer science. My classes cover programming and databases, and I like the projects where we have to build something that actually works. For a database assignment, I enjoyed deciding where to store the information and then checking whether I could find it again easily.

questions.prompt: Do you like your subject?

answers.basic: Yes. I like the moment when a piece of code finally works and I can see what all the smaller steps were for. A recent example was getting a little app to save my notes, which felt more useful than just finishing an exercise.

questions.prompt: Why did you choose to study that subject?

answers.basic: I enjoyed solving problems and wanted to make things I could use myself. Once I'd built a small program, I wanted to see what else I could do. I liked that I could start with something as simple as a list and gradually add features that made it easier to use.

questions.prompt: Do you think that your subject is popular in your country?

answers.basic: Yes, quite a few people choose it because software is used in so many jobs. There are also lots of projects you can try outside class. Several students I know started with a small website and kept learning once friends actually wanted to use it.

questions.prompt: Do you have any plans for your studies in the next five years?

answers.basic: I'd like to finish my degree and get some experience on a real software team. I'm particularly interested in how websites and apps work behind the scenes. An internship would be a good chance to see what happens between writing a feature and making it available to users.

questions.prompt: What are the benefits of being your age?

answers.basic: It's a good time to try different things and see what suits me. I can spend an afternoon on a small project just because I'm curious. If I find a subject I like, I can take a short course or build a small example before making a bigger decision.

questions.prompt: Do you want to change your major?

answers.basic: I'm happy with computer science for now. There are still plenty of areas I haven't tried, so I'd rather explore those first. For instance, I'm curious about how servers handle lots of requests, and I'd like to try building something that lets me see that.

questions.prompt: Do you prefer to study in the mornings or in the afternoons?

answers.basic: I prefer mornings for anything that takes real concentration. In the afternoon I'm usually better at reviewing something I've already learned. I might write new code before lunch, then go over my notes or tidy up a project later in the day.

questions.prompt: How much time do you spend on your studies each week?

answers.basic: Outside class, I usually spend an hour or two studying on weekdays. I put in extra time when there's a project due. In a typical week that works out to several hours at my desk, mostly trying examples from class and checking what I understand.

questions.prompt: Are you looking forward to working?

answers.basic: Yes. I want to see how a team builds something people actually use. I think I'd learn a lot from seeing how more experienced engineers work. I'd especially like to see how they decide what to fix first when there are several things going wrong at once.

questions.prompt: What technology do you use when you study?

answers.basic: I use my laptop for coding, a notes app to keep track of questions and Git to save my work. I often check the official documentation when I'm stuck. Keeping my work in Git means I can try a change and go back to an earlier version if it breaks something.

questions.prompt: What changes would you like to see in your school?

answers.basic: I'd like more classes where students work on a small project together. It would give us a chance to see how the ideas fit together. For example, one student could build a simple page while someone else works on saving the information it needs.

questions.prompt: What work do you do?

answers.basic: I work full-time as a backend software engineer. I also coach badminton part-time, which gives me a very different way to spend time after work. On a typical day I work on the parts of an app users don't see, then head to the court to teach.

questions.prompt: Why did you choose to do that type of work?

answers.basic: I like figuring out how things work behind the scenes. With backend development, I get to solve the problems that let an app do what people expect it to. I especially like tracing a problem from what the user sees all the way back to the piece of code that caused it.

questions.prompt: Do you like your job?

answers.basic: Yes. My favourite part is taking a problem that seems confusing at first and figuring out where it actually starts. It's satisfying when a fix holds up. For example, if something runs slowly, I enjoy narrowing it down until there's one small change I can test.

questions.prompt: What requirements did you need to meet to get your current job?

answers.basic: I needed to be able to write code, work with databases and explain how I'd solve a problem. Being able to work with other engineers mattered too. I remember that explaining why I'd make a particular choice mattered almost as much as being able to write the code.

questions.prompt: Do you have any plans for your work in the next five years?

answers.basic: I'd like to get better at designing reliable systems and take more responsibility for projects. I also want to keep coaching and build up my personal website. For example, I'd like to make more decisions about how a service is put together and write about what I learn.

questions.prompt: What do you think is the most important at the moment?

answers.basic: Right now it's keeping a steady pace. I want enough time to do my job well, coach and still have energy left for the things I'm learning. On a week with evening lessons, that might mean setting aside one quiet night for reading or catching up on sleep.

questions.prompt: Do you want to change to another job?

answers.basic: I'm happy working in backend development at the moment. There are still problems I want to learn how to solve, so I'm in no hurry to change fields. I still want to get better at designing services that are easy to maintain when more people start using them.

questions.prompt: Do you miss being a student?

answers.basic: Sometimes I miss having more time to explore a subject just because it interested me. I still get to do that now, but I have to make time for it. I used to be able to spend an entire afternoon figuring out a small program, which is harder to fit around work and coaching.

questions.prompt: What technology do you use at work?

answers.basic: I spend a lot of time with a code editor, Git and database tools. When something goes wrong, I usually start with the logs to see what happened. If an app fails to save something, I can follow the request from the error message to the database.

questions.prompt: Who helps you the most? And how?

answers.basic: My teammates help the most. They often know why a part of the system works a certain way, which can save me hours of guessing. One short conversation can explain why a decision was made and point me towards the right place to make a change.

questions.prompt: What kind of house or apartment do you want to live in in the future?

answers.basic: I'd like an apartment with good light and space for a desk. Being near a subway station and a badminton hall would make it a great fit for me. I'd especially like a window by the desk so I can sit down to read without having to turn the light on.

questions.prompt: Are the transport facilities to your home very good?

answers.basic: Yes, I can get to the subway without much trouble. That's useful when I go straight from work to a court on the other side of town. I can carry my gear on the subway and get there without having to worry about parking after work.

questions.prompt: Do you prefer living in a house or an apartment?

answers.basic: An apartment makes more sense for me in Shanghai. I don't need a lot of space, and I'd rather be able to get to places easily. A flat close to the subway works well on nights when I need to get home from a lesson with my racket bag.

questions.prompt: Please describe the room you live in.

answers.basic: It's a simple room with a bed, a desk and a place to put my clothes. My badminton bag usually ends up next to the door. I use the desk to read or work on my site, so I try to leave enough space to open a notebook.

questions.prompt: What part of your home do you like the most?

answers.basic: I like the spot by the desk best. That's where I write notes for my blog or work on a small project when I have a free evening. The light is quite good there, and having a regular place to sit makes it easy to pick up a half-finished idea.

questions.prompt: How long have you lived there?

answers.basic: I've lived in my current place for a while now. I've had time to find a grocery shop and a few courts I can reach easily. The routes feel familiar enough now that I can decide where to shop or play without looking at a map first.

questions.prompt: Do you plan to live there for a long time?

answers.basic: I can see myself staying here for the time being. I'd consider moving if my commute changed or I needed more space. At the moment I can get to work and reach several badminton halls, so it suits the way I spend my week.

questions.prompt: What’s the difference between where you are living now and where you have lived in the past?

answers.basic: Where I grew up in Hunan felt less rushed. In Shanghai I have more places to go and better transport, but I appreciate how quiet my place feels when I get home. In Hunan I could go out without much planning, whereas in Shanghai I often check the subway route before heading somewhere new.

questions.prompt: Can you describe the place where you live?

answers.basic: It's a fairly simple apartment in Shanghai, with enough room to work and relax. There are shops nearby, which is handy when I come home late. Inside, the main things I need are a comfortable desk, somewhere to keep my sports gear and a quiet place to sleep.

questions.prompt: What room does your family spend most of the time in?

answers.basic: When we're all together, my family usually spends the most time in the living room. That's where we sit and talk after a meal. If we're visiting around a holiday, someone usually puts the kettle on and we end up there until it's time to eat again.

questions.prompt: What's your favorite room in your apartment or house?

answers.basic: My favourite room is the one with my desk. I can sit down, work on my site for an hour and leave my notes ready for next time. I keep a notebook within reach there, so an idea from a badminton lesson can turn into a post later.

questions.prompt: What makes you feel pleasant in your home?

answers.basic: A quiet room and a bit of natural light do a lot for me. I also like getting home and knowing I can put my bag down and switch off. On a busy evening, even ten minutes by the window with a cup of tea can make it feel like I'm properly home.

questions.prompt: Do you think it is important to live in a comfortable environment?

answers.basic: Yes. A comfortable place makes it easier to rest after work. Even something small, like a chair that fits you, can change how you feel at home. I notice it on evenings when I need to read or practise English, because it's easier to settle down somewhere quiet.

questions.prompt: Do you live in an apartment or a house?

answers.basic: I live in an apartment in Shanghai. It's a practical size for me and easy to look after when the week gets busy. I have a spot for my desk and a place by the door for my racket bag, so the space works well.

questions.prompt: Who do you live with?

answers.basic: I live on my own at the moment. I like being able to keep my own hours, especially on days when I get back late from coaching. If I finish a lesson late, I can unpack, shower and eat at my own pace without disturbing anyone.

questions.prompt: What do you usually do in your apartment?

answers.basic: I usually cook something simple, get my gear ready for the next session or work on my blog. Some evenings I just sit down and read. On Sundays I often check my racket bag and put a clean top by the door before I settle down with a book.

questions.prompt: What kinds of accommodation do you live in?

answers.basic: I live in a small apartment. I have enough room for a proper desk and somewhere to leave my badminton gear, which is about all I need. That makes it easy to keep tidy, even when I come in late and have to leave for work early the next morning.

questions.prompt: Where is your hometown?

answers.basic: I grew up in Hunan, in central China. I live in Shanghai now, but Hunan is still what I think of when someone asks where I'm from. A lot of my early memories, including when I started playing badminton at around ten, are tied to growing up there.

questions.prompt: Is that a big city or a small place?

answers.basic: I'd call it a smaller place compared with Shanghai. It has the things you'd need day to day, and the streets feel less crowded to me. It feels possible to do several things on one short trip because the places I know are closer together.

questions.prompt: Please describe your hometown a little.

answers.basic: It's the part of Hunan where I spent my school years. I remember the spicy food, familiar streets and afternoons when I could go out and play badminton. Even now, the smell of chillies cooking can take me back to walking home hungry after playing for an hour.

questions.prompt: How long have you been living there?

answers.basic: I lived in Hunan for most of my childhood. I moved away later and now live in Shanghai, so these days I go back to visit. When I'm back, familiar streets still make me feel like I know my way around, even if some shops have changed.

questions.prompt: Do you think you will continue living there for a long time?

answers.basic: I'm based in Shanghai for work now, so I expect to stay here for a while. I'd still like to go back to Hunan when I get the chance. Most of my work and coaching are in Shanghai now, so going back to Hunan feels more like a break.

questions.prompt: Do you like your hometown?

answers.basic: Yes, I feel at home there. Even small things like the way people speak or the smell of a familiar dish remind me of growing up. For instance, hearing someone speak with the same accent as my relatives can make a place feel familiar quite quickly.

questions.prompt: Do you like living there?

answers.basic: I enjoyed living there, and I like going back now. After a busy few weeks in Shanghai, it's good to spend time somewhere that feels familiar. I especially like coming back when I have a few days free and can take my time over a family meal.

questions.prompt: What do you like (most) about your hometown?

answers.basic: I probably miss the food most. A spicy meal in Hunan tastes like what I grew up eating, and I always look forward to that when I go back. Stir-fried pork with chillies is one of those things I'd order straight away because it tastes like home to me.

questions.prompt: Is there anything you dislike about it?

answers.basic: The humid summer weather can wear me out a bit. If I go out to play in the afternoon, I feel like I need a second shower afterwards. I remember wanting to get out early for a game, before it was so hot that moving around felt like hard work.

questions.prompt: What's your hometown famous for?

answers.basic: Hunan is well known for its spicy food. A dish like stir-fried pork with chillies is the kind of thing many people think of first. When friends ask what to try first, I'd suggest one dish with fresh chillies so they can taste what makes it familiar to me.

questions.prompt: Did you learn about the history of your hometown at school?

answers.basic: Yes, we learned a little local history at school. I remember the stories better when they were connected to places I'd actually seen. A story about a street or building nearby was easier to picture than a list of dates we had to remember.

questions.prompt: Are there many young people in your hometown?

answers.basic: Yes, there are young people studying and working there. Some move to bigger cities for a few years, so you tend to see more familiar faces during holidays. It's nice to go back at those times because people I knew at school may be back visiting their own families too.

questions.prompt: Is your hometown a good place for young people to pursue their careers?

answers.basic: It depends on what they want to do. Staying close to family can be a real advantage, and a bigger city may offer more options in a specialised field like backend development. For a local business, knowing the area and the people might matter more than having lots of companies to choose from.

questions.prompt: Have you learned anything about the history of your hometown?

answers.basic: A little. I learned some local stories at school, and talking to older people helped me picture what the area was like before I grew up there. Hearing how relatives got around or bought things years ago made local history feel connected to places I already knew.

questions.prompt: Did you learn about the culture of your hometown in your childhood?

answers.basic: Yes. Most of it came from daily life, like the food we made at home, the way people spoke and how we spent holidays together. For instance, I learned which dishes felt right for a holiday long before I knew where the traditions behind them came from.

questions.prompt: Do you like the area that you live in?

answers.basic: Yes, it's easy to get around and I can pick up most things near home. Having places to play badminton within reach is a big plus. I can buy a few things on my way home and still get to an evening lesson without making a special trip across town.

questions.prompt: Where do you like to go in that area?

answers.basic: I usually head to a badminton hall or take a walk if I've been at my desk all day. I like knowing I have both options nearby. If I've got a whole evening, I'll play badminton, and if I've only got twenty minutes I'll take a short walk instead.

questions.prompt: Do you know any famous people in your area?

answers.basic: No, nobody famous comes to mind. I recognise some people from playing badminton, but most of us know each other through the courts. I'll often see a familiar player several times before I learn much about them outside the game.

questions.prompt: What are some changes in the area recently?

answers.basic: I've noticed a few shops change hands and some small improvements around the street. I tend to notice those things when I take the same route home every day. For example, a new place to eat on my route can make it easier to grab dinner after a late lesson.

questions.prompt: Do you know any of your neighbors?

answers.basic: I know a few faces in my building. We usually say hello in the lift, and sometimes we talk for a minute about the weather. Those little conversations make the building feel more familiar, even though we don't often see each other for long.

questions.prompt: Are the people in your neighborhood nice and friendly?

answers.basic: Yes, in a quiet sort of way. People hold the door for each other or help out with a delivery, even when they don't know each other well. When my hands are full of groceries and sports gear, having someone keep the lift door open makes a difference.

questions.prompt: Do you live in a noisy or a quiet area?

answers.basic: It's fairly quiet once I'm inside. You can hear the traffic on the main road, but it fades quite quickly when you turn into the smaller streets. By the time I'm home, it's usually quiet enough to read for a while without having to put my headphones on.

questions.prompt: What city do you live in?

answers.basic: I live in Shanghai. I moved here after growing up in Hunan, so living in such a big city was a change for me. I got used to it by finding places I could go regularly, especially badminton halls where I started recognising a few faces.

questions.prompt: Do you like this city? Why?

answers.basic: Yes. I can do the kind of work I want and find people to play badminton with, even if I decide quite late in the day. On a free evening I can find a court or get something to eat with friends without having to plan the whole day around it.

questions.prompt: How long have you lived in this city?

answers.basic: I've been here for a while now. It feels like home in the sense that I have my work, my usual courts and a routine here. I noticed it started to feel familiar when I could get to most of my usual places without checking a map.

questions.prompt: Are there big changes in this city?

answers.basic: Yes, some areas change quite quickly. I tend to notice it in smaller ways, like a new shop or a route that suddenly gets easier to walk. That matters to me more day to day than a new tower, because it changes where I can stop on the way home.

questions.prompt: Is this city your permanent residence?

answers.basic: Shanghai is where I'm based at the moment, and I expect to stay for work. I haven't made a decision about where I'll live long term. Being able to do backend work and coach in the same city is a good reason for me to stay at this stage.

questions.prompt: Are there people of different ages living in this city?

answers.basic: Yes, my neighbourhood has families, younger people who go out to work and plenty of older residents. I often see them using the same small public spaces at different times. A park can be full of older people exercising in the morning and children running around when school finishes.

questions.prompt: Are the people friendly in the city?

answers.basic: Generally, yes. People may look busy on the subway, but I've had strangers give me directions or hold the lift when my hands were full. When I first moved, I remember how helpful it was when someone pointed me towards the right subway exit.

questions.prompt: Is the city friendly to children and old people?

answers.basic: In many areas, yes. A nearby park and good public transport help both groups. Some busy crossings could still be easier to get around. I notice the difference near a park where there's somewhere to sit and the nearest crossing is easy to find.

questions.prompt: Do you often see your neighbors?

answers.basic: I see a few of them in the lift or on my way out. We usually exchange a quick hello and go on with our day. It's usually when we're both coming back from work, so saying hello is enough to make it feel friendly.

questions.prompt: What's the weather like where you live?

answers.basic: Summers in Shanghai are hot and humid. In winter the damp can make it feel colder than I expect, so I usually check the weather before heading out. If I'm taking my racket bag across town in summer, I usually bring a spare shirt because the walk can feel quite warm.

questions.prompt: Would you recommend your city to others?

answers.basic: Yes, especially if they enjoy walking, good food and seeing different parts of a city. It's easy to get around by subway, so they can explore at their own pace. I'd tell a friend to leave part of the day free for a walk by the river, then stop somewhere for food.

part2And3.title: 对结果开心的重要决定

part2.prompt: Describe a time you made an important decision and were happy with the result
cuePoints: How easy it was for you to make the decision
And explain why you were happy with the result

answers.basic:
One decision I'm really glad I made was to start coaching badminton part-time. I'd been playing since I was ten, and somewhere along the way I realised that I understood a shot better when I tried to explain it to someone else. That's the idea I took from the Feynman technique. If I couldn't explain a movement in simple words, there was usually a part I hadn't understood myself.

I noticed that most clearly when people asked me for tips between games. I could show a movement quite easily, but sometimes I had to stop and think when someone asked what to do with their feet first. I'd try giving them one thing to focus on, then watch what happened on their next attempt. If the movement got easier, I had a better idea of what I'd explained well. If they were still confused, I'd go back and work out which part of the movement I was taking for granted. Those little conversations made me want to spend more time teaching.

I liked the idea straight away, but committing to it took some thought. I work full-time as a backend engineer, and I wondered whether I'd have the energy to teach after work. I also knew that doing a shot and helping someone else do it were different skills. What makes me happy now is that little moment when a student stops, tries the movement again and goes, 'Oh, I get it.' It still feels good every time.

part3.prompt: Which is better, to make a decision quickly or slowly?

answers.basic: For everyday choices, I think it's better to decide quickly. If the choice could affect your life for years, like moving to another city, it's worth taking your time. With something like choosing lunch, spending ten minutes comparing options probably costs more than getting it slightly wrong. A move is different because you might need to check the commute and talk it over with your family before you know whether the new place would work on an ordinary weekday.

part3.prompt: Do you think most people's decisions are made in their 20s?

answers.basic: A lot of firsts happen in your twenties, like choosing a job or moving out. But people make important decisions at every age, especially when their family or work situation changes. In your twenties, a lot of decisions feel connected because one choice about work can affect where you live and who you see every day. Someone in their forties might have to weigh a different set of things, like whether a new job would leave enough time to care for a parent.

part3.prompt: What if people in a group have different opinions on a decision?

answers.basic: I'd let everyone explain what matters to them first. Once we know what we agree on, it's easier to choose something the whole group can live with. At work, for instance, two engineers can prefer different designs because one is worried about speed and the other is worried about maintenance. I'd try to agree on which concern matters most for this release, and if we're still stuck, I'd test both ideas on a small example.

part3.prompt: What little decisions do people make every day?

answers.basic: People decide what to wear, what to eat, and how to get to work. They also make small choices about whether to reply to a message now or later. Many of these choices follow a routine, so you barely notice making them until something changes. If it's raining when I leave work, for instance, I have to decide whether to walk to the usual station or take a bus that's closer but might get stuck in traffic.

part3.prompt: Do you think it is a good idea to make a small decision every day?

answers.basic: Yes. Making small decisions helps you notice what you actually want. Picking what to cook, for example, can make the day feel a bit more like your own. It gives you practice at choosing without making every little decision feel like a big test. For instance, when I decide whether to take a walk or go straight home, I can check how much energy I have and see whether the choice leaves me feeling better an hour later.

part3.prompt: How can we tell the difference between an important and an easy decision?

answers.basic: An important decision has lasting consequences, while an easy decision is simply one you can make without much effort. Sometimes an important choice is easy because you already know what matters most to you. I'd ask what would happen if I changed my mind a week later. Ordering the wrong meal is easy to put right the next day, whereas accepting a job can affect your schedule for years, even if you feel sure it's the right choice the moment you hear about it.

part2And3.title: 做困难事情并成功的人

part2.prompt: Describe a person you know who did something difficult and was successful
cuePoints: What difficult thing this person did
And explain how you feel about this person

answers.basic:
I'd talk about a colleague who helped fix a slow service. The difficult part was that it worked fine most of the time, so we couldn't just open the app and see the problem. When things got busy, though, one request would take much longer than it should.

It was awkward to investigate because people noticed the delays at different times and described them in different ways. Some of us thought the service needed more capacity, but it was hard to tell from a general report that the app felt slow. He asked us to find one example with a clear time and an action we could repeat. We then tried the same action when the system was quiet and when more requests were coming in. That gave us a much better place to start, because we finally had a pair of results we could compare.

My colleague picked one slow request from the logs and followed it step by step. He found that the service was asking the database for the same information several times. He changed that one part, then checked the result under a similar load before calling it fixed. I remember him showing us two timings side by side. The difference was obvious. I admire the way he worked. When several people had theories about what might be wrong, he stayed patient and found a way to test one of them.

part3.prompt: In which sectors are companies more likely to succeed in China?

answers.basic: I'd look at sectors that solve everyday problems, like healthcare and services for older people. I can also see room for small tech companies that make simple tools people are willing to pay for. A business that makes booking appointments simpler, for example, is dealing with something customers already do and can see the point of. I'd also look at how easy it is to reach those customers, because a good product can go unnoticed if nobody knows where to find it.

part3.prompt: Is it easy to start up a company?

answers.basic: The first step can be quite simple, especially if you sell a service online. Finding enough customers and keeping the business running are the harder parts. Someone can start offering badminton lessons with a small group and find out whether people want to come back. To turn it into a business, they'd still need to cover court fees, find a dependable schedule and give people enough reason to choose those sessions again next month.

part3.prompt: Other than making money, what is more important for a company?

answers.basic: A company needs people to trust it. If it keeps its promises to customers and treats its staff well, people are more likely to stick with it. One test is what happens when the company gets something wrong. If a shop sends the wrong product and sorts it out quickly, I'd feel comfortable buying from it again, and that sort of confidence matters when you want customers and employees to stay with you for years.

part3.prompt: Does money equal success?

answers.basic: Money is one sign that a business is doing well. I'd also count building a product people rely on or creating a workplace where people want to stay. A business can have a good month because it offered a heavy discount, so I'd want to know what happens when the offer ends. If people keep coming back at the normal price and the staff can handle the work comfortably, that tells me a lot more about its future.

part3.prompt: How can companies help protect the environment?

answers.basic: They can cut back on packaging and design products that are easier to repair. They can also check how much energy they use and fix the obvious sources of waste. A small retailer could start by checking which orders really need a large box and which could go in something smaller. The change is easier to keep up if it also saves money or time, because then the people packing orders have a practical reason to make it part of the routine.

part3.prompt: Is it difficult to do business in today's world?

answers.basic: Yes, because customers can compare prices and reviews in seconds. At the same time, a small business can reach people online without opening a shop, which helps. That gives a new company a chance to try an idea with a few customers before spending much. It also raises expectations, because if a delivery takes longer than promised, customers can tell other people about it straight away and the business has to respond while it's still dealing with the original problem.

part2.prompt: Describe a happy person you know
cuePoints: And explain why you think he/she is a happy person

answers.basic:
A friend I play badminton with comes to mind. When I arrive at a court and hear someone laughing before I've even changed my shoes, there's a good chance it's him. He gets a lot of enjoyment out of small things, like finally getting a serve in after missing it several times.

What I like is that his mood doesn't depend on whether he's playing well. Sometimes he arrives after a long day and says he only wants an easy game. Half an hour later he's usually chatting away and asking how everyone else's week has been. He also notices people who've been standing by the court for a while and invites them to play. I remember turning up tired once and thinking I'd go home after a game or two. Spending a bit of time around him made it much easier to forget the day I'd just had.

You can tell when he's happy because he talks more, laughs easily and starts looking for someone else to join the game. Once he hit the frame of his racket and the shuttle somehow went over the net. He laughed so hard that we had to stop for a minute. He has bad days like everyone else, but he pays attention to the parts that went well. Even after a game he's lost, he'll remember one good rally and ask if we can play again next week.

part3.prompt: When do you think people are happiest?

answers.basic: I think people are happiest when they can relax with people they trust. An ordinary dinner with close friends can be more enjoyable than a big event. With good friends, there's no pressure to keep the conversation going every second or look as if everything is going well. I notice that after badminton, when everyone is tired and we can still sit over a bowl of noodles for ages, talking about one funny point from the game.

part3.prompt: How can the arts spread positive emotions in society?

answers.basic: A song or a film can help people see a familiar problem in a kinder way. A local performance can also give neighbours something to enjoy together. For instance, an outdoor concert gives people who would normally pass one another in the street a reason to stop and listen together. They may start talking afterwards, and even those who went on their own can leave feeling that they shared something with the people around them for a while.

part3.prompt: Do you think teachers are able to spot the unhappy children?

answers.basic: Some teachers notice when a talkative student suddenly goes quiet. But some children hide their feelings well, so a private chat can tell a teacher more than watching from across the classroom. A teacher might ask what break time has been like lately, since that gives the student something easier to talk about than their feelings in general. It also helps when the same adult checks in again later, because some children need a bit of time before they're ready to say anything.

part3.prompt: Should teachers know what children are doing all the time?

answers.basic: Teachers should know enough to keep children safe at school. Children also need some room to play, make choices and solve little problems on their own. If two children disagree about whose turn it is in a game, a teacher can stay nearby and see whether they work it out. They can step in if someone is being hurt, and the children still get a chance to practise speaking up for themselves in a fairly safe situation.

part3.prompt: What would make a student happy at school?

answers.basic: Having a friend to sit with can make a big difference. It also helps when there is at least one subject or activity a student looks forward to. I remember school feeling easier on days when there was something to do together after class. Even a small success can help, like working out a problem that felt impossible the day before, because it gives you a reason to want to come back and try the next one.

part3.prompt: Do you think doing a job that you like is more important than other things?

answers.basic: Liking your job matters because you spend so much time at it. I'd still weigh it alongside pay, health and whether the job leaves enough time for life outside work. For example, a job can be interesting and still leave you too tired to enjoy anything once you get home. I'd look for work that gives me enough of a challenge during the day and still lets me do things I care about, like teaching badminton in the evening.

part2.prompt: Describe a time you watched a famous person being interviewed
cuePoints: When and where you watched the interview
And explain how you felt about the interview

answers.basic:
I remember watching an interview with Lin Dan, the badminton player. I'd come home from playing one evening and was looking at badminton clips on my phone. I came across a longer interview and stayed to watch because I wanted to hear him talk about playing under pressure.

I'd watched plenty of match highlights before, so I expected to skip to the parts about famous games. Instead, I found myself listening for the smaller things that go into being ready for one match. I thought about my own reaction to a bad session, when I often want to change everything at once. Watching him made me think about how useful it might be to work on one thing long enough to see a difference. I went back to a bit I'd half heard the first time, because I wanted to follow the whole conversation at my own pace.

The part I found interesting was hearing him discuss preparation. When you watch a match, the camera follows the shuttle and you mainly see who won the point. An interview gives you a chance to think about what the player has been doing for weeks before that point. I remember putting my racket bag down halfway through so I could pay proper attention. I came away feeling a bit less impatient about my own training. Some improvements take a lot of quiet practice before anyone watching would be able to notice them.

part3.prompt: What should people wear to a job interview?

answers.basic: I'd wear something clean and fairly simple, like a neat shirt and trousers. For a more formal workplace, I'd go a step further and wear a jacket. I'd check how people usually dress in that field and aim to look like I've made an effort. For a software interview, for instance, I'd choose something comfortable enough to sit and talk in for an hour, so I can put my attention on the questions when the interview starts.

part3.prompt: Why do we need to attend interviews when applying for jobs?

answers.basic: An interview lets both sides ask questions. The employer can hear how you handled real situations, and you can find out what the job is actually like. For example, I could ask a software team how they handle a problem that comes up outside working hours. Their answer would tell me something about what the job feels like on a difficult day, and my explanation of a past problem would give them something concrete to ask me about.
