part3.prompt: What should people do to prepare for a job interview?

answers.basic: I'd read about the company and prepare two or three examples from my own experience. It's also worth practising how to describe each example out loud. I usually find that a story is easier to remember if I know what the problem was, what I did and how it turned out. I'd also think of one genuine question about the job, because it's much easier to ask something useful when you've looked into the role beforehand.

part3.prompt: Why do some people think interviews are a waste of time?

answers.basic: Some interviews feel pointless when the questions have little to do with the work. A long process is especially frustrating if the company never tells you how it went. Someone might take time off work for several rounds and still get asked the same questions each time. I can see why they'd prefer a shorter interview where they get to talk through something that actually happens in the role and know when to expect an answer.

part3.prompt: Why do some people dislike being interviewed?

answers.basic: Some people get nervous when they know they're being judged. Others simply need time to think and find it hard to give a good answer on the spot. The format can make that worse when several people are looking at you and the next question comes before you've finished thinking. I find it easier when an interviewer gives me a moment to choose an example, because then I can talk about something I've actually done and explain it clearly.

part3.prompt: What kinds of people are usually interviewed?

answers.basic: Job applicants are the most obvious example. Journalists also interview public figures, experts and ordinary people who have seen or done something interesting. A sports reporter might interview a player after a match to find out what changed during the game. If there's news about a neighbourhood, it can be useful to hear from someone who lives there, since they'll know what the change means for people who use the area every day.

part2.prompt: Describe a person you know who is very organized
cuePoints: What this person usually does to stay organized
In what situations you have noticed this quality
And explain why you think being organized is important to him/her

answers.basic:
One organised person I know is a colleague on my software team. When we get a new job to do, she writes down the next few steps and keeps any decisions in the same place. If someone asks what we agreed last week, she can usually find it while the rest of us are still searching through messages.

What I noticed over time was how little effort it took to use her system. The notes were usually a few lines long, and she'd put the decision at the top so we could find it without reading the whole conversation. In meetings she'd write down questions that were still open and leave the rest for later. I started doing something similar on my own tasks because it was useful to have a record I could come back to the next day. It made more sense once I saw how much time we saved by doing it regularly.

I noticed this when we were getting a feature ready to release. She had a short list of things to check and, next to each one, the name of the person doing it. When one test took longer than expected, she moved the other tasks around and told us what we could do in the meantime. I think being organised matters to her because she hates making people wait for information. It also lets her finish work without carrying the whole project around in her head.

part3.prompt: Do you think it is important for managers to be well organized?

answers.basic: Yes, because a manager has to keep track of several people's work at once. A clear plan helps everyone see who is doing what and when it is due. A small example is having one place to check who owns each task. If someone is off sick, the manager can see what's about to be held up and move things around before the rest of the team has spent half a day waiting for an answer.

part3.prompt: Should parents teach their children to be organized?

answers.basic: Yes, and I'd start with little habits like putting school things in the same place. Doing it together a few times can help the child remember the routine. A child might start by packing their bag with a parent and then check it on their own once the steps feel familiar. In the morning they get to see the benefit for themselves, because they can find their things and leave the house without a last-minute search.

part3.prompt: What can people do to become more organized?

answers.basic: I'd start by writing tasks down in one place and choosing the most important one each morning. A system you can stick with is more useful than a complicated one. If a task is too big to fit on that list, I'd write down the first action, like asking a colleague for a file. Once that step is clear, it's easier to start, and at the end of the day you can see what is actually left to do.

part3.prompt: Are organized people more likely to be successful at work or in their studies?

answers.basic: Usually, yes. They are more likely to meet deadlines and have time to check their work. They still need the skills to do the work well. For instance, a student who starts an assignment early can ask a question while there's still time to use the answer. Someone else might know the subject just as well and end up rushing, so organisation helps the first student make better use of the knowledge they already have.

part3.prompt: Do you think children should learn to be organized from a young age?

answers.basic: Yes. Small routines like packing a school bag the night before are easy to learn. They also let children do more things for themselves over time. It can be as simple as asking a child to put a book back where they found it. The benefit becomes obvious when they want the book again the next day, and they can apply the same idea to other things without needing an adult to remind them every time.

part3.prompt: Why is it important for people to be organized?

answers.basic: It saves time and makes life less stressful. When you know where things are and what needs doing, you can spend more energy on the work itself. I notice it most when I'm switching between work and coaching on the same day. If my equipment is packed and my lesson notes are in one place, I can arrive thinking about the student in front of me, which makes the first few minutes of the lesson easier.

part2.prompt: Describe a noisy place you have been to
cuePoints: And explain why you feel it’s a noisy place

answers.basic:
One noisy place I know is a badminton hall in Shanghai. I went there one Saturday evening to play doubles with a few friends. The courts were all booked, and we had to walk past several games just to reach the one at the back.

We arrived a few minutes before our booking and waited near the net while the previous group finished. I was trying to tell my friends who I'd play with first, but everyone seemed to be talking louder than usual just to finish a sentence. During the warm-up I could see people giving little signals with their rackets across the court. I ended up doing the same thing whenever my partner was too far away to hear me. Nobody seemed particularly annoyed by it, because most of us were making just as much noise once our own games began.

The noise came from a bit of everything. Shoes squeaked on the floor, people shouted the score, and you could hear a sharp crack every time someone hit a hard shot. The ceiling was quite high, so the sound seemed to bounce around. At one point my partner was trying to tell me whose serve it was, and I had to walk over to hear him. I got used to it once we started playing. When I stepped outside at the end, though, I suddenly noticed how quiet the street was.

part3.prompt: How can people consider others' feelings when chatting in public?

answers.basic: People can keep their voices down and use headphones for videos. If they need to take a long call, they can step outside or move somewhere quieter. On a crowded train, I try to think about whether the people next to me have any way to move away from the noise. A quick call to say I'm running late is understandable, and a long conversation can usually wait until I get off at the next stop.

part3.prompt: How would people usually respond to noises in your country?

answers.basic: I think people are fairly patient with ordinary street noise. If a neighbour plays loud music late at night, someone might ask them to turn it down or speak to building management. People are more likely to say something when the same noise keeps coming back at a time when they're trying to sleep. A short conversation in the daytime can help, because the neighbour may have no idea how clearly the sound carries into another flat at night.

part3.prompt: Which area is exposed to noise more, the city or the countryside?

answers.basic: I'd say cities are usually noisier because of traffic, construction and the number of people sharing a small space. The countryside can be loud too, but the noise is often less constant. In Shanghai, I can walk past a busy crossing and still hear traffic after I've turned into the next street. A village can have a loud morning when there's farm work going on, but there may be longer stretches in the day when you can hear someone talking from quite far away.

part3.prompt: What kinds of noises are there in our life?

answers.basic: We hear traffic, building work, people talking and phones going off. At home, even a washing machine can feel loud when you're trying to concentrate. There are also noises I actually enjoy, like the sound of a good shot at a badminton hall. How I feel about a noise depends on what I'm trying to do at the time, so the same group of people chatting can sound friendly during dinner and distracting during a work call.

part3.prompt: Should children not be allowed to make noise under any circumstances?

answers.basic: Children should be able to make noise when they're playing outside or joining a game. In a library or on a quiet train, they can learn to lower their voices. I'd explain the reason in terms they can see, like pointing out that someone nearby is trying to read. If children also have a place where they can run around and call to each other, it's easier for them to understand why the expectation changes from one place to another.

part3.prompt: Do you think it is good for children to make noise?

answers.basic: It can be healthy when they're playing and expressing excitement. As they grow older, they can learn to notice when their noise is bothering someone. When a child calls for the shuttle in a game, for instance, they're learning to communicate with another player. I think adults can show them how to do that clearly and also show them when to give someone a little quiet, such as while another child is listening to instructions.

part2.prompt: Describe a natural place in your city that you enjoy visiting
cuePoints: Who you often go there with
And explain why you enjoy visiting there

answers.basic:
I like walking by the Huangpu River in Shanghai. There are stretches with trees and a path along the water, and you can watch boats go past without having to cross a busy road every few minutes. I try to go every few weeks when I have a free afternoon. Sometimes a friend comes with me, especially if we both feel like a break after playing indoors.

I usually start at a spot where the path is wide enough that people can walk at their own pace. At first I still find myself checking my phone, especially if I've come straight from work. After a while there's usually something that makes me look up, like a boat turning or a patch of light moving across the water. If I'm there with a friend, the conversation tends to slow down as well. We can stop halfway through a sentence to watch something and pick it up again without feeling we need to hurry.

We usually pick a direction and walk until we feel like turning back. I like hearing the water and feeling the wind, because most of my week is spent at a desk or in a sports hall. I don't normally plan anything else around the walk. It's enough to get some air, talk for a bit and go home feeling like I had a proper break.

part3.prompt: Which is more important, protecting the environment or developing the economy?

answers.basic: If I had to choose, I'd protect the environment first, because damage to clean water or air can be hard to undo. I'd look for ways to grow the economy within those limits. For example, factories can still create jobs if they have to account for how they handle waste. There may be an extra cost at first, but leaving a river polluted can take away other ways people earn a living and make the area less pleasant for everyone who lives there.

part3.prompt: Do you think staying in a natural place would help change people’s mood?

answers.basic: Yes. Walking somewhere green makes it easier to stop thinking about work for a while. I usually feel calmer when there's space to walk without much traffic around. The change can be quite small, like feeling less impatient after ten minutes by the river. I think part of it is that you have fewer demands on your attention there, so you can let a thought go instead of immediately having to deal with another sound or message.

part3.prompt: Do you think there should be many natural places in cities?

answers.basic: Yes, and I'd spread them around the city. Even a small neighbourhood park can make a difference if people can reach it on foot after work. A large park across town is great for a weekend, but a small one near your building can become part of your daily routine. I'd make sure people have a safe way to walk there and somewhere to sit, because those details matter if you're older or looking after a child.

part2.prompt: Describe a time when you saved money to buy something special
cuePoints: Why you wanted to buy it
How you saved money for it
And explain how you felt after buying it

answers.basic:
I once saved up for a badminton racket I really wanted. I'd been using the same one for a while, and it was fine, but I'd tried a friend's racket and liked how quickly I could get it into position. I wanted to buy something I'd actually enjoy playing with for a few years.

I didn't want to buy it just because it felt good for a few minutes, so I tried it again during a normal game. What I noticed was that I could get it up in time for the next shot without gripping it so tightly. I also checked what it would cost to get it restrung, because that was something I'd need to pay for eventually. Once I had a realistic price in mind, I could work out roughly how long I'd need to wait. It felt easier to be patient when I had a clear amount to aim for.

I put a little money aside each month and waited until I could afford it comfortably. I kept playing with my old racket while I saved, which gave me time to see if I still wanted the new one. I did, so I went back to the shop and bought it. I was looking forward to the next session as soon as I left. I also felt pleased that I'd taken my time, because I could explain exactly why I'd chosen it.

part3.prompt: Should people spend time on charity, or just money?

answers.basic: It depends on what the charity needs. Money can pay for supplies, and time can be more useful when a local group needs volunteers to help with an event. If I'm free on a Saturday, I could help set up tables at a community event, where an extra pair of hands makes an immediate difference. If my work schedule makes it hard to turn up regularly, a small donation I can manage each month may be more dependable.

part3.prompt: What kind of things do people usually save money for?

answers.basic: Big goals include a home, education and travel. People also save for smaller things they really want, like a laptop or a gift for someone. Putting money aside can also give people some room when something unexpected happens. For instance, I'd rather have a small amount ready if my computer needs replacing, because then I can choose what suits my work instead of having to take whatever I can afford that particular week.

part3.prompt: Is it easier to spend money or save money?

answers.basic: Spending is easier because you get something straight away. Saving gets easier if you set aside a fixed amount as soon as you get paid. With online shopping, it's easy to tap a button without stopping to think about the total. Saving for a racket felt easier once I had an actual item in mind, because I could see how much closer I was getting each month and knew what I was waiting for.

part3.prompt: Do you think it is easier to teach teenagers how to manage money when they are around 16 or 17 years old?

answers.basic: Yes, because at that age many teenagers already decide what to buy with their own money. They can practise making a budget while a parent is still around to help. A teenager could start by deciding how much of their money to use for transport, food and going out with friends. If they spend too much one week, they can see what needs to change the next, while the consequences are still fairly small and someone can help them think it through.

part3.prompt: Should parents teach their children to spend money freely or to save money?

answers.basic: I'd teach both. Give children a little money they can spend as they like, and help them put some aside when they're saving for something bigger. If a child is saving for a game or a new racket, it helps to let them see the amount grow each week. They can still choose a small treat now and then, and they learn from experience how that choice affects when they'll be able to buy the bigger thing.

part3.prompt: Should schools teach children how to manage money from a young age?

answers.basic: Yes. Schools can start with simple examples, like planning what to buy with a fixed amount. It's a practical skill children can use outside the classroom. One lesson could ask students to plan an afternoon out with friends and work out what they can afford after paying for transport. Comparing two possible plans would give them something useful to discuss, because they'll face that kind of choice themselves well before they earn a full-time wage.

part2.prompt: Describe a new skill you learned when you were a child
cuePoints: And explain how you felt about learning the skill

answers.basic:
I started learning badminton when I was about ten. At first I thought it was mostly about swinging hard enough to get the shuttle over the net. An older player at the court showed me how to hold the racket and asked me to try hitting the shuttle with a much smaller swing.

The first few times, I wanted to stand at the back and hit the shuttle as far as I could. The person helping me moved me much closer and asked me to see whether I could send it back to roughly the same spot twice. That was harder than I expected, because I was still changing the way I held the racket every time. I practised with a friend and we counted how many shots we managed before somebody dropped the shuttle. Keeping track of that number gave us a reason to try again even when progress was quite slow.

Once I could return the shuttle a few times near the net, we tried to keep a short rally going. My feet used to stay where they were after I hit, so I had to learn to get ready again before the next shot. I remember how good it felt when we finally kept the shuttle in the air for several hits. That was enough to make me want to come back. I still remember how quickly one small improvement can change the way a game feels, and I see that now when I teach.

part3.prompt: Is it important for everyone to have a specialized skill?

answers.basic: I think it's helpful to have one skill you can do well. It gives you confidence and something useful to offer, whether it's cooking, fixing things or writing code. A specialised skill can also open up conversations with people you might not meet otherwise. Badminton did that for me, because getting better at a particular shot made me curious about how other people learned it, and that eventually helped me find a way into teaching the sport as well.

part3.prompt: Can a child learn skills from another child?

answers.basic: Yes. A child may feel more comfortable asking a friend to show them a new move in a game. They can take turns and learn by copying each other. On a badminton court, two beginners can work out a simple rally together, then swap tips about what helped them keep the shuttle in the air. An adult can step in when they need help, but a friend often gives them the courage to try again right away after a mistake.

part3.prompt: Do you think it is easier for children to learn new skills than for adults?

answers.basic: It depends on the skill. Children often pick up sounds and movements through play, while adults can set a clear goal and find good instructions. An adult learning a badminton movement might understand an explanation about foot position very quickly. A child might get there by playing a game that naturally puts their feet in the right place, so I think the best approach depends on what the learner can already do and what keeps them interested.

part3.prompt: What are the differences between the way adults learn and the way children learn?

answers.basic: Children often learn by trying things and watching others. Adults are more likely to look for an explanation and connect the new skill to something they already know. A child might learn to catch a ball by asking for another throw until it feels natural. An adult often wants to know what to look for before they try again, which can be helpful when the movement is unfamiliar and they have only a short practice session.

part3.prompt: What are the differences between learning in a group and learning by yourself?

answers.basic: In a group, you can ask for help and see how other people do things. On your own, you can repeat a tricky bit without holding anyone up. I like combining the two when I'm learning badminton. A group gives me someone to play against and shows me where a shot breaks down, then I can go back and practise the first step by myself until I feel ready to try the whole thing at the next session.

part3.prompt: What skills should children learn before they go to school?

answers.basic: I'd focus on everyday skills like taking turns, asking for help and looking after their things. Those habits make the first weeks of school a bit easier. For example, a child who can say they don't understand an instruction is already in a better position to get help. Being able to wait for a turn also makes shared activities feel fairer, so the teacher can spend more time helping everyone enjoy what they're doing.

part2.prompt: Describe a person you know who really likes taking photos
cuePoints: When and how you got to know him/her
And explain how you feel about him/her

answers.basic:
A friend I met through badminton loves taking photos. We got to know each other after joining the same group session in Shanghai. Most of us packed up as soon as the last game finished, but he asked if we could stay for a quick group photo. By the next morning he'd sent everyone a copy.

After that I began to notice how he did it. He'd spend a few minutes looking around when he arrived and sometimes move a couple of steps before taking a photo. On a walk in Shanghai, for example, he waited until the light reached one side of a shop window. I would have taken a quick picture and gone on, but he wanted to see what changed if he stayed there. When he showed me the result, I could understand what he'd been looking at, even though we'd been standing in almost the same spot.

He takes photos at sports halls, on walks and whenever he visits a new part of the city. I like the ones he takes while people are getting ready to play. Someone might be tying a shoe or looking for a shuttle, and somehow he catches the moment in a way that makes me remember the whole evening. I like that he notices things the rest of us walk past. I don't take many photos myself, so I'm always glad when he brings his camera.

part3.prompt: Some people don't mind others walking into their shot when they're taking photos.

answers.basic: I can see why. A few people in the background can make a street photo feel more alive. If I were taking a portrait, though, I'd probably wait for a clear shot. A market photo can feel a little empty if everyone steps aside and leaves the stalls looking deserted. At the same time, I'd pay attention to whether the person is just passing in the distance or has become the main subject, because I'd ask permission in the second case.

part3.prompt: Why do tourists like taking photos while they are travelling?

answers.basic: Photos help people remember little details from a trip. They also give travellers an easy way to show friends what a place looked like and what they did there. A small photo often brings back something that isn't in the picture itself, like how warm it was or who suggested stopping there. I notice that when I scroll through pictures later, because an ordinary meal can make me remember a trip just as clearly as the main attraction.

part3.prompt: Do you think it’s ok to take photos everywhere?

answers.basic: I'd check the rules first. Some museums and private spaces have limits, and I'd ask before taking a close-up photo of a person I don't know. Even where photos are allowed, I'd think about what's happening around me. Taking a quick picture of a street is usually quite different from pointing a camera at someone who is having a private moment, and it's easy to wait or choose another angle if they look uncomfortable.

part3.prompt: What kind of photos do people often take?

answers.basic: People often take pictures of meals, pets, family events and places they visit. They also photograph useful things, like a shop's opening hours, so they can look them up later. A lot of phone photos are little records that nobody else will ever see. I might take a picture of a notice at a badminton hall so I remember when it closes, then use the same camera to take a group photo after the last game of the evening.

part3.prompt: Why are some people keen on taking photos?

answers.basic: Some people enjoy looking for interesting light or a different angle. Others like having a record of daily life and seeing how things have changed over the years. For someone who enjoys the creative side, finding a good angle can turn a street they know well into something new. Someone else might take the same walk for years and enjoy having a record of a favourite shop or tree changing without paying much attention to how the picture is framed.

part3.prompt: When do people like taking photos?

answers.basic: People often take photos on holidays or at birthdays and family dinners. An ordinary day can be worth a picture too, especially when the light is good. I also see people take photos just before they go home, when it occurs to them that everyone is together in one place. At a regular badminton session we might forget completely, but if someone is visiting from another city, we're more likely to get everybody into the shot.

part2.prompt: Describe someone who is older than you that you admire
cuePoints: What kinds of things you like to do together
And explain how you feel about this person

answers.basic:
There's an older player I've met through badminton in Shanghai who I really respect. We got to know each other by turning up to the same regular session. The first time we played doubles together, I kept trying to hit hard. He just told me to leave a bit more room between us and watch where the other pair was standing.

It was a small suggestion, but it changed the way the next few points went. When I left him enough space, he could see the same opening I saw and take the shot without us getting in each other's way. Between games he explained that he watches where people move after they hit, because it gives him a clue about what might come next. I've tried to do the same since then. It gives me something useful to pay attention to, especially against players who can hit harder or move faster than I can.

We still enjoy playing doubles together when our schedules line up. I like talking about one or two rallies afterwards because he usually remembers a detail I've missed. What I admire is how calm he stays. If someone makes the same mistake three times, he can point it out in a way that makes them want to try again. As a coach myself, I know that takes patience. I always come away from a game with him with something useful to think about.

part3.prompt: What do old people usually do in their daily life?

answers.basic: It depends on their health and interests. Some older people go for walks or meet friends in the park. Others spend time cooking, reading or looking after grandchildren. In a neighbourhood park, for example, I often see people exercising together in the morning and stopping for a chat afterwards. Having somewhere nearby to go can make a big difference to the routine, especially for someone who enjoys meeting people but doesn't want to make a long trip.

part3.prompt: Why is there a generation gap between the young and the old?

answers.basic: They grew up with different technology and expectations. For example, younger people may text someone about a problem, while their parents would rather pick up the phone. The gap can also come from what was normal at work or at home when each generation was younger. If someone remembers how hard it was to change jobs, for example, they may give quite different advice to a younger person who sees changing jobs as a normal step.

part3.prompt: Has old people's life quality improved when compared to the past?

answers.basic: In many ways, yes. It's easier to find medical care and stay in touch with family now. Some older people still feel lonely, especially when their children live far away. A video call can be a real improvement for someone whose children live in another city, because they can see each other without arranging a trip. It still helps to have a neighbour to talk to in person, especially on a day when they need practical help with something nearby.

part3.prompt: What can young and old people learn from each other?

answers.basic: Older people can pass on practical skills and share what they've learned from setbacks. Younger people can help them use new technology and show them how daily life is changing. An older relative might show a younger person how they cook a family dish without measuring everything. The younger person could help them keep a video of the recipe so other relatives can use it, and both get something useful out of spending the time together.

part2.prompt: Describe a time when someone talked about something you were not interested in but you kept listening
cuePoints: And explain how you felt about the experience

answers.basic:
A friend once spent most of a subway ride telling me about a phone he was thinking of buying. We'd just finished playing badminton and I was pretty tired. He had several models open on his phone and wanted to compare the cameras and all the different settings. After the first few minutes, I was having trouble remembering which one he was talking about.

The trouble was that most of the differences sounded the same to me by that point. He'd move from one page to another and ask whether I thought a particular feature was worth paying for. I was listening enough to know he wanted an answer, but I couldn't have repeated half of what he'd said. I remember looking up at the station names and realising we'd still be on the train for a while. I decided to put my own phone away so I could at least give him my full attention and see what he was trying to decide.

I kept listening because I could see he'd put a lot of thought into it. Eventually I asked what he actually wanted to take pictures of. That turned out to be a question he was happy to talk about, and it made the conversation easier for me to follow. I was relieved when we moved on, but I'm glad I stayed with it. He needed someone to help him think aloud more than he needed someone who knew about phones.

part3.prompt: How can we tell if a listener is listening carefully?

answers.basic: A careful listener usually asks a question that relates to what you've just said. They can also sum up the main point, which tells you more than a polite nod. I pay attention to whether their next question picks up a specific detail, such as why I changed my mind halfway through a decision. Some people listen quietly without much eye contact, so what they say when it's their turn can be a better clue than how attentive they look.

part3.prompt: What would happen if the listener didn’t listen carefully?

answers.basic: They might miss a detail or give an answer that has little to do with the conversation. The speaker can also feel ignored and stop sharing. At work a missed detail can mean someone spends an afternoon doing the wrong task. In a personal conversation, the effect may be harder to see, because the speaker might carry on politely and simply decide to share less the next time they have something important to say.

part3.prompt: What kind of topics do young people like to talk about today?

answers.basic: People I know often talk about work, travel, sport or something they saw online. The topic usually depends on what the group has in common. With my badminton friends, we can spend ages talking about a shot because everyone knows why it was tricky. The same people might talk about a show or a place to eat in another group, where a sport they play every week would be harder to bring everyone into.

part2.prompt: Describe a time when you received good service in a shop/store
cuePoints: When you went to the shop
What service you received from the staff
And explain how you felt about the service

answers.basic:
I had a good experience at a badminton shop in Shanghai when I was looking for new shoes. I went in on a weekend because my old pair was wearing out, and I wanted to try a couple of sizes. I told the person helping me that I could feel my foot slide sideways when I changed direction.

Before suggesting anything, he asked how often I played and what I noticed towards the end of a long session. I hadn't thought to mention that my toes felt squeezed after I'd been moving for an hour, so that question helped narrow things down. He showed me how to lace one pair and asked me to stand up before deciding on the size. He gave me a bit of time to walk around by myself as well. I liked being able to notice how the shoes felt before hearing what he thought of each one.

He gave me enough room to take a few side steps in each of the two pairs. He also asked me to check whether my heel was lifting. One pair was more expensive, but the other felt better, and he said that was the one he'd choose for my feet. I was relieved because I'd been expecting the usual sales pitch. I left with shoes I felt comfortable moving in, and I remember thinking I'd go back there the next time I needed help.

part3.prompt: Can consumption drive economic growth?

answers.basic: Yes. When people buy more goods and services, businesses can get more orders and hire more staff. That works best when households can afford what they're spending. A small restaurant is a good example, because a steady increase in customers can justify adding another shift or buying more from a local supplier. If people are buying on credit they can't comfortably repay, though, that extra spending may be followed by a period when they have to cut back.

part3.prompt: What are the advantages and disadvantages of shopping online?

answers.basic: Online shopping is convenient, and it's easy to compare prices. The main drawback is that you can't try things first, so sometimes you end up sending them back. Reviews can help when lots of people mention the same thing, like whether a shoe runs small. They still can't tell me how the shoe feels on my own feet, so I might end up spending longer ordering and returning a pair than I would have spent trying it in a shop.

part3.prompt: What are the differences between online shopping and in-store shopping?

answers.basic: Online I can search quickly and read reviews. In a shop I can see how something fits or feels and take it home straight away. I often go online when I already know the model and want to see who can deliver it quickly. For a new racket, a good shop gives me a chance to ask how two options feel in use, which is more helpful to me than comparing a long list of measurements.

part3.prompt: Why do some people not like shopping in small shops?

answers.basic: Some small shops have a limited range or shorter opening hours. A few people also feel awkward browsing when the owner is standing right next to them. People who are short on time may also want to check several things in one trip, which is easier in a big store. A small shop can be excellent at one thing, but if you're picking up groceries, clothes and a charger at once, you might find that you need several stops.

part3.prompt: What are the advantages and disadvantages of shopping in small shops?

answers.basic: The service can feel more personal, and a local shop may stock things a chain doesn't carry. The trade-off is that prices and return policies can be less predictable. A badminton shop owner can remember what a regular player asked for last time, which saves a lot of explaining. I'd still check what happens if something turns out to be the wrong size, because that can be less straightforward when a shop has only one location or very little stock.

part3.prompt: Why are shopping malls so popular in China?

answers.basic: In cities like Shanghai, a mall can be a convenient place to eat, shop and meet friends in one trip. It's especially handy on a very hot or rainy day. A family can choose a restaurant while someone else looks for a particular shop, then everyone can meet without going back outside. Good subway access helps too, because it turns the mall into a useful meeting point even for people who just came to see friends.

part2.prompt: Describe a person who is good at making things by hand
cuePoints: What materials or technologies he/she uses
And why you think this person is good at making things by hand

answers.basic:
A friend of mine makes small wooden things at home. He's made a phone stand and a little rack for keys, and he sometimes makes something for a friend when he knows what they need. The pieces are simple, but when you pick them up you can tell he's taken his time.

The phone stand is a good example of how he works. It looks like a small piece of wood with a groove in it, but the angle has to be right if you want to see the screen while sitting down. He tried it on the desk before deciding how much wood to take away. Then he checked whether he could tap the screen without knocking the whole thing over. I thought that was an interesting way to make something, because every small change came from seeing how the object behaved when somebody actually used it.

He usually starts with leftover pieces of wood. He marks the shape in pencil, cuts it with a small saw and sands the edges by hand. I once watched him make a stand a little wider so a phone would fit with its case still on. That extra bit of work is what makes me think he's good at it. He tests things as he goes and notices details other people might leave for later. The things he makes feel like they belong in someone's daily life.

part3.prompt: Does art, like music or theater, have an impact on society?

answers.basic: Yes. A play or a song can get people talking about something they usually avoid. It can also bring people together when they enjoy the same performance. A play about a family disagreement can make people recognise a situation they've been in and understand the other person's side a little better. The conversation afterwards is often where the effect shows up, because people have a scene they can point to instead of having to start with a personal story.

part3.prompt: Is it good to have creative people in a team?

answers.basic: Yes, creative people can suggest a different way to solve a problem when the team gets stuck. It's useful to have someone who can turn that idea into a practical plan, too. If a team is trying to make a form easier to use, someone might ask whether half the questions need to be there at all. That suggestion is useful if the team can try it on a small example and see what would actually change for the people filling it in.

part3.prompt: What impact can artistic buildings have on society?

answers.basic: A distinctive building can give people a reason to explore an area. If the building is also useful, like a good public library, people may visit regularly and feel attached to it. A good building can change the way people spend time in a neighbourhood, especially if there's room to sit or something anyone can go in and do. A library with a bright reading room can draw people back long after they've got used to seeing its unusual shape from the street.

part3.prompt: Do children these days still like doing arts and crafts?

answers.basic: Many do, especially when they can choose what to make. A screen can show them how to fold paper or paint a model, and then they get to try it themselves. I think the pleasure is still there when children have enough time and can get hold of simple materials. Making a paper plane, for instance, lets them see immediately what a different fold does, and that can be just as absorbing as something they watch on a screen.

part3.prompt: Why do some children enjoy making things by hand?

answers.basic: They get to see an idea turn into a real thing. It feels good to show someone a model or a drawing and say, 'I made that.' Something like a cardboard model gives them lots of small decisions to make, from the shape to where the pieces go. If it falls apart, they can try another idea and see the difference themselves, which feels more satisfying than just being told what the right way is.

part3.prompt: Do you think art classes are important for children?

answers.basic: Yes. Art gives children time to make choices and try again when something goes wrong. It's also a way for quiet children to share ideas. A child who finds writing difficult might show what they've understood about a story by drawing one scene from it. I also like that art makes room for several good answers, because children can explain their choices and see how someone else took the same task in a different direction.

part2And3.title: 和朋友度过的愉快夜晚

part2.prompt: Describe an enjoyable evening you had with your friends
cuePoints: Who you spent the evening with
And explain why it was enjoyable

answers.basic:
One Friday evening, I met three friends at a badminton hall in Shanghai. We'd all had a long week, so we booked a court and decided to warm up while we waited for everyone to arrive. Once everyone was there, we swapped partners a few times and stayed until our booking ended. One rally went on so long that both pairs started laughing before it was over.

I remember the first game feeling a bit scrappy because everyone was still getting used to moving after sitting at work all day. Nobody minded much, and we kept changing sides until the games felt reasonably even. At one point somebody missed a very easy shot and tried to blame the lighting, which made the rest of us laugh. By the end of the session I'd completely forgotten what I'd been worrying about on my way there. One friend suggested noodles because the place was still open and we could walk there together.

Afterwards we went to a small place nearby for noodles. We were still talking about the game at first, and then the conversation wandered to work and weekend plans. I remember looking at the time and being surprised we'd been sitting there for over an hour. I enjoyed it because none of us had to make a big plan. We got to move around, eat something warm and talk without anyone needing to rush off.

part3.prompt: What are the differences between young people’s leisure time activities and those of old people?

answers.basic: Younger people may choose faster activities or go out later. Some older people prefer a walk or a chat in the park, although plenty of people enjoy the same sports at different ages. Some of it comes down to time and energy, because people have different routines at different stages of life. I see that at badminton, where someone in their twenties may want a fast game after work and an older player may prefer a quieter morning session with time to talk afterwards.

part3.prompt: What can we do to bring family members closer together?

answers.basic: A regular meal or a short walk together can give everyone time to talk. When people live far apart, a quick call can keep them involved in each other's lives. A shared activity helps because the conversation can start with something simple, like what to cook or where to go. If you're away from home, even a short call while you're walking back from work can give your family a better idea of what your ordinary week is like.

part3.prompt: How do people get along in a big family?

answers.basic: It helps if people agree on everyday things like chores and quiet hours. In a big family, giving people a bit of space matters as much as spending time together. For example, it helps to talk about who can use the kitchen when several people come home at different times. If there's a disagreement, I'd raise the specific problem early, because small habits are usually easier to change before everyone has spent weeks getting annoyed about them.

part2.prompt: Describe an activity you do regularly that you think is a waste of time
cuePoints: And explain why you think it is a waste of time

answers.basic:
I have a habit of scrolling through short videos after work. It usually starts when I sit down to answer a message or look up a badminton clip. If I'm already tired, it's easy to watch whatever comes next instead of deciding what I actually want to do.

It happens most easily on evenings when I get home without a plan. I sit down while I'm waiting for dinner or before I get ready for bed, and the next clip is already playing by the time I think about getting up. A lot of the videos are things I'd never look for on my own. I watch because they're short and I can always tell myself there's only one more. Occasionally I look at the time and realise that the gap I meant to fill has turned into a big part of the evening.

Some videos are useful. I sometimes save a drill I can try at the court. The problem is the extra twenty or thirty minutes after I've found what I came for. I put the phone down and can't remember most of what I watched. That annoys me because I'd been meaning to read a few pages or get to bed a bit earlier. These days I try to save the clip I want and close the app. It's a small thing, but it makes the evening feel longer.

part3.prompt: Why do some people refuse to abide by rules?

answers.basic: Some people break rules because they think the rule is unfair or makes life harder for no good reason. Others simply copy the people around them. A rule is easier to follow when people can see who it helps and when it applies to everyone in the same way. If a player sees other people staying on a booked court after their time is up, for instance, it becomes harder to see why they should leave on time themselves.

part3.prompt: What kinds of things make people feel pressured?

answers.basic: Deadlines, money worries and comparing yourself with other people can all create pressure. It gets worse when several problems arrive at the same time. Sometimes it's the uncertainty that makes a problem feel heavy, like knowing something is due but having no idea how long it will take. I feel more in control if I can name one thing to do next, even if I still have several other things to deal with later.

part3.prompt: Will you continue doing something when you are aware that it’s a waste of time?

answers.basic: I might keep doing it for a while if it has become a habit. Once I notice that, I try to replace it with something I actually enjoy, like playing badminton. With short videos, I find that the first useful clip makes it easy to justify watching another five. If I save what I came for and leave my phone by the door while I make dinner, I have a better chance of spending the rest of the evening the way I intended.

part3.prompt: How do you balance life and work?

answers.basic: I try to finish the main work task before I leave. Having a badminton session booked after work helps me stop checking messages and switch off. I also try to be realistic about how much I can fit into one evening. If I've had a difficult day at work, it helps to have either a short game or a quiet night planned, so the time outside work actually feels like something I get to choose.

part2.prompt: Describe a crowded place you went to

answers.basic:
I went to a weekend food market in Shanghai with a friend one Saturday afternoon. We had planned to walk through and pick up something to eat. By the time we got there, the narrow space between the stalls was so full that we had to keep stopping every few steps.

From the entrance we could smell something cooking before we could see which stall it came from. It took a while just to get close enough to read the signs, and if one person stopped to order, everybody behind them had to squeeze past. My friend spotted something he wanted and pointed across the path, but a group came between us before I could see what he meant. We tried staying together for a few minutes after that. By the time we reached the middle, my friend wanted to try a stall on the other side and I wanted to get a better look at the food near us.

We split up for a few minutes to look at different stalls and immediately lost sight of each other. After that we agreed to meet beside a drinks stand that was easy to spot. We bought a couple of snacks, found a quieter spot outside and shared them there. The food was good, and I liked watching the people coming out with bags in both hands. I would probably go earlier next time. It would be nice to see what was on sale without feeling that I had to keep moving.

part3.prompt: Do you think it is a good trend to have more big cities?

answers.basic: Big cities can offer more jobs and better transport. I think growth makes sense when housing and public services grow with them, so daily life stays manageable. A city like Shanghai gives people more choice about where to work and what to do in their free time. If it becomes hard to find an affordable place within reach of those jobs, though, people can end up spending so much time commuting that they see very little of those benefits.

part3.prompt: Do you think there are some people who enjoy crowded places?

answers.basic: Yes. Some people enjoy the energy of a full stadium or a night market. Being surrounded by people can make an event feel more exciting. At a close sports match, hearing people react to the same point can make the whole thing feel bigger. Someone who finds a crowded subway exhausting might still enjoy that, because they chose to be there and the people around them are paying attention to something they care about.

part3.prompt: Why do people go to crowded places?

answers.basic: Sometimes they have to, like on the subway at rush hour. Other times the crowd is part of the fun, for example at a match or a festival. It also matters whether there's a good reason to go at that particular time. A busy food market might have several stalls you can't find elsewhere, and people can be willing to wait if the visit is something they've looked forward to all week and they can go with a friend.

part3.prompt: Will people use bikes more or less in cities in the future?

answers.basic: I think more people will cycle for short trips if cities build safe routes. Where the roads feel dangerous, people will probably stick with the subway or the bus. For example, if someone can ride from their apartment to a station without having to mix with fast traffic, a bike may save time. Having somewhere easy to leave it matters too, because even a good route feels less useful if you're worried about the bike once you arrive.

part3.prompt: Will there be more or less green space in cities in the future?

answers.basic: I hope there'll be more. Large parks take space, but cities can still plant trees along streets and turn small unused areas into places people can sit. A city could also make the green space it already has easier to reach, for example by adding crossings or opening another entrance to a park. To me the important question is whether people can get somewhere green on an ordinary afternoon, because that affects how often they actually use it.

part3.prompt: Which cities are overcrowded in your country?

answers.basic: Some parts of Shanghai and Beijing feel very crowded at rush hour. In Shanghai, the difference between a busy interchange and a quiet residential street can be quite striking. Part of the issue is that many people are trying to reach the same places at the same time. On a weekday evening, for instance, a station where several lines meet can be packed, and walking a little farther from the main route can make the area feel completely different.

part2.prompt: Describe a person who learns history and loves history
cuePoints: And explain how you feel about him/her

answers.basic:
A friend I know through work enjoys reading about the history of Shanghai. He sometimes visits an old street or a small museum at the weekend. Then he looks up what used to be there and compares old photos with what he saw in person. He's shown me a few pictures on his phone when we've walked past a building together.

One time he showed me a photo of a street I'd walked down earlier that week. I recognised the corner from the shape of one building, even though the shopfronts and the way people were getting around looked completely different. He'd found the picture after noticing a small detail on the building that made him curious about its age. He went back another day to check which parts were still there. I would normally have walked past without looking up, so it was interesting to see how one question had sent him back to a place we both knew.

I asked him once why he spends so much time on it. He said he likes finding out what ordinary people did in places he already knows. I can see the appeal. The street you walk down to get lunch feels different once you know what was there fifty years ago. I like listening to him because he tells one story at a time. I usually remember it the next time I'm in the area.

part3.prompt: Besides big historical events, what else is important when learning history?

answers.basic: It's worth learning what ordinary people ate, how they travelled and what work they did. Those details make it easier to picture the period. An old photo of a street can tell you something about how people got around and what they could buy nearby. Those ordinary details also help explain bigger events, because you get a better idea of what a change meant to a family trying to get on with daily life.

part3.prompt: Do you think people should learn ancient history before learning modern history?

answers.basic: A rough timeline helps, but people can begin with whichever period interests them. A modern event often gives them a reason to go back and look at what came before it. For example, someone who is curious about how their city looks today might start with an old photo of a street they know. Once they have a question they actually want answered, they're likely to remember earlier events better because those events help them make sense of something familiar.

part3.prompt: Is it important to learn how people in the past lived their lives?

answers.basic: Yes, because daily life shows what people had to deal with. Comparing how families travelled then and now can make a big change easier to understand. A child can understand what a new railway meant if they first hear how long a visit to relatives used to take. I like examples like that because they put the dates into a story about a real choice, like whether people could afford the time to travel at all.

part3.prompt: How do children learn history before they attend school?

answers.basic: They can hear stories from relatives, look at family photos or visit a museum with their parents. Those experiences give them a first idea of how life changes over time. A grandparent might show a child a photo of their old school and explain why everybody dressed differently. The child is likely to ask about something they recognise, like the playground, and that one question can be enough to get a conversation going about how life used to be.

part3.prompt: At what age do you think people should begin to learn history?

answers.basic: I'd introduce simple stories around primary school age. Dates and more complicated ideas can come later when children have more context. I'd start with short stories about a person or a place they know, because that gives them something to picture. Once they can put a few events in order and connect them to a place they've visited, they can start asking bigger questions about why things changed and what different people thought at the time.

part3.prompt: Do you think children should begin learning history from an early age?

answers.basic: Yes, if it starts with something close to them. Finding out what school was like for their grandparents is a good way to get curious. It could be as simple as walking past an old shop and talking about what was there before. I think that kind of history is easier to remember at first, because the child can compare the story with what they see in front of them on the way home.

part2.prompt: Describe a person who taught you a new skill
cuePoints: And explain how you felt about this person

answers.basic:
I'd talk about a coach whose badminton lessons I watch online. He helped me understand how to take the first step when moving back for a shot. I used to concentrate so much on getting to the back of the court that I hardly thought about what my feet were doing at the start.

I'd watched other demonstrations before and could recognise what a good version looked like, but that didn't tell me why my version felt rushed. In this lesson, the coach let the clip run at normal speed first so I could see the whole problem. Then he slowed it down and showed where the player was before the shuttle went up. That made me notice that my first move was often taking me slightly away from where I needed to go. For the first time I knew what to watch for when I tried it again.

What I liked about his lesson was that he separated the movement into stages. He showed the first step on its own, explained what it was for, and then put the rest of the movement back in. I paused the video and tried that first part slowly the next time I went to the hall. I was grateful for the way he explained it. It made the skill easier to learn, and it changed how I coach. Now I ask myself which part a student needs to see first.

part3.prompt: Why is self-discipline important when learning a new skill?

answers.basic: Progress comes from regular practice. When I work on a badminton shot, short sessions spread across a few weeks help me build a more reliable movement. It's easy to feel motivated when you first see someone do a skill well, then get discouraged when it takes longer than you expected. Keeping a regular time to work on one small thing helps you notice progress, because you can compare what felt difficult last week with how it feels today.

part3.prompt: What are the differences between learning from a teacher and learning by oneself?

answers.basic: A teacher can spot an error you don't notice and give you something specific to work on. Learning alone gives you more control over the pace and schedule. If I'm practising by myself, I can pause a video and repeat the same movement until I have a question about it. A teacher can then help me find out whether the part I'm focusing on is really what's causing trouble, which can save a lot of practice in the wrong direction.

part3.prompt: How do adults learn a new skill?

answers.basic: Most adults learn when they have a clear reason to. They might watch a lesson, try it on a real task and ask someone for feedback when they get stuck. I often learn a new tool for work by trying to use it on one small problem first. If I can get it to do something useful, I have a better reason to read the instructions and a clearer idea of what to ask when I need advice.

part3.prompt: How can parents and teachers teach children new skills?

answers.basic: I'd show one small step, let the child try it and point out one thing they did well. Then I'd give them another go with one simple correction. On court, for example, I'd have a beginner practise the grip before asking them to think about their feet as well. Once they feel what the grip is supposed to be like, they can use that feeling to check their own movement, and the next instruction is easier to take in.

part3.prompt: Where can children learn new skills?

answers.basic: They can learn at home, at school or through a sports club. Playgrounds are also good places to practise things like taking turns and working with other children. What matters is whether they get a chance to use what they've been shown. At home they can help make a simple meal, while a sports club gives them a different kind of practice, because they have to listen and work with people who may do things a little differently.

part3.prompt: Why should children learn new skills?

answers.basic: New skills give children more ways to spend their time and solve problems. Finding something they're good at can also make them more confident. It's useful for children to have the experience of being a beginner and getting a little better with practice. When a child finally manages to keep a rally going, for instance, they have a real example of progress they can remember the next time something feels too difficult at first.

part2.prompt: Describe your least favourite movie
cuePoints: And explain why it’s your least favourite movie

answers.basic:
One film I really didn't enjoy was a science fiction film I watched at home one Saturday night. I can't remember the title now, but it was about a rescue crew looking for people on a damaged spaceship. I thought it would be interesting to see how they made decisions with very little information.

At the beginning, the crew received a message and had to decide whether they had enough time to reach the ship. I liked that part because it gave them a choice that seemed to matter. Once they arrived, though, the film kept adding another emergency before the previous one had been explained. There was a scene where someone went back for a piece of equipment, and I couldn't tell why it was worth the risk. By then I was mostly waiting for the film to slow down long enough to let me understand what was happening.

In the end, most of the film was people running down dark corridors while something went wrong behind them. The characters hardly had time to talk, so I never got to know any of them well enough to care what happened. I remember pausing it to get a glass of water and realising there was still nearly an hour left. I like science fiction when it gives me an idea to think about afterwards. With this one, I mostly remembered how loud it was.

part3.prompt: Can movies help people better understand the cultural background of a country?

answers.basic: Yes. Films can show how people speak to relatives, what they eat and how a neighbourhood feels. I'd watch more than one film to get a fuller picture. For example, a scene at a family dinner might show who serves the food and how people talk to someone older. Those details can give me questions to ask, and seeing them in several different stories helps me remember that one family on screen only represents one way of living.

part3.prompt: Are movies more likely to help people become more creative than books?

answers.basic: Both can help in different ways. A film can inspire someone with sound and images, and a book gives readers space to imagine how a scene looks for themselves. A film can make me notice how music changes the mood of a scene, which might give me an idea I can use somewhere else. With a book, I do more of the work myself, like imagining what the room looks like from only a couple of details on the page.

part3.prompt: What are the differences between watching movies at home and in a cinema?

answers.basic: At home you can pause, get a snack and watch whenever you want. A cinema has a bigger screen and fewer distractions, which helps you get into the film. At home I'm much more likely to check my phone when the story takes a while to get going. In a cinema, even hearing other people laugh can change the experience, although I'd still choose home if I wanted to stop and talk about the film as I watched it.

part3.prompt: What kinds of movies are the most popular in China?

answers.basic: Comedies and action films often draw a lot of attention, especially around holidays. Family films are also an easy choice when several generations go out together. I think it matters who people are going with as much as what kind of film they usually like. A comedy can be an easy choice for a group of friends, whereas when I watch something on my own I'm more likely to pick a story based on one subject I already enjoy.

part2.prompt: Describe a short trip you often take but do not like
cuePoints: And explain why you do not like the trip

answers.basic:
A short trip I don't enjoy is the subway journey I sometimes make from work to a badminton hall on a weekday evening. I go there to teach, and it's a good place once I arrive. The journey takes about half an hour on a normal day, but I often have to make a change during the evening rush.

I usually try to get everything into one bag before I leave work, because I know the change between trains can be tight. On a quiet day the walk between platforms is easy, and I can use the journey to think about what I want to teach. At rush hour I spend most of that walk watching where people are going. The bags, the announcements and the people coming from several directions all make it hard to settle down. Sometimes I arrive at the next platform and realise I've been holding my shoulders up the whole way.

The annoying part is carrying a racket bag through a crowded station. I'm always checking that it isn't in someone's way, and I sometimes have to wait for another train if the first one is full. I also like to get to the court a little early, so I keep an eye on the time more than I'd like. I still make the trip because I enjoy the lesson itself. The walk out of the station is usually when I start to relax.

part3.prompt: Which is better for knowing more about a country? Travelling or reading books about it?

answers.basic: I'd choose travel if I wanted to see how people live day to day. A book is better for background, so I'd read a little before going if I had the time. You can see things on a trip that are hard to imagine from a description, like how people actually use a public square on a weekday. A book can explain why the square is there in the first place, which can make what you see more interesting once you arrive.

part3.prompt: How much time do you think people should spend on a trip abroad?

answers.basic: I'd give myself about a week for a first trip if I could. That allows time to settle in, visit a few places and have a day without a full schedule. A longer stay makes more sense if you're crossing several time zones, because the first day may be spent getting used to the schedule. For a place a short flight away, I'd be happy with a few days in one city if I could spend the time walking around and trying local food.

part3.prompt: Who prefers travelling abroad? The young or the old?

answers.basic: Younger people may be more willing to try a cheap trip with a loose plan. Older people can have more free time, and many of them are just as interested in going abroad. I'd put more weight on money, time and confidence than on age alone. A younger person might be ready to take an overnight bus to save money, while an older person with enough time might book a slower trip that gives them a chance to see several places without rushing.

part3.prompt: Do Chinese people like travelling abroad?

answers.basic: Many do. Some want to try different food or see how people live elsewhere. Cost, time off work and the distance can affect where they actually go. For example, a family with only a few free days might choose somewhere close enough to reach in one flight. Someone who's been saving for a particular trip may be willing to travel much farther, because seeing the place is the main reason they're taking the time off.

part2.prompt: Describe a popular person
cuePoints: What kind of person he or she is
And explain why you think this person is popular

answers.basic:
There's someone I often see at a regular badminton session who seems to know everyone. He's usually there when I arrive at the weekend. If a new player is standing by the door looking unsure, he'll go over, ask their name and find them a game. He does it so casually that they don't feel like they're being singled out.

I saw him do it one evening when a new player came on their own and spent most of the warm-up watching. He asked if they'd like to do a few easy rallies with him, then brought two more people over once they felt comfortable. A little later they were laughing and working out who would serve next. He didn't make a big deal of helping, so there was no awkward moment where everyone had to stop and pay attention. He was just making room for another person, which is something he does pretty regularly.

I think that's the main reason people like him. He's quite a good player, but he's just as happy to have a relaxed game with someone who's learning. He also remembers who's coming back after a break and asks how they're getting on. When he can't make a session, people usually ask where he is. I can understand that. The atmosphere is a little warmer when he's there, especially if you don't know many people yet.

part3.prompt: Why do people want to be popular?

answers.basic: Being popular can make people feel accepted and give them more chances to meet others. Some people also like knowing that others pay attention to their ideas. That can matter in practical ways as well as emotionally, because being known makes it easier to invite people to something. At a sports club, for instance, the person who knows everyone can often get a game going, and seeing people turn up makes them feel like they belong there.

part3.prompt: Is it easier to become popular nowadays?

answers.basic: It's easier to get noticed through social media. Staying popular is harder because there is always something new for people to look at. Someone can reach thousands of people with one funny clip, even if they had no audience the day before. Keeping those people interested takes more work, because one clip gives them very little reason to remember your name unless you keep making things they actually want to see.

part3.prompt: What are the qualities of being a good teacher?

answers.basic: A good teacher explains things clearly and notices when someone is confused. When I coach badminton, I find that one correction a player can actually try is often enough. With a badminton beginner, I might ask them to show me what they just tried so I can see where the instruction stopped making sense. The ability to change your explanation matters, because a student who didn't understand the first example may pick it up quickly from a simpler one.

part3.prompt: Do you think good teachers are always popular among students?

answers.basic: No. A teacher who gives demanding feedback may be unpopular at first, and students may appreciate the same teacher later when they can see their progress. A teacher who asks students to rewrite a weak answer might seem strict in the moment. If the feedback is clear and the next answer is easier to write, those students may appreciate the effort later, even if they weren't happy to be given the extra work at the time.

part3.prompt: Is it important for a teacher to be popular?

answers.basic: It helps if students feel comfortable asking questions. I'd put being fair and explaining things well ahead of being everyone's favourite teacher. For instance, a student may like a teacher because they tell funny stories, but that doesn't necessarily help the student understand the next chapter. A quieter teacher who explains a confusing idea and takes questions seriously can make just as much of a difference to how the class feels about learning.

part3.prompt: Why are some students popular in school?

answers.basic: Some are outgoing and make an effort to include others. Others get noticed because they're good at a sport or something the school values. I remember that the people who got everyone involved were often the ones you wanted to see outside class as well. Being good at a sport can get someone noticed early on, but inviting others to join in gives them a reason to stay interested after the match is over.

part2.prompt: Describe a successful sportsperson you admire
cuePoints: What he/she is like in real life

answers.basic:
A sportsperson I admire is Lin Dan. He's a Chinese badminton player and won Olympic gold in men's singles twice. I started playing when I was ten, and later I watched clips of his matches to see what a really good player does when the other person is putting him under pressure.

One thing I look for when I watch is what he does after a shot that doesn't go as planned. It's easy to admire a great winner, but I learn more from the way he gets back into position and gives himself another chance. I remember replaying a short rally because I thought he'd rushed to the back of the court. The second time I noticed how early he seemed to read the other player's movement. It made sense that he looked so calm, because he'd done some of the work before the shuttle even arrived.

The thing I notice is how much time he seems to have. He can keep a rally going at one pace and suddenly change it when he sees an opening. I don't know him personally. In interviews, he comes across as quite direct when he talks about his game, and on court he looks very focused. Winning Olympic gold twice is a remarkable achievement. What sticks with me when I go back to those matches is how clean his basic movements look, even when the score is close.

part3.prompt: Why are there so few top athletes?

answers.basic: At that level, athletes need years of practice, good coaching and the chance to compete. Even talented people can be held back by an injury or a lack of time. Reaching the top also means performing well against other people who've made the same commitment. A badminton player can be the strongest person in their local club and still need years to get used to facing people who react faster, move differently and know how to take away their best shot.

part3.prompt: What is the most popular sport in your country?

answers.basic: I'd say basketball is one of the most widely played sports in China. Badminton is very popular too, and I like that people can keep playing it at different ages. Basketball is easy to see at schools because a court can serve a lot of people through the day. Badminton fits a different routine for me, since I can book a hall in the evening and get a good game even if only one other person can make it.

part3.prompt: Is it easy to identify children’s talents?

answers.basic: Sometimes it shows early, but children develop at different speeds. I'd give them time to try several sports and see what they enjoy and keep improving at. A child who looks average at first might just have had fewer chances to practise. In a badminton lesson I notice who keeps trying a movement after a mistake, because if they're still curious after a difficult session, they may improve much more over the next few months than you'd expect.

part3.prompt: Is talent important in sports?

answers.basic: Talent can help someone learn faster at the start. Over time, regular practice and the ability to handle setbacks make a big difference too. Someone with good timing might find it easier to return a fast shot on their first day. After a while, though, they still need to build a movement they can repeat under pressure, and that takes the kind of practice where you pay attention to what happens on the days you play badly.

part3.prompt: What qualities should an athlete have?

answers.basic: I'd put patience and consistency near the top. An athlete has to repeat basic movements and stay calm enough to think clearly when a match is going badly. I'd also add being willing to listen when someone points out a weakness. A player who's used to winning a certain way may need to change when they meet a stronger opponent, and being able to try a new approach without losing confidence makes a difference across a whole season.

part3.prompt: Should students have physical education and do sports at school?

answers.basic: Yes. School sport gives children a chance to move regularly and try an activity they might enjoy for years. There should be options for people who prefer different kinds of exercise. For example, a child who avoids competitive team games might enjoy swimming or playing badminton with a friend. Giving them a few options makes exercise feel like something they can choose to keep doing later, which matters much more than whether they win a match while they're at school.

part2.prompt: Describe a building you enjoy visiting (e.g. a library, a shopping mall, etc.)
cuePoints: And explain why you enjoy visiting it

answers.basic:
I enjoy visiting a public library in Shanghai that I found while looking for somewhere quiet to read. It's a short walk from a subway station. From outside it looks quite plain, but inside there are high ceilings and long tables by the windows. The light is good enough that I can sit there for an hour without getting tired of looking down at a page.

I first went inside on an afternoon when I only meant to stay for a short while. There was space to walk around without having to squeeze past people, and I found a table where I could see the trees outside. I remember opening my notebook and being surprised at how quickly I stopped thinking about the trip there. There wasn't much to distract me once I sat down. Now I know which part of the room I like best, so I can get on with reading instead of spending the first twenty minutes trying to settle in.

I usually take a book or a few English notes and find a spot away from the entrance. At home it's easy to open my laptop and get distracted by something I meant to fix on my website. In the library I can get through what I came to read. I also like the quiet sound of other people working around me. It feels good to leave with a page of notes and the rest of the afternoon free.

part3.prompt: Do you think all old buildings should be demolished?

answers.basic: I'd look at each building separately. If it's safe enough to repair and people still use it, keeping it can give an area a sense of history. An old building near a main street can still be useful if the inside is adapted for something people need, like a library.
