If repairs would cost a lot and the place can no longer be made safe, I'd want people to be clear about the reasons before deciding what to do with it.

part3.prompt: Do you think old buildings are valuable?

answers.basic: Yes, old buildings can show what a place used to be like. They can also become useful spaces, like a library or a small museum, if they're looked after. For example, walking into an old public hall can give you a better idea of how people used to gather than seeing its picture in a book. A building becomes more valuable to the people around it when they can actually use it and form their own memories there.

part2.prompt: Describe a party for a special event that impressed you a lot
cuePoints: When and where it was held
What the party was held for
And explain why it impressed you a lot

answers.basic:
A party that stayed with me was a friend's birthday dinner in Shanghai. It was held on a Saturday evening in a small private room at a restaurant. There were about ten of us, including a few people I'd met through badminton. We ordered dishes to share and spent a long time talking before anyone even thought about bringing out the cake.

The meal had started like a fairly ordinary birthday dinner, with people arriving a few at a time and trying to work out who knew whom. I sat next to someone I usually only see on court, so it was nice to hear what they did outside badminton. The person who had brought the photos had kept them on a phone until everybody was there. I remember thinking they were just going to show us one picture. Instead, people started leaning closer to see which year each photo was from, and the whole table got involved.

What made it memorable was that one friend had put together a few photos from different years. Some were from ordinary days our friend had almost forgotten. Everyone had a different memory of when a photo was taken, so we kept interrupting each other to fill in the details. The birthday person laughed so much they had to wait before blowing out the candles. I liked how personal it felt. It took more thought than simply booking a table.

part3.prompt: What special events are celebrated in your country?

answers.basic: People celebrate weddings, birthdays and family milestones. During the Spring Festival, getting together for a meal is a big event for many families. A wedding is a chance for two families to meet and spend time together. At the Spring Festival, the occasion can be more about coming back to the same table each year, where even a dish someone makes in the usual way can remind everyone of the last time they were together.

part3.prompt: Do most people prefer to hold a party in a restaurant or in a pub?

answers.basic: I'd say a restaurant is more common for a family celebration because it's easier to serve a full meal. A pub might suit a small group of friends. A restaurant is easier when you're inviting people of different ages and want them to sit and talk over food. A pub can work well for friends who only plan to stay for a drink, especially if they already know the place and can come and go when it suits them.

part3.prompt: Do most people prefer to hold a party in a public place or a private place?

answers.basic: Some prefer a private place because they can talk freely and set their own schedule. A public venue is convenient if there's a big group and nobody wants to host at home. I'd probably book somewhere for a large celebration, because there's room for everyone and fewer things for the host to take care of during the party. For a small dinner with friends, I'd enjoy being at home, where we can stay at the table as long as the conversation lasts.

part3.prompt: When do people like to hold a party?

answers.basic: People often choose weekends or holidays when guests are free. For a birthday, the nearest Saturday can be easier than the actual date. If you're inviting people who work different hours, getting a date early can matter more than picking a special venue. A Saturday afternoon might suit a family with children, while an evening after work can be easier for a few friends who are already in the same part of town.

part2.prompt: Describe a person whose health and fitness you have helped to improve
cuePoints: And explain whether it was easy or difficult

answers.basic:
I'd talk about a beginner who wanted to get more active and came to me for badminton coaching. They spent a lot of the day sitting and wanted an activity they could look forward to. They got out of breath quite quickly at first, and trying to cover the whole court made it hard to enjoy the game.

They told me they liked the idea of playing a real game, but they didn't want to spend the whole lesson feeling like they were behind. I asked what felt hardest in the first few minutes, and they said it was trying to move and think about the racket at the same time. That gave me something clear to work with. I could make the area smaller and keep the shots predictable, so there was time to get back into position. We could then make one small change as soon as they felt ready for it.

We started with short rallies near the net and took breaks between them. I showed them one movement at a time and tried to keep the first sessions easy enough that they'd want to come back. After a few sessions they could keep a rally going for longer and were happy to practise between lessons. The hardest part for me was judging when to make things a little harder. It felt good when they asked if we could try another round. That was a better sign than anything I could have said.

part3.prompt: What effect does stress have on health?

answers.basic: When stress lasts a long time, it can affect sleep and make it harder to keep good habits. A stressful week can leave people with less energy to cook or exercise. For example, someone may stay up worrying about work, then wake up too tired for the walk they usually take before breakfast. If that happens repeatedly, they can lose some of the activities that would normally help them feel better, so the effect goes beyond how they feel at their desk.

part3.prompt: Which group pays more attention to health, young people or old people?

answers.basic: Older people may think more about regular check-ups and staying mobile. Younger people may focus on fitness or appearance, although a lot depends on what each person needs. At a badminton hall, I see some younger players check how much exercise they've done, while older players may pay more attention to how their knees feel after a game. Both are looking after their health in a practical way, because they're thinking about what will let them keep playing.

part2And3.title: 喜欢或不喜欢的高建筑

part2.prompt: Describe a tall building you like or dislike
cuePoints: And explain why you like/dislike it

answers.basic:
A tall building I like is Shanghai Tower in Lujiazui. It houses offices and has an observation area for visitors. I usually see it from across the Huangpu River, where it's easy to pick out among the other tall buildings. The outside is covered in glass and the shape seems to twist gently as it goes up.

I remember first paying attention to it when I was walking with someone by the river. We stopped because the top was just coming out of low cloud, and it looked quite different a few minutes later when more of the building came into view. I hadn't noticed how slowly the outline seems to turn when you follow it with your eyes. The buildings beside it look much straighter, which makes that shape stand out even more. I sometimes use it as a point to look for when I'm trying to work out which direction I'm facing by the water.

I like it best when I can see it from a distance on a clear day. Up close, a very tall building can look like a wall of glass. From the river you can see the whole shape and how it fits into the skyline. It also looks different depending on the light. Sometimes I'm just out for a walk and catch myself looking up at it again. It's one of the things that makes that part of Shanghai easy to recognise.

part3.prompt: Are there many tall buildings in your country?

answers.basic: Yes, especially in large cities like Shanghai. There are tall apartment blocks in residential areas and much higher office towers in some business districts. A tall residential building can put a lot of homes within a short walk of the subway, which is useful in a busy city. In smaller towns there's often more room to build outwards, so the height of the buildings can change quite a lot as you travel between places.

part3.prompt: What are the differences between those tall buildings in your country?

answers.basic: Some are designed for offices and have large open floors. Others are apartment blocks, where good light, lifts and shared spaces matter more to the people using them. An office tower might have a large entrance for people arriving around the same time in the morning. In a residential building, I'd notice different details, like how far I have to carry groceries from the lift and whether there is somewhere quiet to sit near the entrance.

part3.prompt: Why are different places laid out and designed differently?

answers.basic: Places have different needs and different amounts of space. A busy district near a subway station can fit more offices and flats, while an older street may keep its small shops. A street with lots of small shops needs room for people to stop and look around, which is different from an area designed for people changing trains quickly. The way each place is laid out can make those everyday activities easy or quite awkward, even if the buildings look good individually.

part3.prompt: What are the advantages of living in tall buildings?

answers.basic: On a higher floor, you might get more light and a better view. A large building can also put many homes near the same shops and transport. It can be convenient if there are enough lifts and the things you need are close by. For me, a good example would be getting home with a racket bag after a late lesson and being able to pick up dinner on the short walk from the station.

part3.prompt: Why do some people like to remodel and decorate their homes themselves?

answers.basic: They can choose details that match how they live. For example, they might set up a corner for working from home or add shelves exactly where they want them. If they use a room for work during the day and dinner at night, they might want furniture they can move easily. Doing some of the work themselves also lets them try a small change first and see what it feels like before they spend money on the whole room.

part3.prompt: What kind of interior design style do most people like?

answers.basic: I think many people like light colours and simple furniture because they make a room feel open. Personal touches, like photos or a lamp, can make it feel less plain. People living in a small flat may also choose furniture that can do more than one job, because it leaves more of the room free. I'd keep my own desk area fairly plain and let things like books or a favourite picture give it some character over time.

part2.prompt: Describe an interesting video
cuePoints: When and where you watched it
And explain how you feel about it

answers.basic:
I watched an interesting badminton video at home one evening after work. It was from the online coach I follow. He was explaining why a player kept arriving late to the back of the court. I'd been thinking about how to explain a similar problem in a lesson, so I wanted to see what he noticed.

The thing that caught my attention was how ordinary the first clip looked. The player reached the shuttle, so at normal speed it was tempting to assume they just needed to move faster. I watched it twice and still couldn't say where the problem began. The coach let us see the same movement from another angle, with enough space to watch the player's feet. I moved my phone a little closer and tried to work it out before he explained it. It was the first time I'd thought to look that early in the movement.

He replayed the movement slowly and asked viewers to look at the first step. Once I spotted it, I understood why the rest of the movement felt rushed. I liked that he gave me one thing to look for and enough time to see it for myself. I paused the video and wrote down how I'd explain it in my own words. It was only a small part of the lesson, but it was the bit I kept thinking about afterwards.

part3.prompt: What kind of videos do people in your country like to watch?

answers.basic: Short clips about food, comedy and daily life seem popular. People also watch longer videos when they want to learn something, like how to cook a dish or fix a device. I think short videos fit into gaps in the day, like the time you spend waiting for a train. For something practical, I'd look for a longer video, because if I'm learning a badminton drill I want to see the setup, the movement and what to do if it goes wrong.

part3.prompt: Which is more helpful, watching videos or reading books?

answers.basic: I'd use a video to learn a movement, like a badminton serve. A book is useful when I need to work through an idea at my own pace. With a serve, I can slow a clip down and see exactly when the racket makes contact. For an idea that has several steps, I like being able to keep a page open, go back to an earlier example and think about it for as long as I need.

part3.prompt: What skills can people learn from watching videos?

answers.basic: People can learn simple repairs, cooking and sport techniques. The important part is trying the skill yourself, because watching someone else can make a difficult step look easy. Someone learning to cook can pause after the first step, try it and check whether their food looks anything like what's on the screen. That kind of feedback is harder to get with a skill like singing, where it's useful to have somebody listen and point out what you can't hear yourself.

part3.prompt: Are there any differences between the videos that young people and old people like to watch?

answers.basic: There is plenty of overlap. Younger viewers might follow more short clips or gaming streams, while some older viewers use video for news, cooking tips or exercise. Part of the difference may be how people find the videos in the first place. Someone who follows gaming accounts will keep seeing more of those clips, and somebody who was sent a cooking video by a friend may go on to look for more recipes from the same person.

part3.prompt: Are there any differences between the videos that young men and young women like to watch?

answers.basic: There may be some differences on average, but I'd expect interests to matter more. Two people who play the same sport may watch similar videos whatever their gender. For example, people I know who play badminton often send each other the same clips about footwork. The recommendations on each person's phone can also make a difference, because once you've watched a few videos on a subject, you're likely to be shown more of them whether or not that was your main interest.

part3.prompt: What makes a video go viral online?

answers.basic: It helps if the point is clear in the first few seconds. People also share clips that are funny or useful, especially if they immediately think of someone who would enjoy them. For example, a clip that shows a common mistake and fixes it in twenty seconds is easy to send to someone who makes that mistake. Timing matters as well, because if it arrives while lots of people are already talking about the same thing, it gives them a simple way to join in.

part2.prompt: Describe a boring place
cuePoints: And explain why you think it is a boring place

answers.basic:
A place I found quite boring was the waiting area in a shopping mall in Shanghai. I went with a friend who needed to get a phone repaired. We thought it would be quick, but the shop asked us to come back in an hour. We sat on a bench outside and talked for a bit while people went past.

At first we thought we might look around, but neither of us needed anything and the shops closest to us all seemed to sell the same sort of thing. We walked as far as the next set of lifts and ended up back on the bench. My friend didn't have his phone, so we tried guessing how long the repair would take without asking again. That got old quite quickly. People kept walking past with things to do and places to go, which made me more aware that we were just filling time until we could leave.

After a while we ran out of things to say. The same ad kept playing on a screen across from us, and there wasn't much to look at apart from the entrances to other shops. I kept taking out my phone to check the time. I think it felt especially dull because we were just waiting for something to happen. If I went back, I'd find a café or take a walk and set an alarm for when we needed to return.

part3.prompt: Why do most children think education is boring?

answers.basic: Children can lose interest if they spend too much time listening and can't see why a lesson matters. Giving them something to try can change how it feels. For example, a lesson about how things move is easier to get into if students can roll something across a table and see what happens when they change the angle. The activity gives them a reason to want an explanation, and that's when the information is more likely to stick.

part3.prompt: Why aren’t young people willing to listen to the experiences of older people?

answers.basic: Advice can feel like a lecture if it arrives before anyone has asked for it. Young people may listen more willingly when the story connects to a problem they actually face. Someone worried about a first job might want to hear how an older person dealt with being new on a team. That same advice could be irritating if the younger person was trying to talk about something else, because it would feel like the adult had decided what they needed before listening.

part3.prompt: What can people do when they feel bored?

answers.basic: They could take a walk, message a friend or try a small task they've been putting off. I often feel better once I've moved around a bit. I like choosing something small enough to start straight away, because being bored can make a bigger plan feel like too much work. A ten-minute walk often changes how I feel, and if I'm still restless afterwards I've at least worked out that I want something more engaging to do.

part3.prompt: Why are some teachers’ classes boring? Are there any solutions?

answers.basic: A lesson can drag when the teacher talks for a long time without checking what the class understands. A short activity or a real example can give students a reason to pay attention. For instance, a teacher can show two possible answers to a maths problem and ask the class to work out which one makes sense. Having to make a choice keeps people involved, and what they say gives the teacher a better idea of where they got lost in the first place.

part3.prompt: Why do some young people feel bored when talking with old people?

answers.basic: They may have few topics in common at first. Asking about something specific, like a first job or a favourite sport, can make it easier for both sides to join in. It can also feel one-sided if one person gives a lot of advice and never asks about the other person's life. A conversation about a first job can go much better when both people get to say what was difficult for them and compare the parts they recognise.

part3.prompt: Do most people think news about celebrities is boring?

answers.basic: It depends on the story. Some people enjoy a good interview, but a small rumour can feel pointless if it has nothing to do with the person's work. If an athlete talks about coming back from a difficult season, people who follow the sport may want to hear what changed. A story about where that same athlete went for dinner might interest a few fans, but it gives most readers much less to talk about or remember.

part2.prompt: Describe a time when you got up early
cuePoints: And how you felt about it

answers.basic:
I got up early to catch a train from Shanghai back to Hunan for a holiday. My alarm went off while it was still dark. I'd packed the night before, so all I had to do was get dressed, make sure I had my phone and keys, and get out of the door.

Outside, the street was much quieter than I was used to, and for a minute it felt like I was leaving in the middle of the night. Once I got to the station, I found there were already quite a few people there with bags and breakfast. I checked the board twice because I hadn't been fully awake the first time. Then I sent a quick message home to say I was on my way. That was when I started looking forward to getting there, even though my main thought had been getting back into bed.

I chose an early train so I could get there in time to have a meal with my family. At first I was half asleep and kept wondering if I'd forgotten something. Once I was through the station and sitting by the window, I felt much better. I bought something warm to eat and watched the sun come up as we travelled. I wouldn't want to get up that early every day, but that morning I was glad I had a good reason to do it.

part3.prompt: Do you know anyone who likes to get up early?

answers.basic: Some people I meet through badminton like to play first thing in the morning. They say the hall is quiet and they can still use the rest of the day for other things. I can see the appeal because it's easier to hear your partner and practise the same shot for a while when only a few courts are in use. It also makes sense for someone with a busy weekend, because the game is finished before other plans start to compete with it.

part3.prompt: Why do people get up early?

answers.basic: Some have to start work or catch transport early. Others like having a quiet hour to exercise or do something for themselves before the day gets busy. There can be a big difference between getting up early because you have to and doing it because you like the extra time. Someone who wants a quieter training session can choose the hour that works for them, while a commuter may simply need to be on the first train.

part3.prompt: What kinds of occasions need people to arrive early?

answers.basic: It's sensible to arrive early for a flight, an exam or a job interview. Having extra time can help if you need to find the right room. For example, with a new exam venue I'd want enough time to find the entrance and settle down before the start. Being a little early also means a small delay on the subway doesn't turn into the thing I'm thinking about when I should be concentrating on the exam.

part3.prompt: Why do some people like to stay up late?

answers.basic: Late at night may be the only quiet part of their day. Some people also stay up because they get caught up in a show or in a conversation with friends. An evening can feel like the first part of the day that belongs entirely to you, especially if you've been dealing with work or family plans. It's easy to keep going for another hour when you finally get to watch something you enjoy, even if you know you'll feel tired in the morning.

part3.prompt: Is it good to arrive early in any situation?

answers.basic: A few minutes early is useful for most appointments. For dinner at someone's home, turning up very early can put pressure on the host while they're still getting ready. For a job interview I'd get to the area early, then wait nearby until it's close to the agreed time. The same idea works with a visit to a friend's home, because I get the benefit of having extra time and they still get the time they expected to prepare.

part3.prompt: What kind of people like getting up early?

answers.basic: People who enjoy quiet mornings or who have a regular morning routine often get up early. Others do it because of work or family commitments. Some people find it easier to focus before their phones start going off, so they use the morning for reading or exercise. People who work or coach late may get a better start a bit later, because the routine that suits them depends on what the rest of the day looks like.

part2And3.title: 喜欢在家 / 花园种菜的人

part2.prompt: Describe a person who loves to grow plants (e.g. vegetables, flowers) at home or in the garden
cuePoints: And explain why he/she loves growing plants

answers.basic:
A relative of mine in Hunan likes growing plants at home. She has a few pots of spring onions and chillies in a sunny spot. Whenever I visit, I notice that the pots have been moved around a little, depending on which ones need more light.

On one visit I asked her how she knew which pots to move, and she took me outside to show me where the sun reached in the afternoon. I hadn't realised how much difference it made to move a pot even a short distance. She checks the plants when she's already out there doing something else, so it fits quite easily into her day. If one isn't doing well, she tries a different spot and waits a while to see what happens. It's quite an ordinary routine, but she enjoys knowing which little changes made a difference.

She saves the root ends from the spring onions she buys, puts them in soil and waters them when the surface feels dry. When she's cooking, she'll step outside, cut a handful and bring it straight back to the kitchen. She likes having something fresh right there, and I think she also enjoys seeing a bit of progress every day. She'll point out a new chilli before she tells me anything else about the week. It makes her happy in a way I can understand. It's a small thing she's looked after herself.

part3.prompt: What are the advantages of growing vegetables or flowers at home?

answers.basic: You can pick a few fresh herbs whenever you need them, and flowers can make a small balcony feel more welcoming. Looking after plants can be relaxing too. A balcony with a few plants gives someone a reason to step outside and pay attention to something that changes slowly. It's practical as well, because if you only need a handful of spring onions for a meal, you can cut exactly that amount and leave the rest growing.

part3.prompt: Is it easy to grow plants at home?

answers.basic: Some plants are easy if they get enough light and you water them properly. It takes a bit of trial and error to find what grows well in your space. A sunny balcony may be fine for one plant while a dark room suits something quite different. I'd try one or two small pots first and watch what happens, because it can take a while to learn how often the soil actually dries out where you live.

part3.prompt: Do many people grow vegetables or flowers at home in your country?

answers.basic: Some families grow things like spring onions or flowers on a balcony. In a big city, I'd expect it to depend a lot on how much space and light people have. Back in Hunan I've seen people use a sunny corner for a few pots, even if they don't have a proper garden. In a Shanghai flat the setup may be smaller, but there can still be enough room for something like spring onions that you can cut when you're cooking.

part3.prompt: Why do some people like to grow plants?

answers.basic: It gives people something to look after and a small sign of progress each week. It can also be a good way to spend a few quiet minutes after work. For someone who spends all day looking at a screen, watering a pot or noticing a new leaf is a different kind of activity. There isn't much to hurry along, and I can see how it would feel rewarding to come back a week later and find something has grown.

part3.prompt: Why do some people prefer to grow their own fruits and vegetables instead of buying them from the market?

answers.basic: They enjoy eating something they've grown themselves, and they can pick it when they need it. For herbs, a small pot can be more convenient than buying a whole bunch. There's also the pleasure of deciding what to plant and watching it turn into something you can eat. Growing everything yourself would take quite a bit of time and space, but a couple of things you use often can make cooking feel a little more personal without much extra work.

part3.prompt: Do you think students should learn to grow plant?

answers.basic: Yes, even a small classroom pot could work. Watching a seed grow can teach students patience and help them understand where their food comes from. If students grow the same plant in different places, they can compare what happens when one gets more light. That gives them a small experiment they can keep coming back to, and it helps them see why looking after something for a few minutes each day can add up.

part2.prompt: Describe a new law you would like to introduce in your country
cuePoints: Whether this new law will be popular
How you came up with the new law
And explain how you feel about this new law

answers.basic:
I'd introduce a rule that requires employers to show a realistic salary range in job ads. I thought of it because someone can read a whole description, prepare for an interview and only then find out the pay is far from what they need. That seems like a lot of time for both sides to spend before discussing something so basic.

Imagine seeing two ads for fairly similar jobs and having no way to tell whether either fits your needs. You might spend a few evenings getting ready for an interview before you find out something that could have saved you the trouble. I would want the range to be fairly narrow and to mean something in practice. If the highest figure were only available in very unusual cases, the advert could explain what experience it was based on. That would still leave some room to talk about the offer after both sides know a bit more.

With the rule, an applicant could decide earlier whether the job was worth applying for. A company could still offer a different amount based on experience, but it would have to give people a useful starting point. I think applicants would welcome it. Some employers might find it awkward at first, especially if they've never shared that information. I'd feel good about a change that made the first conversation a bit more straightforward for everyone.

part3.prompt: What rules should students follow at school?

answers.basic: Students should arrive on time, respect other people and follow safety rules. I'd also expect them to hand in their own work and ask before borrowing things. A good rule should help make it clear what students can expect from one another. If everyone has to put shared equipment back after using it, for example, the next class can get started without waiting for a teacher to find something that should already be in the room.

part3.prompt: Do people in your country usually obey the law?

answers.basic: I think most people follow basic rules in daily life. How consistently a rule is followed depends in part on how clear it is and how fairly it's enforced. For example, people are more likely to follow a crossing signal when they can see that the traffic will stop and that waiting won't take very long. Clear signs and consistent behaviour around them can make following the rule feel like the ordinary thing to do.

part3.prompt: What kinds of behavior are considered as good behavior?

answers.basic: I'd count keeping your word, giving others space and taking responsibility when you make a mistake. Small things like waiting your turn matter too. In a shared space, good behaviour often means noticing how your actions affect people who didn't choose to be there with you. Playing a video through headphones on a crowded train is a small example, and the effect is obvious to anybody who has been stuck next to a loud speaker.

part3.prompt: Do you think children can learn about the law outside of school?

answers.basic: Yes. They see rules in action when they cross the street, use a library or play sport. An adult can explain the reason at the moment it matters. If a parent explains why cars and people have to take turns at a crossing, a child can see the purpose of a rule straight away. Later, the same child may start asking why some rules apply to everyone and who gets to decide how they should be enforced.

part3.prompt: What are the benefits for people to obey rules?

answers.basic: Shared rules help people know what to expect. On a road, for example, everyone is safer when drivers and pedestrians follow the same signals. Rules can save time as well as keep people safe, because each person can make a plan based on what others are likely to do. If everyone leaves a sports court when their booking ends, the next group can start on time without having to interrupt a game and negotiate.

part3.prompt: How can parents teach children to obey rules?

answers.basic: Parents can explain the reason and follow the rule themselves. If they ask children to put things away, it helps when they do the same. I'd start with something the child can see, like how much faster everyone gets out of the door if the shoes are in one place. Once they've experienced the benefit a few times, they're more likely to remember why the rule exists and follow it even when nobody is watching.

part2.prompt: Describe a friend from your childhood
cuePoints: Where and how you met each other
And explain what made you like him/her

answers.basic:
One of my childhood friends was a boy I met at school in Hunan. We first talked because we both wanted to play badminton after class. I was around ten when I started playing, and at that age we were mostly trying to keep the shuttle going for as long as we could.

We didn't have many ideas about how to practise at first, so we'd make up little games. One was seeing whether we could send the shuttle back to the same patch of ground without moving too far. We were both quite pleased when we managed a decent rally, even if we lost count halfway through. I remember that he was usually willing to keep playing after a mistake. If one of us missed an easy shot, the other would just pick up the shuttle and start again, so there was no reason to feel embarrassed about it.

We used to play whenever we found some space. When it got too windy, we'd put the rackets down and go buy a snack. Sometimes we argued over whether the shuttle had landed in, then forgot about it by the time we walked home. I liked him because he was easy to be around. If I was having a bad day, I didn't have to explain much. We could play for a while and I'd usually feel better. That's one of the things I miss about being a kid.

part3.prompt: Do you still keep in touch with your friends from childhood? Why or why not?

answers.basic: Living in Shanghai makes it harder to see people I knew growing up in Hunan. A message now and then is a simple way to keep in touch, even when both sides are busy. When I go back for a holiday, I sometimes send a message to see whether anyone else is in the area. It's harder to have the kind of regular contact we had at school, but getting together for a game or a meal can make it easy to catch up.

part3.prompt: How important is childhood friendship to children?

answers.basic: It's quite important. Friends give children someone to share little problems with and help them learn to take turns and make up after an argument. Children get to make some choices together without an adult deciding everything, which is useful practice for later. If two friends both want the same turn in a game, they can learn to work it out and find that a small argument doesn't have to spoil the whole friendship.

part3.prompt: What do you think of communicating via social media?

answers.basic: It's handy for making plans and sending small updates. For a serious conversation, I'd rather call so I can hear how the other person is feeling. I use group chats to arrange badminton because everyone can answer when they get a minute and we can all see the plan. For a personal conversation, tone matters more, and a call makes it easier to notice if somebody needs time to say what they're actually thinking.

part3.prompt: Do you think online communication through social media will replace face-to-face communication?

answers.basic: I think social media will stay useful, especially for friends who live apart, and people will still want to meet in person. Being in the same room still makes it easier to notice a pause, share a joke or do something together. For example, it's easy to send an old friend a photo of a court where you used to play, even if they're in another city. To find out how life is going for them now, I'd still enjoy having a meal together, where there's time for the conversation to move naturally.

part3.prompt: What's the difference between having younger friends and older friends?

answers.basic: An older friend may have useful experience with a problem you're facing. A younger friend may introduce you to a different way of doing something. Shared interests matter more to me than age. For example, someone who's been in the same line of work longer might help me put a bad week into perspective. A younger friend might show me a new way to learn a skill, and in both cases the friendship works better when people are curious about each other's ideas.

part3.prompt: Has technology changed people's friendships? How?

answers.basic: Yes. It's easier to keep a friendship going across cities, but a quick reaction can become a substitute for a proper conversation if people are busy. I can send someone a clip that makes me think of them even if we haven't talked for weeks, which is a nice way to keep a connection. If I want to know how they're really doing, though, I need to make time for more than a quick reply or reaction.

part2.prompt: Describe a person you know who would like to choose a career in the medical field (e.g. a doctor, a nurse)
cuePoints: When he/she started to think about that
What he/she would like to do
And explain why he/she would like to choose this career

answers.basic:
A younger cousin I'd known since we were kids told me she was thinking about becoming a nurse. She started seriously considering it towards the end of secondary school. Someone in the family had spent time in hospital, and she noticed how much calmer they felt when a nurse explained what was about to happen.

What struck me was that she remembered the small things people did for the family, like checking whether they understood an instruction before moving on. When she talked about it later, she was interested in how the nurses made people comfortable enough to ask questions. She also wanted to know what an ordinary shift was like, because she knew that one good experience could only show her a small part of the job. We talked about how she might find out more before deciding what to study. She seemed quite willing to take her time with the decision.

She told me she'd like to work in a hospital ward, where she'd get to see how people recover over several days. She's interested in the practical side of the job and in talking to people who are worried or in pain. I remember her saying she wanted to be useful when someone had no idea what to expect. I could see why the job appealed to her. She's the sort of person who'll wait while you ask the same question twice.

part3.prompt: Do you think being a doctor is easy or difficult?

answers.basic: I think it's difficult. Doctors need years of training, and they have to make careful decisions even when the day is busy or a patient is worried. They also have to explain complicated choices in a way that makes sense to someone who may be in pain or hearing the information for the first time. I think that combination of technical knowledge, good judgment and being patient with people is what makes the work particularly demanding.

part3.prompt: Do you think learning biology is interesting for children?

answers.basic: It can be very interesting for children. I'd start with things they can see for themselves, like how a plant grows or why their heart beats faster after running. For example, planting two seeds and watching what happens over a week gives children something to notice and talk about. Once they've seen a difference for themselves, learning the words for what happened can feel like a way to answer a real question instead of an exercise in remembering terms.

part3.prompt: Why do some children want to become doctors?

answers.basic: Some want to help people after seeing a doctor care for someone in their family. Others get interested in how the body works and want to learn more. Having a positive experience with a doctor can make that job seem like something a child could do one day. At the same time, once they get older and learn what's involved, their interest may change, so it helps to give them a chance to explore what the work is actually like.

part3.prompt: Do you think governments should put a large amount of money into medical research?

answers.basic: Yes, particularly for research that could improve care for many people. I'd want the funding to be shared across prevention and treatment and reviewed as results come in. Some projects take years to show results, and a private company may have less reason to pay for work that won't lead to a product quickly. Public funding can make room for those questions, as long as people can see how the money is being used and why the work matters.

part3.prompt: Why is some doctors’ pay high and others’ low?

answers.basic: Pay can vary with experience, specialty, location and the kind of hospital someone works in. Some roles also involve longer hours or harder-to-fill shifts. For instance, a post that requires years of extra training or a specialist who is difficult to recruit may come with higher pay. A difference in pay doesn't tell you how useful each doctor is to the people they see, because different roles solve different problems for the community.

part3.prompt: Do you think doctors should be paid more?

answers.basic: I'd support better pay where long hours and responsibility are poorly reflected. Workload and enough time to rest are worth improving alongside salary. If a hospital is struggling to keep people in a particularly demanding role, better pay may help experienced staff stay. I'd also ask why they're leaving, because if the main problem is that their shifts are constantly being changed, a pay rise alone may make very little difference to daily life.

part2.prompt: Describe a person you know who has a successful business
cuePoints: How you got to know him/her
Why and how he/she started the business
And explain why you think the business is successful

answers.basic:
I'd talk about the owner of a badminton shop in Shanghai. I first met him when I went in to have a racket restrung. He asked how often I played and what I wanted the racket to feel like, then talked me through a couple of options. I got the impression he'd had that conversation hundreds of times and still paid attention to the answer.

I went back another time because I wanted to understand why one setup had felt better in a game. He remembered the sort of thing we'd talked about and suggested I try a small change so I could feel the difference. I liked that he explained what to pay attention to, because it meant I could come back with a better question if it still felt wrong. After a few visits I realised I knew several players who did the same thing. The shop had become somewhere people went for advice as well as somewhere to buy equipment.

He told me he'd started by stringing rackets for people he played with. He found there were enough regular customers to rent a small shop, and now he also sells rackets, shoes and other gear. I think it's successful because people trust his advice and keep coming back. If I ask around at a court where to get a racket fixed, his shop comes up quite often. That says more to me than how big the shop is.

part3.prompt: Why do some people start their own business?

answers.basic: Some want more control over their work. Others notice a problem customers keep having and think they can build something better around it. A person who has worked in a sports shop, for instance, might notice that players keep asking for a repair service they can't get nearby. Starting a business gives them room to try that idea, and it also means they're responsible for finding out whether people will pay enough to keep it going.

part3.prompt: Should governments provide financial support to start-ups?

answers.basic: Some support can help, especially when a new idea needs time to be tested. I'd make the terms clear and check whether the money is actually helping the business develop. For instance, a small grant could help someone make an early version and try it with real customers. I'd want the next decision to depend on what they learn from that trial, so a useful idea has a chance to grow and money doesn't keep going into something people rarely use.

part3.prompt: Do most people prefer shopping at big stores or small stores?

answers.basic: For a big weekly shop, a large store can be convenient. A small shop can be a better choice when you need one thing quickly or want advice from someone who knows the product. I don't think the same person chooses one type of shop for everything. I might go to a large store if I need several unrelated things, then visit a small badminton shop for a particular racket because the owner can tell me how it feels compared with the one I already use.

part3.prompt: What makes a business successful?

answers.basic: A business needs to solve a real problem and give customers a reason to come back. It also needs enough control over costs to keep doing that. A local shop can do well by being especially useful to one group of people, such as players who need to get a racket repaired quickly. Repeat visits make it easier to know what to keep in stock, and that helps the owner avoid spending too much on things customers rarely ask for.

part3.prompt: What makes a business fail?

answers.basic: Some businesses run out of money before they find enough customers. Others grow too fast and stop giving people the good service that made them popular in the first place. A shop that takes on a much bigger space might suddenly need more staff and more customers just to cover its bills. If it hasn't worked out why people came in the first place, it can end up making the service slower while still trying to pay for the extra room.

part3.prompt: Is it easy to set up a new business in your country?

answers.basic: It depends on the type of business. Testing a small online service can be fairly simple, while opening a shop involves more money, staff and practical arrangements. For example, someone who gives lessons can test whether there is enough interest by booking a court one evening a week. If they want to open their own hall, the scale changes, because they need a place people can reach and enough regular bookings to pay for it.

part2.prompt: Describe a plan that you had to change recently
cuePoints: What made you change the plan
And how you felt about the change

answers.basic:
One weekend a few friends and I had planned to play badminton together in Shanghai. We'd all left the afternoon free, but we found out quite late that the court we'd expected to use was unavailable. We checked a few other halls and everything nearby was booked.

We spent a while looking at the booking apps because none of us wanted to give up on the game too quickly. Someone found a court farther away, but the only time was late enough that one of us would already have to be heading home. At that point it made more sense to ask what we could still do with the afternoon. We had all left the time free, and it would have been a shame to stay home just because one part of the plan hadn't worked. That got us talking about food instead.

Our new plan was to meet for an early dinner instead. One friend suggested a place we could all reach by subway, so we left our rackets at home and went there. At first I was a little annoyed because I'd been looking forward to playing all week. Once we sat down, I realised we hardly ever had that much time to talk during a session. We booked another court for the following week and spent the rest of the evening catching up. In the end I was glad we still met.

part3.prompt: Do people often change their plans?

answers.basic: Yes, especially when a plan depends on other people or the weather. I usually leave some room to move things around when I make weekend plans. A group might decide to go for a walk and then find that it's raining heavily when everyone is free. If they've already thought of somewhere to eat indoors, changing the plan doesn't have to mean giving up the chance to see each other, and there is less rushing around at the last minute.

part3.prompt: Would you tell others if you change your plan?

answers.basic: Yes, if the change affects them. I'd tell them as soon as I knew and suggest another time if we'd already agreed to meet. A quick message can stop another person from making a trip they no longer need to make. If we had booked a badminton court together, for instance, I'd say whether I could still help find another player, because my change affects what everyone else can do with the booking.

part3.prompt: Why do you think parents still make plans for their children nowadays?

answers.basic: Parents often know what needs to be arranged and want to give their children a good start. It helps to let children make more choices as they grow. Sometimes a parent sees things a child doesn't have to think about yet, like whether they can get home from an activity safely. Once those practical details are clear, the child can still have a say in what they do, which gives them some experience making plans of their own.

part3.prompt: How does technology help people make plans?

answers.basic: A shared calendar lets everyone see when they're free, and map apps help estimate travel time. It's also easy to tell people when a plan has changed. For a game after work, I can check the route to a hall and share it in the same chat where we decide who is coming. Everyone can work from the same information, although I still like confirming the time in one message so people can find it easily later.

part3.prompt: What kind of plans do people often make?

answers.basic: People plan trips, work deadlines and meals. Even a quick plan for when to do the shopping can make a busy weekend feel easier. Some plans are about saving time, such as shopping on the way home instead of making another trip. Others make it possible for people to get together, because if friends work different hours, it often takes a little planning to find an evening that suits everybody.

part3.prompt: Do you think people like the process of making plans more, or the moment of carrying them out?

answers.basic: I think planning is fun when you're choosing something like a holiday. For routine things, the best part is usually doing them and seeing that the plan worked. Looking through photos and choosing a place to visit can be fun in its own right because you get to imagine the trip before it happens. With a regular badminton booking, I spend as little time as possible on the arrangements and look forward to the moment we actually start playing.

part2.prompt: Describe a time when you worked in a group
cuePoints: And explain why you worked in the group

answers.basic:
At work I helped build a feature that needed changes on both the server and the screen people use. I handled part of the backend and worked with a frontend engineer and someone who tested the feature. We had to do it together because each person's work depended on what the others expected to happen.

Before writing much code, we walked through what somebody would do from the moment they opened the page. That helped us notice that we were making different assumptions about when a choice would be saved. I was thinking about what the server needed in order to store the information. The frontend engineer was thinking about what the person on the page would see if something was missing. The person testing it started asking what should happen if somebody went back and tried again. Having all three questions on the table gave us a better way to test the feature.

One problem came up when we tested what would happen if a user left a field empty. My part returned a general error, and the person working on the screen needed to know exactly what to show. We made a short list of cases and agreed on what the service would return for each one. Then we went through them together. I liked how quickly things moved once we were looking at the same example. A short conversation saved us from going back and forth all afternoon.

part3.prompt: Why do some people prefer to work by themselves?

answers.basic: Some tasks take concentration, and it can be easier to stay focused alone. People also like being able to decide their own pace and order of work. If I'm looking for the cause of a bug, for example, I often need half an hour without anyone asking me to switch to another task. Once I've made some progress, it can be useful to talk to the team, especially if someone else has dealt with a similar problem.

part3.prompt: What should a leader do to make team members want to follow him or her?

answers.basic: A leader should explain why the work matters and give people a chance to raise concerns. Following through on small promises also makes it easier to earn trust. A good example is telling the team which parts of a project can wait when the deadline is close. People are more likely to follow that decision if they understand the reason and have been able to point out anything important the leader might have missed.

part3.prompt: Should students learn to do group work?

answers.basic: Yes, because they'll probably have to work with other people later. Group work gives them a chance to practise sharing tasks and disagreeing politely. In a class project, somebody can have a good idea and still need to explain it in a way the group can actually use. It helps if the teacher gives everyone a role, so the same student doesn't end up doing all the work while the others watch.

part3.prompt: What group tasks are there in schools?

answers.basic: There are science projects, presentations and team games. A group can also plan a small event where everyone has a clear job to do. For a presentation, one student might find examples, another might organise the main ideas and a third might practise explaining them to the class. They still need to look at it together before they present, because the different pieces have to tell a story people can follow.

part3.prompt: What advantages are there for students experiencing teamwork at school?

answers.basic: They learn to explain their ideas and listen when another person suggests a different approach. They also see how their own work affects the rest of the group. For example, if one student is gathering information and another is making slides, they have to agree on what is worth including. That is a useful early lesson in doing work somebody else can pick up, which applies in many jobs even when each person has a separate task.

part3.prompt: How can you tell if a person is a good leader?

answers.basic: I'd look at how the team works when there's a problem. A good leader listens, makes a clear decision and takes responsibility for how it turns out. I'd notice whether people feel able to say something has gone wrong before it turns into a bigger problem. For instance, if a deadline is at risk, a good leader can help the team decide what can still be done instead of letting everybody spend the meeting guessing who is to blame.

part2.prompt: Describe an important decision that you made
cuePoints: What the results of the decision were
And explain why it was important

answers.basic:
One important decision I made was to start a personal website. I'd been learning things through work and badminton and wanted somewhere to share them. I also wanted to build a personal brand around the things I actually do. I thought about posting everything on social media, but I liked the idea of having my own place to keep longer notes and improve them over time.

What made me take the idea seriously was looking back at how I kept notes. Some were saved in chats and others were in files I hardly opened again. I wanted to see whether I could turn one of them into something that would still make sense to me a few months later. I tried writing about a small thing I'd learned and realised how much I enjoyed choosing the example and explaining it in my own words. The idea of keeping several of those pieces together made the website feel like something I would actually use.

I decided to start with a simple blog and see what I wanted to add once I'd used it for a while. Now I have a place to publish posts and build tools for my own practice. It also gives me a reason to explain what I've learned in a way someone else could follow. That matters to me because it's the same habit I value as a coach. Writing things down shows me which parts I still need to think about.

part3.prompt: Do you think children sometimes have to make important decisions?

answers.basic: Yes. Choosing whether to leave an activity or tell an adult about a problem can feel important to a child. They can make some decisions with a bit of support. Leaving a sports club, for example, can mean giving up a routine and seeing some friends less often. An adult can help a child think about those consequences, and the child can still say whether they want to try a different group or take a break.

part3.prompt: What important decisions do teenagers need to make after graduation?

answers.basic: They may need to choose between more study and work, or decide which subject to focus on. Some also have to consider whether they're ready to move away from home. For example, a course that looks interesting might be in another city, so they have to think about living costs and being away from people they know. These choices can feel hard because a teenager is often deciding what kind of day-to-day life they want without having tried it yet.

part3.prompt: Who can children turn to for help when making a decision?

answers.basic: Parents, teachers or another adult they trust can help. A good person to ask will listen first and help the child think through what might happen. A parent might know more about practical things like costs, while a teacher may be able to explain what a new course involves. If a child can hear both views and say what worries them, they have a better chance of making a choice that feels like their own.

part3.prompt: Do you think advertisements can influence our decisions when shopping?

answers.basic: Yes. An ad can make a product feel familiar, so it comes to mind first when we're shopping. A limited-time offer can also make people rush. If I've seen the same pair of shoes several times before I walk into a shop, I'm more likely to recognise it and pick it up. Whether I actually buy it will depend on things like fit and price, so advertising can influence which choices I consider without deciding everything for me.

part3.prompt: Do you think the influence of advertising is good?

answers.basic: It can be helpful if the ad explains a feature or lets you know about a real offer. It becomes less useful when it creates pressure or leaves out important details. For example, a video that shows how a product works can help me decide whether it's worth trying. I get more cautious if the advert keeps telling me to buy immediately, because a little time to check the details can change how good the offer seems.

part3.prompt: How do people usually make important decisions?

answers.basic: People often talk to someone they trust and compare a few options. I find it helpful to think about what each choice would look like on an ordinary day. When I was thinking about coaching alongside my job, I had to picture what an evening lesson would feel like after a full day at work. Talking it through and starting on a small scale made the decision easier, because I had a better idea of how it would fit.

part2.prompt: Describe a live sports event you watched and liked
cuePoints: When and where you watched it
And explain why you liked it

answers.basic:
I once watched a local badminton doubles tournament in a sports hall in Shanghai. It was on a weekend, and I went with a friend I usually play with. We sat close enough to hear the players call to each other between shots, which is a detail I rarely pick up when I watch a clip on my phone.

We had gone expecting to watch for a little while and see how good the local players were. Once we were inside, it was easy to get caught up in the way people reacted around us. There were a few quiet seconds whenever somebody got ready to serve, and then you could hear people shifting in their seats as the rally went on. My friend and I would try to guess where a player was about to put the shuttle. We got it wrong often enough that it became another reason to watch closely.

One match got very close near the end. One pair kept putting the shuttle into the same corner until the other pair changed where they were standing. My friend pointed it out, and from then on we were both watching their feet as much as the shuttle. I liked being able to see that sort of thing live. The crowd was following every point, and on the way home we were still talking about which shots we'd try in our next game.

part3.prompt: Why do some people like to watch sports events?

answers.basic: It's exciting to see how players deal with pressure. I also like watching badminton to see what choices players make when a rally starts going against them. A live match also gives people something to share, especially if they're following the same player or have been looking forward to the game for a while. If the score gets close, even somebody who knows the rules quite well can be surprised by how differently two players handle the next point.

part3.prompt: Where do people normally watch sports events?

answers.basic: Many people watch at home on a TV or phone. If there's a venue nearby, they might go in person, especially for a team or player they follow. I might watch a big match on my phone if it's happening far away, then go in person to a smaller event near where I live. The distance, the cost and the people I'm watching with can all affect which option feels worth making time for.

part3.prompt: What are the advantages of watching sports events online?

answers.basic: It's easy to watch from anywhere, and you can often replay a key point. That's useful when a shot is so fast you miss it the first time. If I'm watching badminton, I can go back and see what a player did with their feet just before an unusual shot. It's also convenient when the event is far away, because I can still follow the important points without arranging the rest of my day around travelling to the venue.

part3.prompt: What sports matches are suitable for children to attend?

answers.basic: I'd pick a short local match in a sport the child enjoys. A smaller venue can make it easier to see what's happening and leave if they get tired. For example, at a local badminton match you can see the court quite well and explain the score without having to shout. If the child can follow what's going on and still has the option to take a break, they're more likely to leave wanting to see another game.

part3.prompt: Why do some people spend a lot going to other countries to watch sports events?

answers.basic: They may want to see a favourite athlete or experience an event they've followed for years. For some people, it's also a good reason to visit a new city. Someone who's watched an event online for years might enjoy hearing the crowd and seeing what goes on between points. Going with a friend can make the cost feel more worthwhile, because the match becomes part of a trip they've been able to plan and look forward to together.

part3.prompt: What sports games are popular in your country?

answers.basic: Basketball, football, badminton and table tennis all have a following. I hear about badminton most often because a lot of the people I know play it themselves. Which sport you notice most probably depends on where you live and what your friends do. I see basketball in public spaces and at schools, while in my own week a badminton hall is where I'm most likely to meet people who want to talk about a recent match.

part2.prompt: Describe a food that people eat on special occasions/events
cuePoints: And explain why people eat it on that special occasion/event

answers.basic:
A dish I'd talk about is a whole steamed fish at a Lunar New Year meal. The word for fish sounds like the word for having something left over in Chinese, so people serve it as a wish for plenty in the coming year. It also looks good in the middle of a table where everyone is sharing the food.

I remember being more interested in the way it looked when I was younger. Somebody would carry the plate to the table, and the first thing I'd notice was that the fish still had its head and tail. When I got a bit older, I asked why people made an effort to serve it that way. The explanation about wishing for plenty made sense once I saw how much of the meal was about being together and hoping the next year would go well. It's the sort of detail I remember even if the other dishes change.

The fish is usually cleaned and steamed whole. You can add ginger and spring onions, and some people pour a little soy sauce over it at the end. In Hunan, I enjoy a version with chopped chillies because it has the kind of heat I grew up with. For me, the best part is when someone brings the plate out and everyone makes room for it. That moment feels like the start of a proper family meal.

part3.prompt: Why are there special foods on special occasions or events?

answers.basic: Food gives people a familiar way to mark the occasion. When the same dish turns up every year, its smell or taste can bring back memories of earlier celebrations. Sharing a particular dish also gives people something familiar to do together, even when the group at the table changes over time. At Lunar New Year, for instance, seeing a whole fish brought out can make dinner feel like a celebration before anybody says a word about the occasion itself.

part3.prompt: What are the differences between everyday food and festival food?

answers.basic: Everyday food is often quick and practical. Festival food may take longer to make, and preparing it together can be part of the occasion. On a workday I might cook one simple thing and eat as soon as it's ready. For a festival meal, people may come early to help prepare several dishes, so the time spent cooking and waiting for everyone to sit down is part of what makes it feel different.

part3.prompt: Are there any differences between the food people eat today and the food people ate in the past?

answers.basic: People have easier access to food from other places now. Some families still cook the dishes they grew up with, but they may buy ingredients or ready-made versions more often. For example, a family might still prepare a familiar dish for a holiday but buy a sauce or ingredient that used to take longer to make at home. That can make it easier to keep the tradition going, and it also changes which cooking skills get passed from one person to another.

part3.prompt: Do people today prefer eating at home or in a restaurant?

answers.basic: For ordinary days, home can be cheaper and more relaxed. A restaurant is often convenient when a large group wants to celebrate and nobody has time to cook. After work I like being able to make a simple meal whenever I get home. If I'm meeting friends who live in different parts of Shanghai, a restaurant near a station is often easier for everybody, and it means one person doesn't have to spend the evening cooking and clearing up.

part2And3.title: 擅长学习和说语言的人

part2.prompt: Describe a person who is good at learning and speaking new languages
cuePoints: How you got to know him/her
How he/she learns a new language
And explain how you feel about him/her

answers.basic:
One colleague of mine is good at picking up languages. I got to know her through work, and I first noticed it when she could move between Mandarin and English in the same conversation without losing her train of thought. She also speaks some Japanese, which she started learning because she wanted to understand shows without reading every subtitle.

I asked her about it after hearing her explain a problem to someone in English during a call. I would have tried to prepare every sentence, but she seemed comfortable getting the main idea across first and adding details when the other person asked. She said she pays attention to short exchanges and tries to remember the kind of reply a real person would give. She also listens to the same bit several times until she can hear where one word ends and the next begins. That made the work behind her confidence feel much more ordinary and achievable.

Her way of studying is quite practical. She takes a short piece of audio, picks out a few lines she'd actually say, and tries using them with someone. She told me she keeps returning to the same lines until she can say them at a normal speed. I admire how patient she is with that process. She doesn't seem embarrassed about getting something wrong the first time. Seeing how she learns has made me more comfortable practising a few useful lines of English at a time.

part3.prompt: Are there many people who can speak foreign languages in your country?

answers.basic: Many people learn English in school, and some use it regularly for work or study. Being able to hold a conversation depends a lot on how often they get to speak. For instance, somebody may understand a page of technical English and still need time to get used to a real conversation. In a city with plenty of chances to speak with other people, they may develop that part faster simply because it comes up more often in their day.

part3.prompt: Does speaking other languages help at work?

answers.basic: Yes. In software, I often read documentation in English, and another language can also help when you work with a team or a customer overseas. Being able to ask a follow-up question directly can also save time, especially when a written message could mean two different things. In a meeting with people in different places, I'd rather hear someone explain the problem in their own words and be able to check what they mean immediately.

part3.prompt: Do people learn any languages other than English?

answers.basic: Yes, people learn languages like Japanese, Korean, French or Spanish for work, travel or an interest in the culture. English is just the one I see most often. For instance, someone who watches Japanese shows might start by wanting to understand a few lines without reading the subtitles. A colleague dealing with customers in another country could have a more practical reason, and both are more likely to keep learning if there is a clear way to use it.

part3.prompt: Why is it easier for children to learn new things than for adults?

answers.basic: Children often have more chances to repeat something through play and are willing to try even when they make mistakes. Adults can make up for that with a clear goal and regular practice. A child can hear the same expression dozens of times in a game without feeling like they're studying it. An adult may have fewer chances for that kind of repetition, but can use what they already know to pick an approach and practise the exact thing they need in a short session.

part3.prompt: How do people learn new things?

answers.basic: I usually start with a small example, try it myself and get feedback. A tutorial can get me started, and using the skill on a real task helps it stick. When I learn a new tool, for example, I try it on something small enough to finish and check what actually happens. Having a result to look at makes the next explanation more useful, because I can connect it to a question I already have instead of trying to remember every instruction.

part3.prompt: What is the most important thing for learning a language well?

answers.basic: I'd say using it regularly for something you care about. Reading helps me find new expressions, and using one in a conversation helps me remember it. For me, it helps to pick a subject I could talk about anyway, like explaining a movement in badminton. When I try to explain it in English, I find out which words are actually easy to reach, and the same expressions become easier to use again when a similar conversation comes up.

part2.prompt: Describe a challenging technological problem you faced
cuePoints: When and where you faced it
And explain how you solved it

answers.basic:
A problem I had with my personal website was that a picture showed up on my computer but disappeared after I published the page. I was working on it at home one evening. Because the preview looked fine, I kept refreshing the live page and wondering if it was just taking time to update.

I tried another browser first because I thought I'd been looking at an old copy of the page. The picture was still missing, although everything around it loaded properly. That gave me a better question to ask, which was why this particular file was the only thing the site couldn't show. I made a small change to the page so I could be sure I was looking at the latest version. When the text changed and the picture still didn't appear, I knew there was little point refreshing it again and started looking more closely at the file.

In the end I opened the browser tools and checked the exact address the page was asking for. The live site couldn't find a file at that address. I compared it with where I'd actually put the image, moved the file into the right place and corrected the path. It was frustrating because the fix was small and I'd spent so long looking in the wrong place. Since then, when something doesn't load, I check the request first. It tells me where to start instead of making me guess.

part3.prompt: What are the advantages and disadvantages of AI?

answers.basic: AI can save time on drafts and help you explore unfamiliar ideas. It can also give a convincing answer that's wrong, so important details still need to be checked. For instance, it can offer several ways to organise a messy set of notes in a few seconds. I'd still compare the result with the notes before sharing it, because an attractive summary can change the meaning of one important point and make that change surprisingly easy to miss.

part3.prompt: Do you think people today should learn about AI technology?

answers.basic: Yes. People can learn where it's useful, how to ask a clear question and how to check the result. Those basics are enough to make better choices about using it. Someone might ask a tool to explain an unfamiliar instruction and then check its explanation against the original source. Practising that on a small task is useful, because you get a sense of which parts save you time and which parts still need your own judgment before you act on them.

part3.prompt: Should children learn to use AI?

answers.basic: I think they can learn with a teacher or parent guiding them. A child can use it to ask for ideas and then check those ideas against a book or an experiment. For instance, a student could ask for ideas for a simple experiment, choose one and see whether the suggested result actually happens. The useful part of the lesson is being able to explain what they observed, and that gives the teacher a way to see whether the student has understood it.

part3.prompt: How can AI help in our lives?

answers.basic: It can explain a confusing instruction, help practise a language or turn rough notes into a starting outline. I find it useful when I have a clear task in mind. For language practice, I might ask it to show me two ordinary ways to say something and then try using one in a sentence. It's easier to get a useful result if I know what I'm trying to express, and I can still check a phrase I'm unsure about with another source.

part3.prompt: Do you think students are overly reliant on AI?

answers.basic: Some are, especially if they turn to it before trying a question themselves. Used after a first attempt, it can give them another explanation or help them spot a mistake. For instance, if a student asks for a complete answer every time, they can miss the practice of deciding where to start. A student who brings their own attempt to the tool has something to compare with the suggestion and can decide which parts of the feedback actually make sense.

part3.prompt: What can teachers do to stop students from relying too much on AI?

answers.basic: Teachers can ask students to show their working or explain one choice aloud. They can also set clear rules about when AI is useful and how students should mention using it. For example, a teacher could ask students to write a first attempt in class and then use AI to suggest one improvement. Asking them to show what they changed and why turns the tool into something they have to think about, and it makes the learning more visible to the teacher.

part2.prompt: Describe an advertisement with a famous person in it
cuePoints: And explain how you feel about the advertisement

answers.basic:
I remember seeing a short ad with Lin Dan in it while I was watching badminton clips on my phone. It was for badminton equipment, and most of the ad was a player getting ready for a rally. Lin Dan was the person I recognised straight away, partly from the way he held the racket before he moved.

It was the sort of ad I could have scrolled past, because it opened with a fairly ordinary view of a court. What made me stop was seeing the player get ready before the shot, which gave me a chance to guess what he would do. The sound of the racket stood out too, because there wasn't much talking over it. By the time the product came up, I already knew what kind of play they wanted people to imagine. I thought that worked well for someone who already enjoys badminton and pays attention to those little details.

The clip caught my attention because I play the same sport. It was more interesting to see the racket moving on court than to hear a list of features. I watched it a second time because I wanted to see the shot again. I liked the ad as a short sports clip, though I'd still want to try the equipment myself before buying it. A great player can make almost any racket look good.

part3.prompt: What are the advantages and disadvantages of advertisements?

answers.basic: Ads can tell us that a useful product exists or that a shop has a sale. They can also interrupt what we're doing or encourage us to buy things we hadn't planned to buy. For instance, a notice about a new local shop can be useful if I already need something it sells. An ad that keeps appearing while I'm watching a video can have the opposite effect, because I start to associate the product with the interruption, even if I might have liked it otherwise.

part3.prompt: Why are many advertisements endorsed by celebrities? How useful are they?

answers.basic: A familiar face can get attention quickly. I think the ad is more convincing when the person has a real connection to the product, like a player showing a racket. A celebrity gives people a reason to pause long enough to see what the ad is about.
