That attention only goes so far, though, because if someone famous recommends a product they've no obvious reason to use, I may remember their face and still have no idea whether the product is any good.

part3.prompt: What is the most important factor in an advertisement?

answers.basic: The message should be clear. After seeing it once, I should know what the product does and why I might want to try it. For example, a racket ad could show what the racket feels like in a quick exchange at the net. A clear demonstration would help me decide whether to try it, and I'd probably remember that detail longer than a video with a lot of quick cuts and very little information.

part3.prompt: Why are some advertisements boring?

answers.basic: Some repeat a slogan without telling you anything useful. Others take too long to get to the point, especially when they're interrupting a video you wanted to watch. It also matters whether the ad understands what someone wants to know before making a choice. If I'm looking at shoes, I'd pay attention to a short clip showing how they grip the floor, whereas a long story that could go with any brand would probably lose me fairly quickly.

part3.prompt: Is advertising important for a company? Why?

answers.basic: Yes, especially when customers haven't heard of the company. Advertising can get people to try something once, and the product itself has to give them a reason to return. A local business could use an ad to let people nearby know it has opened, which can bring in people who would never walk past the door. Once they've come in, I'd expect them to judge the business on how the visit actually went, so good service still matters after the ad has done its job.

part3.prompt: Which is more effective, online advertising or offline advertising?

answers.basic: Online ads can reach people with a specific interest and link straight to the product. An offline sign can be more useful when you want to bring people into a local shop. For example, a specialist online shop can show an ad to players who already follow a sport, even if they live in different cities. A sign outside a badminton hall can reach someone who needs a service right there, so I'd choose the method based on where the customer is likely to act.

part2.prompt: Describe a place you have travelled to that you would like to recommend to others
cuePoints: What you saw and did there
And explain why you would like to recommend it to others

answers.basic:
I'd recommend a trip to West Lake in Hangzhou. It's in the city, so you can spend a day by the water without needing to go far out of town. When I went, I left most of the afternoon free and walked along the lake. I could see boats out on the water and trees along the paths.

I remember taking a look at the map when I arrived and deciding there was no point trying to cover the whole lake. I picked one section that looked easy to reach and turned off the map once I was on the path. Some parts were quite busy, especially where people stopped to take photos, but the walk felt different a little farther along. I found a place where I could see the water between the trees and stayed there for a while. That ended up being the part of the afternoon I remembered most clearly.

I stopped for something to eat and carried on once the path got quieter. I liked having the time to sit for a few minutes without feeling that I had to get to the next stop. I'd recommend it to friends in Shanghai because it's a manageable trip and you can enjoy it without a long list of plans. If a friend asked what to do there, I'd tell them to pick one stretch of the lake and give themselves plenty of time to walk it.

part3.prompt: Where do people in your country often go for holidays?

answers.basic: Some people go to nearby towns or mountain areas for a short break. For a longer holiday, a big city, a beach or a trip back home can all be popular choices. From Shanghai, a nearby city with a lake or a good place to walk can work well for a free weekend. A trip home might make more sense during a longer break, because people have time to see relatives and can spread the journey out over a few days.

part3.prompt: What is the ideal length for a holiday?

answers.basic: About a week works well for me. That's long enough to slow down and do a few things without feeling like every day has to be packed. The first day often goes partly on travel, and it can take another day before I stop thinking about work. With a week, I can pick a couple of things I really want to see and still leave room to spend a whole afternoon somewhere I happen to like.

part3.prompt: How do people usually plan holidays?

answers.basic: People often choose the dates first, then compare transport and book a place to stay. After that they save a few places to visit or ask friends for ideas. If I'm going with friends, the first useful question is when everyone can actually take time off. Then we can agree on things like the price of the train and how far we want to stay from the places we plan to visit, while leaving the smaller choices for later.

part3.prompt: Is it important to plan a holiday ahead?

answers.basic: It's worth booking the main things ahead, especially if you're travelling during a holiday. I like to leave the daily schedule flexible so I can change it if I find something interesting. If transport and a room are sorted, I find it easier to relax once I get there. I'd be happy to change a walk if it rains or spend more time by a lake than I'd planned, because those decisions have very little effect on whether I can get home again.

part3.prompt: Why do many countries try to attract people to visit?

answers.basic: Visitors spend money on transport, hotels, food and activities. Tourism can support local jobs and give people from different places a chance to meet. It can make a difference to a small town if visitors give local cafés and guesthouses enough business to stay open. I think it works best when visitors can also get to know the place a little, because a good experience gives them a reason to recommend it or come back later.

part3.prompt: How do people decide when to travel?

answers.basic: They usually work around holidays, time off and the weather. Some choose a quieter month because prices are lower and popular places are less crowded. If someone wants to take their children, school dates may matter more than the ideal weather. I have a bit more choice for a short trip, so I'd check whether I can take a quieter day off and spend less time waiting for transport or getting into places once I'm there.

part2And3.title: 喜欢拜访但不想住的家

part2.prompt: Describe a home that you like to visit but do not want to live in
cuePoints: Why you like to visit it
And explain why you would not like to live there

answers.basic:
I like visiting a relative's home in Hunan. It's in a quieter area than the part of Shanghai where I live. The rooms are fairly simple, and there's a spot outside where she keeps a few pots of chillies and spring onions. When I visit, we usually eat together and sit around talking for much longer than we meant to.

One thing I enjoy is that people come and go while we're talking. Somebody will step out to check what is cooking and come back with something they remembered halfway through. There is usually room to sit near the door for a while if the weather is good, and I can see the plants without having to move far. It's easy to spend an afternoon there without making a plan for it. At my place in Shanghai I'm more likely to be thinking about when I need to leave for work or whether I've packed for a lesson.

I like going because the day has a different pace. I can put my phone down, have another cup of tea and listen to what people have been doing since I last visited. For everyday life, though, I'd miss being able to get to work and go to different badminton halls by subway. A lot of my routine is in Shanghai now. That home feels right for a visit when I have a few days off. I enjoy coming back to my own routine afterwards.

part3.prompt: Do Chinese people like to visit others’ homes?

answers.basic: Yes, especially if they're visiting family or someone they know well. In a busy city it's also common to meet friends in a café or restaurant for convenience. Visiting someone at home makes it easier to spend several hours together without feeling that you have to leave when the meal ends. I notice that most when I go back to Hunan for a holiday, because having tea and talking after dinner can be the part everybody remembers.

part3.prompt: What do Chinese people do when they visit others?

answers.basic: They usually sit and talk, have some tea or share a meal. If they're staying for a while, they might help prepare the food or play a game together. Food often makes it easier to get a visit started, because people have something to do while the conversation warms up. In a family home, a quick cup of tea can turn into a long meal if someone starts telling a story that everybody wants to add to.

part3.prompt: What kind of place do people in your country like to live in?

answers.basic: It depends on their stage of life. Some want easy access to work and public transport, while others value a quiet street and enough room for family. In Shanghai I'd want somewhere close to the subway because it would affect my work and coaching almost every day. Someone with a different routine might value a bit more space for children to play or a quieter street, especially if they spend more of their time close to home.

part3.prompt: What's the difference between homes in cities and those in the countryside?

answers.basic: City homes tend to be smaller and closer to shops and transport. A home in the countryside may have more room and outdoor space, but daily trips can take longer. That means a city flat can work well for someone who needs to make several short trips in one day. A home with a little outdoor space can be better for someone who likes growing things or having people over, as long as the longer trip to shops fits their routine.

part3.prompt: What kind of gifts do people usually bring when they visit others?

answers.basic: Fruit or a box of snacks is an easy choice. If I know the person well, I'd bring something I already know they enjoy. When I go back to see relatives, something everyone can share after a meal is usually an easy choice. The main thing for me is picking something that suits the people I'm visiting, so a small box of food they enjoy feels more thoughtful than something expensive they may never use.

part3.prompt: How often do you visit your relatives or friends?

answers.basic: I visit people when our schedules line up, usually on weekends or holidays. Living in Shanghai means I see friends nearby more often than relatives back in Hunan. For instance, I can meet friends for a game after work without making it into a whole trip. Seeing relatives in Hunan takes more planning, so I tend to do it when I can stay for a few days and have time to talk over a proper meal.

part2.prompt: Describe a story/book with animals in it
cuePoints: And explain what you think of this story/book

answers.basic:
A story with animals I remember is The Tortoise and the Hare. The hare is so sure he'll win a race that he stops to rest, while the tortoise keeps moving and reaches the finish first. I read it as a child because it was in a book of short stories, and the race was easy to picture.

What made it easy to follow was that I could see why both animals made their choices. The hare had a good reason to feel confident at the start, and the tortoise seemed to know it would have to keep going for much longer. I remember expecting the hare to wake up and still manage to get there first. When that didn't happen, I went back to see how long the tortoise had been moving while the hare was asleep. It was a simple surprise, but it made me think about the race again after I'd closed the book.

When I was little, I thought the funny part was the hare waking up too late. As an adult, I think about the tortoise more. The animal just does the same small thing for long enough to get somewhere. I sometimes feel like that when I'm learning a new movement in badminton. It can look the same for several sessions before I notice that it's easier. I like that a story this short can make sense in a different way years later.

part3.prompt: Should schools teach children about animals?

answers.basic: Yes. Children can learn what animals need and how to behave around them. It also gives them a way to understand things like habitats and food chains. A school could start with animals children already see, like birds in a park, and ask what those animals need to live there. It gives them a reason to look more closely when they go outside, and bigger ideas about the environment become easier to understand once they have a real example in mind.

part3.prompt: Some people think pets should not be kept in cities. What do you think?

answers.basic: I think keeping a pet in a city is fine if the owner can meet its needs. The amount of space and time they have matters, as does keeping shared areas clean. For instance, an owner who can take a dog out regularly may be able to give it a good life even without a private garden. The problems are more likely to appear when the owner is away for long hours or other people have to deal with noise in a shared building.

part3.prompt: Many people regard pets as members of their family. What do you think?

answers.basic: I understand that. A pet is part of someone's daily routine, and people often build a strong bond after years of looking after it. Someone may spend years arranging part of every day around walks, feeding and coming home at a certain time. When I see it that way, it makes sense that the animal's absence would change how the whole home feels, even if a visitor only ever sees a quiet dog by the door.

part3.prompt: Do many people keep pets in your country?

answers.basic: I see quite a few people walking dogs in Shanghai, and cats seem popular with people who live in flats. How common it is probably varies by neighbourhood. For example, near a park I notice owners who go out at similar times and know each other's dogs. In a building where there's less space or fewer places to walk, keeping an animal may be a much bigger decision, even if the people there like pets just as much.

part3.prompt: What are the advantages of keeping a pet?

answers.basic: A pet can give people company and a reason to keep a routine. A dog can also get someone out for a regular walk and talking to neighbours. The benefit can be as simple as having a reason to take a short walk after dinner every day. There's also the feeling of coming home to something that depends on you, although that daily responsibility is worth thinking through before you decide whether a pet would suit the way you live.

part3.prompt: Why do people always tell children stories with animals?

answers.basic: Animals make stories easy to picture and remember. A child might understand a lesson about sharing more easily when it happens to a fox or a rabbit. An animal character also makes it easy to show a quality quickly, like making a hare confident because it can run fast. A child can follow what happens to the hare and the tortoise before they have the words to explain why doing something steadily can matter more than starting out quickly.

part2.prompt: Describe a person who solved a problem in a smart way
cuePoints: And explain why you think he/she did it in a smart way

answers.basic:
A player I know found a smart way to get more people playing during a busy badminton session. We had several people waiting and only one court, so some of us were standing around for quite a while. A few people wanted to finish full games, which meant nobody was sure when they'd get on.

At first we tried to remember the order by calling out names. That worked until someone went to get water and another pair turned up, and then there were two different ideas about who was next. I could see people getting a little impatient because they had paid for time at the hall and wanted to use it. The person who came up with the idea was waiting with us, so he'd seen exactly where things were getting confused. He asked if we'd try changing the order of play for just the next two games and see how it felt.

He suggested playing shorter games and having the next pair put their rackets beside the court in order. Anyone could look down and see whose turn it was. Within a few minutes people had stopped asking when they were going on and started paying attention to the game again. I thought it was clever because he used something everyone already had and made it easy to see what was happening. We kept playing instead of spending ten minutes arguing about the system.

part3.prompt: Do you think smart children are happier than other children?

answers.basic: I don't think intelligence tells you much about how happy a child is. Having friends, feeling supported and enjoying what they do are probably more important. A child might do very well in class and still spend lunch on their own, which can make school feel difficult. Another child might enjoy learning at their own pace and have friends who make them look forward to going in, even if they get lower marks on a test.

part3.prompt: Is it important for schools to identify and develop each student’s talents?

answers.basic: Yes. Some students are good at things that don't show up in a written exam. Giving them different activities helps them notice what they enjoy and do well. For example, a student who stays quiet in class might be very good at showing another person how to do something practical. A school can give them a chance to see that strength by offering different ways to take part, and that can change what they expect of themselves over time.

part3.prompt: Do you think children are born smart or they learn to become smart?

answers.basic: People may start with different strengths. Practice, encouragement and the chance to try new things can change what a child learns to do well. A child may pick up a movement or an idea faster than others the first time they try it. Over a few months, though, a child who gets good feedback and plenty of chances to practise can catch up or develop a strength that wouldn't have shown up on the first day.

part3.prompt: How do children become smart at school?

answers.basic: They can learn to ask good questions and work through a problem in more than one way. Feedback helps them understand why an answer worked or where they went wrong. In maths, for instance, a student can compare two ways of getting the same answer and decide which one they'd use next time. Over time that makes them better at spotting what kind of problem they're dealing with, so they can choose an approach even when the exact example is new.

part3.prompt: Why are some people well-rounded and others only good at one thing?

answers.basic: It depends partly on what they've had the chance to practise. Someone might focus on one skill for years, while another person has time and interest in several areas. For instance, a player who has spent years practising one sport may know a great deal about it and have little time for another. Someone who moves between several hobbies may get comfortable with different kinds of tasks, and either approach can be useful depending on what they want to do.

part3.prompt: Why does modern society need talents of all kinds?

answers.basic: Most big problems need several kinds of skills. A software project, for instance, needs people who can build it, explain it and understand what users actually need. If a service is confusing, an engineer can fix what happens behind the scenes, but someone still needs to find out where users get lost. Putting those strengths together makes it easier to solve the whole problem, because a person who sees one part clearly may miss what somebody else notices straight away.

part2.prompt: Describe a law on environmental protection
cuePoints: How you first learned about it
And explain how you feel about this law

answers.basic:
I'd talk about the household waste-sorting rules in Shanghai. They ask people to separate things like food waste and recyclables. I first paid attention to them after I moved to Shanghai and saw the different labels on the bins. I remember standing there with a cardboard box and taking a second to work out where it went.

When I first saw the different bins, I could understand the idea before I knew how to deal with everything I threw away. A clean bottle was fairly easy, while a container that still had some food in it made me stop and look at the instructions. I realised that I was more likely to do it properly if I'd already separated things upstairs. So I started leaving dry packaging together somewhere I could see it and taking it down on my way out. That turned a job I had to think about into something fairly ordinary.

The rules help people who collect and process the waste because they don't have to start with everything mixed together. Residents can benefit too if the shared bin area is easier to keep clean. I was a bit slow at it at first, especially with packaging that had more than one material. Once I got into the habit of putting bottles and boxes aside at home, it became much easier. I feel good about having a simple thing I can do regularly.

part3.prompt: What kinds of rules do schools in China have?

answers.basic: Schools often have rules about attendance, behaviour and how students use phones. There are also safety rules for labs, sports and shared spaces. For example, students may need to put phones away during a lesson so everybody can hear and take part. In a sports hall, a different rule might be about where equipment goes after class, because the next group needs the space to be clear before they can start.

part3.prompt: Do you think school rules are important?

answers.basic: Yes, because students need to know what behaviour is expected and feel safe around each other. A rule is easier to accept if the reason is clear. If students know everyone is expected to take turns with shared equipment, they can get on with an activity without arguing about it each time. The reason should be clear enough to explain, because a rule that feels arbitrary can create more arguments than it solves.

part3.prompt: Are children unhappy with the school rules?

answers.basic: Some are, especially if a rule feels unfair or is applied differently to different people. They may accept a rule more readily when it clearly protects someone. A phone rule can be frustrating if students see people get away with breaking it while others are punished. They might accept the same rule more easily if they can see how interruptions affect the lesson and know that everyone will be treated in the same way.

part3.prompt: How can parents and teachers help children understand and follow rules?

answers.basic: They can explain what the rule is for and show how it works in daily life. It also helps to let children ask questions about situations they find confusing. For example, if a child has to wait before using a piece of equipment, an adult can point out who is still using it and what could happen if they go too early. Once the child understands the situation, they have a reason to wait the next time even without a reminder.

part3.prompt: What are the rules people should obey at work?

answers.basic: People should follow safety rules, treat colleagues with respect and take care with private information. They should also tell the team early if something is likely to miss a deadline. In my line of work, that can mean being careful about who is allowed to see a file or piece of customer information. It also means communicating clearly when somebody else depends on your work, because a small delay on your side can affect several people before the end of the day.

part3.prompt: What is the purpose of punishment?

answers.basic: It can show that an action has consequences and discourage people from repeating it. For children in particular, it should also help them understand what to do next time. For example, if a child damages something another person was using, helping them put it right can show them the effect of what they did. A consequence works better when the connection is clear, because the child has something specific to do differently the next time the same situation comes up.

part2And3.title: 很久没收到回复的信息

part2.prompt: Describe a time when you sent a message or an email to someone but received no reply for a long time
cuePoints: Whether you finally received the reply
And explain how you felt about the experience

answers.basic:
I once messaged a friend to ask whether he could join a badminton session at the weekend. I was trying to decide how many people to invite before we booked a court, so I asked him fairly early. The message sat there for a couple of days, and I kept checking it because I didn't want to book the wrong amount of time.

The frustrating bit was that the answer would change the plan for everyone else. I could invite another person, but if my friend said yes later I'd have to work out how to give everybody enough time on court. I remember opening the chat during a break at work and seeing that I'd already checked it earlier that morning. That was when I realised I was spending more time waiting than it would take to explain the situation. I decided to be clear about what I needed and give him a little more time to get back to me.

Eventually I sent a short follow-up and told him when I needed to book. He replied later that evening and said he'd seen the first message while he was busy and then forgotten it. I was a little irritated at first, but it made sense when he explained. Now, if a decision depends on the answer, I say when I need it in the first message. That gives the other person something clearer to respond to.

part3.prompt: In what situations do people spend a long time responding to others’ messages?

answers.basic: People often take longer when they're in a meeting, travelling or thinking about a difficult question. A message can also get buried among newer ones. A simple message can still take time to answer if it involves checking a date or asking somebody else. For example, when I get a question about a lesson during work, I may wait until I can look at my calendar and give a useful answer in one go.

part3.prompt: In what situations do people not respond to messages at all?

answers.basic: They may forget, feel unsure what to say or think that the message doesn't need an answer. Sometimes they simply haven't seen it. A group chat is one example, because someone may assume the question has already been answered or is meant for somebody else. If I need a reply from one person, asking them directly and giving them one clear thing to respond to makes it easier for both of us.

part3.prompt: What would you do if you did not receive a reply after sending out a message?

answers.basic: If it were urgent, I'd call or try another way to contact them. Otherwise I'd wait a bit and send one short follow-up if I still needed an answer. For instance, if I had to book a court that evening, I'd say when the booking had to be made and what I planned to do if I didn't hear back. That way I can make a decision without sending several messages, and the other person can see why the timing matters.

part3.prompt: Why do some people prefer sending a message instead of making a call?

answers.basic: A message lets the other person answer when they're free. It's also useful when you need to share an address or leave a written record. If I'm telling someone where to meet for a game, they can open the message again as they walk from the station. A call makes more sense for something that needs several decisions at once, especially if ten short messages would leave both of us unsure what we've agreed.

part3.prompt: How do you show your respect in your messages?

answers.basic: I keep the message clear, say please when asking for something, and thank the person for helping. If there's a deadline, I explain why it matters. For example, when I ask someone at work to check a problem, I give them enough context to see what I need and when. That shows I respect their time, because they can judge whether they can help without having to spend the first few messages asking for the basic details.

part3.prompt: Why do some people feel angry when others don’t reply to their message?

answers.basic: They might feel ignored or worry that the other person is upset. It feels worse when they've shared something important and expected at least a brief response. When plans depend on a reply, the silence can feel worse because the person doesn't know what to do next. I'd still try to leave room for an ordinary explanation, since someone may have seen the message in a busy moment and forgotten they hadn't actually answered it.

part2.prompt: Describe a long-term goal/ambition you would like to achieve
cuePoints: How long you have had this goal/ambition
And explain why you set it

answers.basic:
A long-term goal of mine is to build a personal brand through my website. I've been thinking about it for a while, and it became more concrete once I started my own blog. I'd like someone who comes across the site to get a clear idea of what I do, from backend engineering to coaching badminton and learning new skills.

I think it will take time because I want the site to show how I actually work and learn. If I write about a badminton movement, for instance, I'd like to explain the bit I struggled with and show the small change that helped. That's the kind of thing I'd look for when I'm reading somebody else's blog. I can also go back and add a better explanation once I've tried it with more people. Over time, I hope the posts feel connected because they're about questions I keep coming back to in my own life.

My plan is to write about specific things I've tried and explain what helped me. I can start with a short post about a problem I solved or one coaching idea that made a difference. If I do that regularly, I'll have something useful to look back on and something other people can learn from. I set the goal because a lot of what I learn would otherwise stay in my head. Sharing it gives me a reason to put the ideas in order.

part3.prompt: Why should children have ambitions?

answers.basic: An ambition can give children a reason to practise and find out what they're interested in. It's fine for the goal to change as they learn more. A child who wants to play in a match, for instance, has a reason to keep working on an ordinary skill like serving. If they try it for a while and discover they enjoy something else more, the effort still helps them understand what kind of practice suits them.

part3.prompt: What do you think of people going after high positions?

answers.basic: I respect it when they want to do useful work and take more responsibility. The title matters less to me than how they handle the people and decisions that come with it. Someone who wants to lead a team may have ideas about how to make the work easier for everyone. I'd judge the ambition by what they do once they get the role, because being able to make more decisions also means being willing to explain and stand by those decisions.

part3.prompt: Why are some young people keen on being fans of superstars?

answers.basic: A superstar can give them someone to look up to or something to share with friends. Following an athlete can also make a sport more exciting to watch. For example, watching a player get better over several seasons can make a young fan curious about how people train. The same interest can give them a way to start talking to other fans, so it can become as much about the people they meet as about the star.

part3.prompt: Is it good for a person to be ambitious?

answers.basic: Yes, when ambition gives someone a direction they care about. It helps to choose goals that fit the rest of their life and leave room to rest. For me, the ambition to get better at coaching is useful because it leads to things I can do, like changing how I explain a movement. A goal that is only about keeping up with somebody else can feel quite different, especially if there's no point at which the person feels satisfied.

part3.prompt: Do you think it is necessary to be ambitious when working in a team in a company?

answers.basic: I don't think everyone on a team needs the same kind of ambition. A team needs people who care about doing the work well. Wanting a promotion is one way to be ambitious, and wanting to become very good at your role is another. A software team can benefit from someone who wants to understand a difficult part of the system and make it easier for others to work on. I'd call that a useful kind of ambition, and it's just as valuable to the team as someone wanting to move into a formal leadership role.

part3.prompt: Should parents support their children in pursuing their ambitions?

answers.basic: Yes, they can help children find a way to try the goal in practice. They can also give them space to change their mind once they understand what it involves. If a child wants to play a sport seriously, a parent can help them get to regular practice and ask how they feel about it afterwards. A trial gives the child more information about the goal, and support can continue even if their idea of what they want changes.

part2.prompt: Describe a time when you changed an important opinion of yours
cuePoints: And explain how you felt about the experience

answers.basic:
I changed my mind about when you're ready to teach someone. When I was learning badminton, I used to think I had to be very good at a movement before I could show it to anybody else. I worried that if I still had questions, I wouldn't have anything useful to say.

At the time I was happy to watch a lesson and try the movement myself. When somebody asked me how I did it, though, I could suddenly see which parts had made sense only while I was watching. One question that often came up was what to do first, and my answer wasn't always very clear. I began to think that if I could talk through one small part honestly, there was still something useful I could share. I could also learn from where the other person got stuck, because it made me look at the movement differently.

That changed when I started trying to explain what I'd learned to other players. Sometimes I'd get halfway through an explanation and realise I couldn't say why a step mattered. I'd go back, watch the movement again and try to explain it more simply. That's what made the Feynman technique click for me. I was a little embarrassed the first time I got stuck, but it was also useful. Now I see teaching as part of how I learn, and I get a real sense of achievement when a student understands the idea too.

part3.prompt: When do most children begin to have their own opinions?

answers.basic: Children start showing preferences very early, like choosing a game or a meal. As they get older, they get better at giving reasons and hearing other views. A young child might say they prefer one game because it lets them play with a friend, even if they can't explain much beyond that. With time and practice, they can start comparing choices and understanding why another person might choose differently, which makes their opinions more considered.

part3.prompt: Whose opinions are more important to children, their parents' or teachers'?

answers.basic: For a family decision, children may listen more to their parents. A teacher's opinion may carry more weight on a subject the child enjoys or finds difficult. For instance, a teacher might help a child see that they're capable of a subject they used to avoid, because the teacher sees their work develop over time. Parents know a different side of the child, so they may have more influence when the choice affects everyday life at home.

part3.prompt: Do children communicate more with teachers or with parents?

answers.basic: They probably talk more with parents about daily life at home. Some children find it easier to ask a teacher about schoolwork or something happening in class. Time and comfort matter as well, because a child may see both adults regularly and still tell them different things. They might ask a teacher about a difficult assignment and only tell a parent how upset they were about it once they've had a chance to relax at home.

part3.prompt: Who do young people like to share opinions with?

answers.basic: Many turn to friends first because they're likely to understand the situation. They may also ask a parent, a teacher or a colleague when they need a different perspective. A friend who is going through the same thing can be a good first person to talk to. For a decision like changing jobs, an older colleague might be more useful later, because they've already had to think about what happens after the first few months in a new role.

part2.prompt: Describe an environmental law you would like your country to introduce
cuePoints: Why people should follow the law
Whether the law will be popular
And explain how you feel about this law

answers.basic:
I'd like a rule that makes large delivery companies offer a convenient way to return packaging. For example, someone could leave a clean reusable bag or box at a collection point they already pass on the way home. The company could then use it again for another delivery.

The idea came to me when I looked at how quickly boxes can build up at home during a busy week. Most of them have only been used for one short trip, and a few are still in good enough shape for something else. I'd ask companies to start with packaging they know can stand up to being used several times. They could collect it in places that already handle deliveries, so people would know where to take it. Clear instructions would help, especially if someone needed to know whether a damaged box could go back.

I think it's worth following because a lot of us order things often. Even if each order only comes with one box, it adds up quickly in an apartment building. I can see people using a return system if it takes less than a minute and the collection point is easy to find. If they have to make a separate trip, it may be less popular. I'd be happy to use it myself. I already flatten boxes before I take them downstairs, so returning one would feel like a small change.

part3.prompt: How does technology affect the law?

answers.basic: New technology can create situations older rules didn't cover, such as how personal data is shared. It can also make it easier to collect evidence and enforce existing rules. For example, a camera can show what happened at a crossing, which can make it easier to check a complaint. The same tool raises questions about who can see the recording and how long it is kept, so technology can help put a rule into practice and also create a reason to update it.

part3.prompt: What kinds of rules do schools in China have?

answers.basic: There are usually rules about being on time, treating classmates respectfully and using equipment safely. Some schools also limit when students can use their phones. Some rules apply across most of the day, while others depend on what the students are doing. For example, putting away a phone during a lesson helps everyone concentrate, and wearing the right equipment in a lab matters for a different reason, because an accident there could affect other people.

part3.prompt: Will there be a law that is universally accepted?

answers.basic: Probably not in every detail. Many people can agree on a goal like safer roads, while still disagreeing about how strict a particular rule should be. One person might support a rule that makes a street safer for children, while another worries about what it does to the deliveries their shop depends on. Hearing both views can help people agree on a workable rule, even if they still give different reasons for accepting it.

part3.prompt: What environmental laws does your country already have?

answers.basic: China has laws covering areas like water pollution, air pollution and the handling of solid waste. The effects people notice most are often the practical rules they follow locally. In Shanghai, for instance, I see separate bins for different kinds of household waste, which makes that area of environmental policy part of an ordinary day. A person living somewhere else might notice rules about water or air more directly, depending on what kinds of problems their area has to deal with.

part2.prompt: Describe a piece of local news that people are interested in
cuePoints: And explain why people were interested in it

answers.basic:
A piece of local news I noticed was that a sports centre in Shanghai was reopening some courts after repairs. I saw the update because someone shared it in a badminton group chat. The centre had put out a notice about the reopening, and people in the group started checking which evenings they could book.

Before it reopened, it was one of those places people in the group kept asking about. It was easy to get to from work, and several players had got used to meeting there on the same evening each week. The notice finally gave people a date they could plan around. I remember someone asking if we could get the old group together again, and a few people answered almost straight away. That made me see how much of the interest was about getting the routine back, because finding a place to play also meant seeing the same people regularly.

It mattered to the people who played nearby because it was already hard to find a court at a good time. A few of them had been travelling farther than usual to play after work. I remember the chat going from quiet to busy quite suddenly as people started tagging their usual partners. It was a small bit of news for most of the city, but for us it meant there was another place to get a game in without a long trip home.

part3.prompt: Do people read the newspaper where you live?

answers.basic: Some still do, especially people who enjoy reading a printed paper. Most people I see in Shanghai check the news on their phones during breaks or on the subway. A printed paper can still be part of somebody's morning routine, particularly if they like sitting down and reading without notifications. For a quick update about a subway delay, I'd check my phone, and that difference in convenience probably explains why so many people I know use both formats differently.

part3.prompt: Do people prefer local or international news?

answers.basic: Local news matters when it affects travel, weather or life in your area. People follow international news when an event interests them or affects the work they do. If a station near my home is closed, the local update is the one I need straight away because it changes my route. Someone who works with a team overseas may also check international news regularly, so I think the preference can change with what people need to know that day.

part3.prompt: Do you think it's important to have a national identity?

answers.basic: It can give people a sense of belonging and a connection to shared history. People can feel that connection in different ways depending on where and how they grew up. It can help people feel part of a bigger community, especially when they recognise a story or tradition they share with somebody from another region. Growing up in Hunan and living in Shanghai gives me different experiences to draw on, and both can contribute to how I understand where I'm from.

part3.prompt: How can people develop their national identity?

answers.basic: They can learn about their region and other parts of their country, listen to family stories and take part in community events. Everyday experiences often make the idea more personal. A family story about moving somewhere for work, for example, can lead to questions about how other parts of the country have changed. Visiting a new place or sharing a holiday meal with someone from another region can give those bigger ideas a connection to something you've actually done.

part2.prompt: Describe a change that you made recently
cuePoints: What you did for the change
And explain how you feel about the change

answers.basic:
I recently changed how I get ready for a badminton lesson. I used to go in with quite a few things I wanted to cover. When a student found one part harder than I'd expected, I'd sometimes try to fit the rest in anyway and end up giving them too much to think about.

I noticed the problem most when someone had understood my first instruction but still needed time to get used to it. I'd be looking at the clock and thinking about the next thing I wanted to show them. In practice, the extra instructions made it harder for me to see which part they were still working on. I started asking myself what the smallest useful change would be for that person. If they could do it a few times with less help by the end of the lesson, that gave us both a clearer idea of what had improved.

Watching my online coach break a movement down so clearly made me rethink that. Now I pick one main thing for the lesson and write down a simple way to show it. After the student tries it, I can see if they're ready for another step. I feel more relaxed teaching that way, and I get more out of the lesson myself. I know what I was trying to explain, so when the student gets it I have a better idea of what helped.

part3.prompt: Do you think it is good to change one’s daily routine?

answers.basic: Yes, if it solves a problem you've been having. A small change, like setting a time to put your phone away, is easier to try than changing the whole day. For example, I could decide to finish work at a clear time on the days when I've booked a court. I'd try it for a week and see whether it helps me leave with enough energy to enjoy the evening, because that's the change I'd actually want to keep.

part3.prompt: Do you think it is good to change jobs?

answers.basic: It can be good when the new job fits your goals or gives you more room to learn. I'd think about the daily work as well as the job title and salary. For instance, a move that gives an engineer more say over how a system is built might be a good step if that's what they want to learn. It makes sense to ask what a typical week looks like, because the actual work can feel quite different from the way a role is described.

part3.prompt: Is it good for people to get a job promotion?

answers.basic: A promotion can bring better pay and a chance to make more decisions. It's worth knowing what responsibilities come with it and whether you'd enjoy that kind of work. An engineer might enjoy helping a team make decisions and want more of that responsibility. Somebody who prefers spending most of the day solving technical problems might feel differently about a role full of meetings, so the benefit depends on what kind of work gives that person energy.

part3.prompt: Do people often make plans around their regular routines?

answers.basic: Yes, people fit plans around things like work, meals and family responsibilities. I usually look at my work schedule before arranging a badminton session. A friend who finishes work late might suggest playing on a weekend instead, and I'd check when we can both get to the hall. Regular routines give people a starting point for making plans, which saves them from having to work out what's possible again every time.

part3.prompt: Who tend to change their daily routine more, young people or old people?

answers.basic: Younger people may change routines more often because they're moving, studying or starting new jobs. Older people can also change a routine when their health, family or interests change. Someone starting a job might need a new commute and have to find another time to exercise. An older person who's recently stopped working can face just as much change, so I think it comes down to how often something happens that makes the old routine impractical.
